Here we prove that the varieties of two-step nilpotent (anti-)commutative algebras are weakly action representable, and we explain that the condition (WRA) is closely connected to the existence of a so-called strong amalgam. Our second aim is to work towards the construction, still within the context of algebras over a field, of a weakly representing object $\mathcal{E}(X)$ for the actions on (or split extensions of) an object $X$. We actually obtain a partial algebra $\mathcal{E}(X)$, which we call external weak actor of $X$, together with a monomorphism of functors ${\mathrm{SplExt}(-,X) \rightarrowtail \mathrm{Hom}(U(-),\mathcal{E}(X))}$, which we study in detail in the case of quadratic varieties. Furthermore, the relations between the construction of the universal strict general actor $USGA(X)$ and that of $\mathcal{E}(X)$ are described in detail. We end with some open questions. This version is preceded by a corrigendum. Theorem 2.11 of the published article, which states that the variety of commutative associative algebras is weakly action representable, is false: we exhibit a $16$-dimensional algebra $X$ with zero multiplication for which the functor $\mathrm{SplExt}(-,X)$ admits no weak representation. Hence this variety is action accessible but not weakly action representable. The corrigendum amends the statements affected by this error, corrects Proposition 2.8, whose "if" part needs a strong amalgam, updates the definition of partial algebra, and lists some further minor corrections.
papers.title: Weak representability of actions of non-associative algebras

papers.abstract: Let $\beta>1$ be fixed. We consider the $(\mathbf{b},\mathcal{D})$-numeration system, where the base sequence $\mathbf{b}=(b_k)_{k\geq 0}$ consists of positive real numbers satisfying $\lim_{k\rightarrow \infty}b_{k+1}/b_k=\beta$, and the digit set $\mathcal{D}\ni 0$ is a finite set of nonnegative real numbers containing at least two elements. Let $r_{\mathbf{b},\mathcal{D}}(\lambda)$ denote the number of representations of a given $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ in the form $\sum_{k\ge 0}\delta_kb_k$ with digits $\delta_k\in \mathcal{D}$. We establish upper bounds for $r_{\mathbf{b},\mathcal{D}}(\lambda)$ as well as asymptotic formulas for its arbitrary moments. Furthermore, we prove that the associated Dirichlet series $\zeta_{\mathbf{b},\mathcal{D}}(s):=\sum_{\lambda>0}r_{\mathbf{b},\mathcal{D}}(\lambda)\lambda^{-s}$ admits a meromorphic continuation to the entire complex plane when $b_k=\beta^{k}$, and to the half-plane $\mathrm{Re}(s)>\log_\beta \mathcal{D}-\gamma$ when $b_k=\beta^{k}+O(\beta^{(1-\gamma)k})$ for any fixed $\gamma\in(0,1]$. Within the regions of continuation, we determine all candidate poles, compute their corresponding residues, and locate the trivial zeros of $\zeta_{\mathbf{b},\mathcal{D}}(s)$. As an application, we resolve several problems posed by Chow and Slattery concerning partitions into distinct terms of certain integer sequences.
papers.title: On the representation functions of certain numeration systems

papers.abstract: Trusted Platform Modules constitute an integral building block of modern security features. Moreover, as Windows 11 made a TPM 2.0 mandatory, they are subject to an ever-increasing academic challenge. While discrete TPMs - as found in higher-end systems - have been susceptible to attacks on their exposed communication interface, more common firmware TPMs (fTPMs) are immune to this attack vector as they do not communicate with the CPU via an exposed bus. In this paper, we analyze a new class of attacks against fTPMs: Attacking their Trusted Execution Environment can lead to a full TPM state compromise. We experimentally verify this attack by compromising the AMD Secure Processor, which constitutes the TEE for AMD's fTPMs. In contrast to previous dTPM sniffing attacks, this vulnerability exposes the complete internal TPM state of the fTPM. It allows us to extract any cryptographic material stored or sealed by the fTPM regardless of authentication mechanisms such as Platform Configuration Register validation or passphrases with anti-hammering protection. First, we demonstrate the impact of our findings by - to the best of our knowledge - enabling the first attack against Full Disk Encryption solutions backed by an fTPM. Furthermore, we lay out how any application relying solely on the security properties of the TPM - like Bitlocker's TPM- only protector - can be defeated by an attacker with 2-3 hours of physical access to the target device. Lastly, we analyze the impact of our attack on FDE solutions protected by a TPM and PIN strategy. While a naive implementation also leaves the disk completely unprotected, we find that BitLocker's FDE implementation withholds some protection depending on the complexity of the used PIN. Our results show that when an fTPM's internal state is compromised, a TPM and PIN strategy for FDE is less secure than TPM-less protection with a reasonable passphrase.
papers.title: faulTPM: Exposing AMD fTPMs' Deepest Secrets

papers.abstract: In this version of the paper, we note important gaps in the previous version.
papers.title: Sharp estimates for the Opdam-Cherednik $W$-invariant heat kernel for the root system $A_1$

papers.abstract: Multiple imputation is widely used for handling missing data in real-world applications. For variable selection on multiply-imputed datasets, however, if selection is performed on each imputed dataset separately, it can result in different sets of selected variables across datasets. MI-LASSO, one of the most commonly used approaches to this problem, regards the same variable across all separate imputed datasets as a group variable and exploits the group LASSO to yield a consistent variable selection across all the multiply-imputed datasets. In this paper, we extend MI-LASSO into the Bayesian framework and propose four Bayesian MI-LASSO models for variable selection on multiply-imputed data, including three shrinkage prior-based and one Spike-and-Slab prior-based methods. To overcome the limitations of traditional, ad hoc threshold-based model selection, we develop a principled four-step projection predictive procedure that provides robust variable selection. This procedure also facilitates approximately calibrated post-selection inference and attains near-nominal coverage under a correct selection model. Simulation studies showed that the Bayesian MI-LASSO outperformed MI-LASSO and other alternative approaches, achieving higher specificity and lower mean squared error across a range of settings. We further demonstrated these methods via a case study using a multiply-imputed dataset from the University of Michigan Dioxin Exposure Study. The R package BMIselect is available on CRAN.
papers.title: Bayesian MI-LASSO for Variable Selection on Multiply-Imputed Data

papers.abstract: We study a social bandit problem featuring the production and diffusion of knowledge. While higher connectivity enhances knowledge diffusion, it may reduce knowledge production as agents shy away from experimentation and free-ride on others' discoveries. In the symmetric mixed-strategy equilibrium, exploration probability falls with connectivity, while expected per-capita equilibrium surplus is constant in the interior mixing region. Under finite-player pure strategies, surplus can fall discontinuously when the integer number of explorers drops. In the large-population limit these jumps vanish, and per-capita equilibrium surplus is weakly increasing in connectivity and eventually flat for intermediate beliefs.
papers.title: The Impact of Connectivity on the Production and Diffusion of Knowledge

papers.abstract: We investigate singularly perturbed nonlinear complex differential systems of the form $\hbar \partial_x f = F (x, \hbar, f)$, where $\hbar$ is a small complex perturbation parameter. We give geometric and analytic conditions under which the formal perturbative solution associated with a fixed regular leading-order branch is locally uniformly Borel summable. This leads to an existence and uniqueness theorem of holomorphic solutions with prescribed perturbative expansion. We give an explicit triangular example and a self-contained application to the singularly perturbed Painlev\'e I equation.
papers.title: Borel Summability for Nonlinear Differential Systems on Characteristic Domains

papers.abstract: We establish the functional relations between generating series of higher-order free cumulants and moments in higher-order free probability, solving an open problem posed fifteen years ago by Collins, Mingo, \'Sniady and Speicher. We propose an extension of free probability theory, which governs the all-order topological expansion in unitarily invariant matrix ensembles, with a corresponding notion of free cumulants and give as well their relation to moments via functional relations. Our approach is based on the study of a master transformation involving double monotone Hurwitz numbers via semi-infinite wedge techniques, building on the recent advances of the last-named author with Bychkov, Dunin-Barkowski and Kazarian. We illustrate our formulas by computing the first few decaying terms of the correlation functions of an ensemble of spiked GUE matrices, going beyond the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem.
papers.title: Functional relations for higher-order free cumulants

papers.abstract: We show that for each ${\mathbf c}_{\mathrm M} \in [1,25)$, there is a unique metric associated with Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) with matter central charge ${\mathbf c}_{\mathrm M}$. An earlier series of works by Ding-Dub\'edat-Dunlap-Falconet, Gwynne-Miller, and others showed that such a metric exists and is unique in the subcritical case ${\mathbf c}_{\mathrm M} \in (-\infty,1)$, which corresponds to coupling constant $\gamma \in (0,2)$. The critical case ${\mathbf c}_{\mathrm M} = 1$ corresponds to $\gamma=2$ and the supercritical case ${\mathbf c}_{\mathrm M} \in (1,25)$ corresponds to $\gamma \in \mathbb C$ with $|\gamma| = 2$. Our metric is constructed as the limit of an approximation procedure called Liouville first passage percolation, which was previously shown to be tight for $\mathbf c_{\mathrm M} \in [1,25)$ by Ding and Gwynne (2020). In this paper, we show that the subsequential limit is uniquely characterized by a natural list of axioms. This extends the characterization of the LQG metric proven by Gwynne and Miller (2019) for $\mathbf c_{\mathrm M} \in (-\infty,1)$ to the full parameter range $\mathbf c_{\mathrm M} \in (-\infty,25)$. Our argument is substantially different from the proof of the characterization of the LQG metric for $\mathbf c_{\mathrm M} \in (-\infty,1)$. In particular, the core part of the argument is simpler and does not use confluence of geodesics.
papers.title: Uniqueness of the critical and supercritical Liouville quantum gravity metrics

papers.abstract: As neural language models approach human performance on NLP benchmark tasks, their advances are widely seen as evidence of an increasingly complex understanding of syntax. This view rests upon a hypothesis that has not yet been empirically tested: that word order encodes meaning essential to performing these tasks. We refute this hypothesis in many cases: in the GLUE suite and in various genres of English text, the words in a sentence or phrase can rarely be permuted to form a phrase carrying substantially different information. Our surprising result relies on inference by iterative shuffling (IBIS), a novel, efficient procedure that finds the ordering of a bag of words having the highest likelihood under a fixed language model. IBIS can use any black-box model without additional training and is superior to existing word ordering algorithms. Coalescing our findings, we discuss how shuffling inference procedures such as IBIS can benefit language modeling and constrained generation.
papers.title: Studying word order through iterative shuffling

papers.abstract: The efficiency of spintronic devices can be improved by generating higher effective magnetic fields with lower working currents. Spin-transfer torques can drive magnetic domain wall motion in a device composed of a single material, but a high threshold current density is typically required to move the domain wall and improving the effective magnetic field in common itinerant ferromagnets is difficult. Here we report magnetism modulation in Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$, a magnetic Weyl semimetal, via spin-transfer-torque-driven domain wall motion. We examine the effect of d.c. current on magnetic reversal using anomalous Hall resistance measurements and domain wall motion using time-of-flight measurements. At 160 K, the threshold current density for driving domain wall motion is less than $5.1\times10^5$ A cm$^{-2}$ at zero external field and less than $1.5\times10^5$ A cm$^{-2}$ at a moderate external field (0.2 kOe). The spin-transfer-torque effective field can reach as high as 2.4 to 5.6 kOe MA$^{-1}$ cm$^2$ at 150 K.
papers.title: Magnetism modulation in Co3Sn2S2 by current-assisted domain wall motion

papers.abstract: This is a preliminary version of a book in progress on the theory of quantum communication. We adopt an information-theoretic perspective throughout and give a comprehensive account of fundamental results in quantum communication theory from the past decade (and earlier), with an emphasis on the modern one-shot-to-asymptotic approach that underlies much of today's state-of-the-art research in this field. In Part I, we cover mathematical preliminaries and provide a detailed study of quantum mechanics from an information-theoretic perspective. We also provide an extensive and thorough review of quantum entropies, and we devote an entire chapter to the study of entanglement measures. Equipped with these essential tools, in Part II we study classical communication (with and without entanglement assistance), entanglement distillation, quantum communication, secret key distillation, and private communication. In Part III, we cover the latest developments in feedback-assisted communication tasks, such as quantum and classical feedback-assisted communication, LOCC-assisted quantum communication, and secret key agreement.
papers.title: Principles of Quantum Communication Theory: A Modern Approach

papers.abstract: We study the Hausdorff measure of noncompactness associated with compatible metrics on Fr\'echet spaces, with the aim of extending its Banach-space properties. After recalling the characterization by complete translation-invariant metrics with convex balls, we calculate the scalar Hausdorff measure for a standard weighted fractional metric. For bounded nonprecompact sets its value is the unique root of an equation involving a finite seminorm gauge determined by the covering radius. This yields an actual Hausdorff-condensing criterion for compact perturbations of maps having separate contraction constants at the seminorm levels. On countable products of Banach spaces we obtain an exact coordinate formula and a sharp scalar contraction bound on bounded domains, without requiring a uniform gap between the coordinate constants and one for strict condensation. For closed subspaces, an exact finite-projection formula retains the compatibility constraints on covering centers. Explicit examples show why separately computed seminorm measures cannot generally be substituted into the metric formula. Applications to spaces of real sequence-valued continuous functions give an explicit oscillation formula and exhibit the compatibility obstruction on an unbounded interval. Classical fixed-point consequences are recorded briefly.
papers.title: Characterization of Fr\'{e}chet Spaces and Application to Hausdorff MNC

papers.abstract: Graph modification problems form a unifying framework for many classical graph problems, where the goal is to remove a minimum number of vertices so that the resulting graph satisfies a desired property $\pi$. In this work, we replace the classical objective of minimizing the solution size with the fair objective [Lin&Sahni: Fair edge deletion problems. IEEE Trans. Comput. 89], which minimizes the maximum number of deleted neighbors incident to any vertex. This fairness criterion aims to distribute deletions evenly across the graph and leads to new algorithmic and complexity challenges. We study fair deletion and evaluation problems in the logical setting, where the target property~$\pi$ is defined by a formula in a logic $\mathsf{L}$. In particular, we consider the Fair $\mathsf{L}$ Vertex Evaluation problem, which asks whether there exists a vertex set $W$ of bounded fair cost such that a given formula $\varphi(X)$ holds in the input graph $G$. Our main result is an FPT algorithm for the Fair MSO$_1$ Vertex Evaluation problem with one free variable, parameterized by the twin cover number of the input graph and the quantifier length of the formula. We further show that extending this result to formulas with $\ell$ free variables is unlikely: the $\ell$-Fair FO Vertex Evaluation problem is W[1]-hard for parameter $\ell$ even on graphs of twin cover one. As a concrete case study, we investigate the Fair Vertex Cover}\ problem, one of the simplest fairness-aware graph problems. We prove that it is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the combined treedepth and feedback vertex set, but admits an FPT algorithm for the parameter modular width.
papers.title: Parameterized Complexity of Fair Vertex Evaluation Problems

papers.abstract: (Due to the limit on the number of characters for an abstract set by arXiv, the full abstract can not be displayed here. See the abstract in the paper.) We study dispersive equations with a time non-homogeneous modulation acting on the linear dispersion term. As primary models, we consider the Korteweg-de Vries equation (KdV) and related equations such as the Benjamin-Ono equation (BO) and the intermediate long wave equation (ILW), imposing certain irregularity conditions on the time non-homogeneous modulation. In this work, we establish phenomena called regularization by noise in three-folds: (i) When the modulation is sufficiently irregular, we show that the modulated KdV on both the circle and the real line is locally well-posed in the regime where the (unmodulated) KdV equation is known to be ill-posed. In particular, given any $s \in \mathbb R$, we show that the modulated KdV on the circle with a sufficiently irregular modulation is locally well-posed in $H^s(\mathbb T)$. Moreover, by adapting the $I$-method to the current modulated setting, we prove global well-posedness of the modulated KdV in negative Sobolev spaces. (ii) It is known that certain (semilinear) dispersive equations such as BO and ILW exhibit quasilinear nature. We show that sufficiently irregular modulations make the modulated versions of these equations semilinear by establishing their local well-posedness by a contraction argument, providing local Lipschitz continuity of the solution map. (iii) We also prove nonlinear smoothing for these modulated equations, where we show that a gain of regularity of the nonlinear part becomes (arbitrarily) larger for more irregular modulations. As applications of our approach, we also include further examples.
papers.title: Nonlinear PDEs with modulated dispersion II: Korteweg-de Vries equation

papers.abstract: We review the theory of inflationary perturbations. Perturbations at both linear and nonlinear orders are reviewed. We also review a variety of inflation models, emphasizing their signatures on cosmic perturbations.
papers.title: Inflation, Cosmic Perturbations and Non-Gaussianities

papers.abstract: Let $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. We prove that for every $n\ge 1$ there is a pair of $n\times n$ matrices with entries in $\mathbb{K}$ that generates a dense subsemigroup of the space $M_n(\mathbb{K})$ of all $n\times n$ matrices. Since the powers of a single matrix are never dense, two generators is optimal. Equivalently, there is a $2$-generator semigroup of linear maps whose action on $(\mathbb{K}^n)^n$ is topologically transitive, whereas no semigroup of linear maps acts topologically transitively on $(\mathbb{K}^n)^{n+1}$. In fact, for such a semigroup every orbit closure in $(\mathbb{K}^n)^k$, for every $k\ge1$, is as large as linear algebra allows. Along the way we give a short self-contained proof of the density of explicit $2$-generator subsemigroups of $GL_2^+(\mathbb{R})$ and of $M_2(\mathbb{R})$, based on a simple criterion for closed subsemigroups of $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$.
papers.title: Maximally transitive semigroups of $n\times n$ matrices (revised and extended version)

papers.abstract: We show that the semigroup of real linear fractional transformations of a proper subinterval of the real line does not contain a dense subsemigroup generated by two elements, while it does contain dense subsemigroups generated by three elements. For the semigroup generated by the two maps $x\mapsto 1+a/x$ and $x\mapsto x/b$ (the only pair not excluded by elementary arguments) we compute the closure exactly, and we describe all of its orbit closures in the plane. Consequently the semigroup of $2\times2$ matrices with nonnegative entries has no dense $2$-generator subsemigroup but has dense $3$-generator ones. In contrast, we prove a general density criterion for subsemigroups of $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ and $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ generated by three explicit matrices, and use a word identity of length seven to produce, for both $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$, uncountable families of pairs of matrices that generate dense subsemigroups; a fully explicit rational example is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1/2\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&-8/3\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Thus the minimal number of generators of a dense subsemigroup is $3$ for the nonnegative cone and $2$ for $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ and $M_2(\mathbb{C})$.
papers.title: Dense 2-generator subsemigroups of $2\times 2$ matrices (revised and extended version)

papers.abstract: Let $\theta(x)=(x-1)/3$ if $x\ge1$ and $\theta(x)=2x/(1-x)$ if $0\le x<1$. We conjecture that the $\theta$-orbit of every nonnegative rational number ends in $0$. A weaker conjecture asserts that no map in the semigroup generated by $3x+1$ and $x/(x+2)$, other than the generators' powers, has a positive rational fixed point; equivalently, the only matrices in the semigroup generated by $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with an integer eigenvalue are their pure powers. We prove sharp two-sided bounds for the smallest eigenvalue of every word in the more general semigroups attached to the maps $\varphi_{a,b}$, which explain why the pair $\{2,3\}$ is distinguished: it is the only pair with $(a-1)(b-1)=2$. Combining these bounds with congruences for the trace, we determine the possible integer eigenvalues of words, and we prove that $\theta$ has no rational $1$-circuits, no rational $2$-circuits and no even rational circuits. We show that, for each $k$, a random $k$-syllable word with exponents at most $M$ has an integer eigenvalue with probability at most $2k(k+\log_2 2k)/M$. Finally, we verify by computer that $\theta$ has no positive rational cycle of length at most $36$.
papers.title: A Collatz-type conjecture on the set of rational numbers (revised and extended version)

papers.abstract: For $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and every $n\ge 1$ we construct two $n\times n$ matrices $A$ and $B$ such that the orbit of every vector $p\in\mathbb{K}^n$ with $p_1\ne 0$ under the semigroup generated by $A$ and $B$ is dense in $\mathbb{K}^n$; the remaining vectors lie in an invariant hyperplane, so the set of vectors with dense orbit is exactly the complement of a hyperplane. Thus two generators always suffice for a hypercyclic semigroup of matrices, in contrast with the commutative case, where $n+1$ generators are needed on $\mathbb{C}^n$. We give a transparent reformulation of the hypotheses, a criterion for the density of $\{a^mb^n\}$ that makes them checkable, and explicit examples with complete proofs. As applications we obtain affine pairs on $\mathbb{K}^n$ all of whose orbits are dense, and, for every $n$, a pair of real matrices with an orbit that is somewhere dense but not dense in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
papers.title: Semigroups of matrices with dense orbits (revised version)

papers.abstract: We present BeAR, the Bern Atmospheric Retrieval code and successor of Helios-r, and its new high-resolution cross-correlation framework for emission and transmission spectra. BeAR performs joint retrievals by adding the log-likelihoods of high- and low-resolution data computed from the same model atmosphere. The framework implements established cross-correlation log-likelihoods, with the line-depth scaling either fitted analytically or sampled as a free parameter, their per-pixel generalization, fast model filtering, and model re-injection adapted to this filtering. The forward model and likelihood run entirely on a graphics processing unit (GPU). One forward model takes about 1 ms on an NVIDIA GH200, allowing millions of models per minute on a GPU cluster. In separate retrievals of Gemini South/IGRINS and JWST/NIRSpec dayside spectra of the hot Jupiter WASP-77Ab, BeAR reproduces published abundances, C/O ratios, and metallicities to within 1.5 sigma, the preference for 13CO, and the thermal structure and line contrast to within 1 sigma. The joint retrieval confirms a sub-solar metallicity and a near-solar C/O ratio. A full IGRINS retrieval with 17 free parameters takes 27 to 42 minutes on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 or about 14 minutes on eight RTX 4090 GPUs. Injection--recovery tests show that the posteriors underestimate the uncertainties of abundance ratios by about a factor of two.
papers.title: BeAR: The Bern Atmospheric Retrieval code - A GPU-accelerated framework for low-resolution, high-resolution, and joint retrievals of exoplanet atmospheres

papers.abstract: We provide an explicit scheme to realize a quantum memory in any 2D non-chiral topological order. For this, we construct syndrome extraction circuits based on the Turaev-Viro path integral as well as a classical algorithm for decoding on the fly. We prove that our scheme has a threshold under a local stochastic circuit-level noise model and discuss how to generalize it to implement topological logical gates.
papers.title: Provable circuit-level thresholds for non-abelian topological phases

papers.abstract: User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings. We then apply the method to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system.
papers.title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes

papers.abstract: Scientific figures give research ideas a visual form through choices of abstraction, composition, and emphasis. Generative AI offers new ways to realize these choices, raising questions about explanatory clarity and purposeful visual expression. We examine these questions through a visual retrospective of 371 motivation and framework figures from 200 papers. The corpus comprises a quota-based main sample of 160 papers spanning four temporal periods and a separate purposive style-contrast sample of 40 papers. A single multimodal judge evaluates six dimensions of communication and design, with three repeated judgments per figure. We attempt source-constrained revisions of all 371 figures, of which 369 pass the recorded fidelity checks. Original-figure ratings show no uniform decline across periods. Revisions increase mean clarity ratings by 0.428 points and decrease aesthetic coherence ratings by 0.111 points on a five-point scale. Gains in the six-dimension average are larger for main-sample motivation figures than for frameworks. Case analyses show that added explanation can clarify comparisons while leaving typographic hierarchy and visual economy unresolved. These model-based findings support researcher-led design, with AI assisting exploration and authors retaining responsibility for explanatory purpose, composition, and scientific relationships. The accompanying atlas and evaluation records are available at https://ntu-ai4x.github.io/Rethinking_Figures/index_en.html.
papers.title: Do You Miss the Nights We Spent Crafting Figures? Rethinking Teaser and Framework Figures in the Age of Generative AI

papers.abstract: Grounded reasoning, where a model outputs text coordinates of relevant locations in chain-of-thought reasoning, is a common strategy for solving complex visual reasoning problems. However, the benefits and limitations of grounded reasoning are understudied. We study where and why grounded reasoning is most useful. To do so, we introduce a chain-of-thought analysis method to measure how much a model uses its outputted grounding in its thinking trace and perform a detailed ablation study of a grounded reasoning training recipe. We find that grounded reasoning improves counting but shows no significant gain over baselines without coordinate grounding across a wide range of spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks. Using several synthetic tasks, we show that grounded reasoning is most useful when a task requires undescribable references, which are visual concepts that are difficult to describe in language. However, we observe that many existing visual reasoning benchmarks are solvable with only describable text references. To close this gap, we introduce BrickVision, a new benchmark that requires undescribable visual references to solve.
papers.title: Where and Why is Grounded Reasoning Useful?

papers.abstract: Observations and theory increasingly indicate that protoplanetary disks are weakly turbulent, implying that magnetized disk winds may dominate their angular momentum transport and long-term evolution. Yet dust evolution in wind-dominated disks remains poorly understood, despite its importance for planet formation. In particular, whether wind-dominated disk evolution can create regions with enhanced dust-to-gas mass ratios that enable planetesimal formation via the streaming instability is unclear. We build a parametric hybrid disk evolution model that includes turbulent accretion, wind-driven accretion, and wind-driven mass loss to investigate dust evolution in magnetized protoplanetary disks. We employ this model to carry out a parameter study in which the initial total accretion rate, the wind-driven mass loss rate, and the turbulence strength are varied. We find that although wind-dominated disks are more favorable to dust growth and concentration than turbulence-dominated disks, conditions suitable for the streaming instability arise only within the inner few au and only under the most extreme conditions: very weak turbulence ($α_\text{turb} = 10^{-5}$) where magnetized winds drive most of the accretion ($\dot{M}_\text{acc,tot} \simeq \dot{M}_\text{wind,acc}$), and wind-driven mass loss comparable to the accretion rate ($\dot{M}_\text{wind,outflow} \simeq \dot{M}_\text{acc,wind}$). Our results therefore imply that, beyond the inner few au, the parametric wind-driven evolution models considered in the literature do not by themselves produce conditions suitable for planetesimal formation via the streaming instability, motivating more physically complete models in which spontaneous, long-lived dust traps can arise.
papers.title: Evolution of Dust In Protoplanetary Disks With Magnetized Winds

papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.
papers.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization

papers.abstract: Defining equilibrium typically requires specifying a three-dimensional spacelike hypersurface. While global equilibrium is hypersurface covariant, calculations involving local equilibrium can exhibit hypersurface dependence. In this work, we use polarization in heavy-ion collisions within the Zubarev response approach as an example to show that the hypersurface dependence arising from the local-equilibrium part of the density operator is canceled by an overlooked nondissipative contribution from its so-called ``dissipative part". We establish a hypersurface-covariant Zubarev framework for general geometries by consistently including both nondissipative and dissipative parts, eliminating dependence on the arbitrary hypersurface vector. The remaining frame dependence is physical: it arises from the medium rest frame entering the particle distribution and the time direction of the dissipative process, which usually coincide. This resolves, in principle, the longstanding and widely discussed conceptual disagreement over hypersurface dependence between two influential studies addressing the sign puzzles of $Λ$-hyperon polarization in heavy-ion collisions
papers.title: Hypersurface covariance in relativistic local equilibrium

papers.abstract: The dispersion measures (DMs) of fast radio bursts (FRBs) trace ionised baryons along the line of sight, probing baryonic feedback. Two complementary observables can be constructed from an FRB catalogue: the DM-redshift (Macquart) relation of host-identified FRBs, and the angular power spectrum of the DM field of the full catalogue. Their joint analysis requires their cross-covariance. We derive it within the halo model and show it is a super-sample effect: only the monopole of an individual DM correlates with the angular power spectrum, yielding an exact, model-independent bound on the correlation coefficient. We validate the calculation against log-normal forward simulations of $10^4$ FRBs. For individual DMs, the correlation with the bandpowers is at the per cent level. Neglecting the cross-covariance changes the width of the $χ^2$ distribution by only 0.8 per cent, so the two observables can be treated as effectively independent for wide-area surveys. In a joint forecast with an LSST-like weak lensing survey, adding the Macquart relation tightens constraints on the physical baryon density by 32 per cent and on the mean host contribution by a factor of 4.1, while improving baryonification parameters by only about 5 per cent, indirectly through the host contribution. Finally, we show that the redshift distribution of FRBs without identified hosts, which enters every DM power spectrum, can be reconstructed by inverting their DMs with the jointly fitted mean relation without biasing the inferred parameters, whereas a 20 per cent error in the mean relation biases the DM power spectrum by up to 2$σ$ per band for $5\times 10^5$ FRBs.
papers.title: Joint analysis of the Macquart relation and the dispersion measure power spectrum: cross-covariance and redshift self-calibration

papers.abstract: We consider polar foliations of codimension two on compact simply connected irreducible symmetric spaces. In rank at least two, we prove that these foliations are hyperpolar, settling the remaining case of the hyperpolarity problem discussed by Lytchak. We show that, for irreducible spherical Coxeter quotients, the horizontal universal cover fails to be a spherical building precisely on the Cayley plane, where every such foliation is congruent to one of the two known homogeneous models.
papers.title: Hyperpolarity of polar foliations of codimension two

papers.abstract: The quantum metric is a fundamental geometric property of Bloch bands that governs a wide range of physical phenomena, yet experimentally accessing it remains challenging. We show that the momentum-space variation of the quantum metric can be probed through the real-space dynamics of a Gaussian wave packet prepared in an isolated flat band. Following the application of a weak constant force, we demonstrate analytically that the leading order change in the wave-packet variance is linear in time and contains a contribution proportional to the wave-packet averaged gradient of the quantum-metric trace. This geometric contribution remains finite despite the absence of band dispersion. We illustrate the effect using a gapped Lieb lattice with an exactly flat middle band and vanishing Berry curvature, allowing the quantum-metric contribution to the spreading to be isolated. The numerical results agree with the analytical prediction and confirm the quantum-metric contribution to the wave-packet spreading. The required lattice preparation, tunable hopping amplitudes, applied force, and density measurements are compatible with established ultracold-atom techniques, providing a possible platform for observing the predicted response. Our results establish wave-packet spreading as a dynamical probe of quantum geometry in flat-band systems.
papers.title: Flat-band systems: A platform to realize the moments of Quantum Metric

papers.abstract: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.
papers.title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

papers.abstract: Modern video models possess strong visual priors, yet do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space. We present EgoGeneralist, which adapts pretrained video generators to unify action-conditioned egocentric video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation. Our role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, making metric motion usable as both a spatial control signal and a recoverable generation target. Cross-stream action-video coupling establishes close correspondence between metric motion and visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior. Together, these designs establish a generalist framework spanning five action-video tasks. Despite adaptation only on controlled laboratory recordings, EgoGeneralist generalizes to diverse unseen scenes and interactions with effective action control and visual quality, bridging pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion.
papers.title: EgoGeneralist: Unifying Egocentric Action-Video Tasks through Video-Native Modeling

papers.abstract: Surface defects carry Weyl and gravitational anomalies that generalize the central charges of two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) and characterize the anomalous response of gapless surface modes to background geometry. These anomalies usually appear as contact terms on the defect. We explain how they are encoded at a distance, in scheme-independent integrated bulk stress-tensor correlators. We derive sum rules for them in terms of defect operator data, establish a lower bound on the boundary Weyl anomaly in three-dimensional CFTs, and illustrate our results with explicit examples.
papers.title: Defect Anomalies at a Distance

papers.abstract: We find numerical evidence for a direct continuous transition from a Laughlin fractional Chern insulator (FCI) to a $c_-=3/2$ topological superconductor (TSC), driven by increasing bandwidth at filling $ν=1/3$ in a repulsively interacting Chern band. At the critical point, the electron correlation length diverges at momentum away from the reference Fermi surface. We develop a generalized theory of superconducting-vortex proliferation for this transition. Magnetic translation organizes the vortices into six valleys, so translation-preserving proliferation requires additional gauge fields. The resulting theory reproduces the momentum structure of the critical spectrum and captures the divergent electron correlation. Upon doping away from commensurate filling, the theory gives rise to a superconducting dome. These results are consistent with an anyonic origin of the topological superconductivity in the absence of a weak-coupling Fermi-surface instability.
papers.title: Direct transition from a fractional Chern insulator to a topological superconductor

papers.abstract: Interpretations have been widely used in the study of provenance of queries on semiring-annotated databases. Here, we consider two different interpretation-based semantics for first-order formulas in negation normal form, namely, the canonical-interpretation semantics and the compatible-interpretation semantics. We show that the resulting query languages cannot express the monus operation on semiring-annotated relations, when the annotations come from the bag semiring or the tropical semiring or the fuzzy semiring. Consequently, the semantics of SQL cannot be captured using the interpretation-based semantics considered here.
papers.title: Monus vs. Interpretations in Semiring Semantics

papers.abstract: Measurements of anisotropic flow provide some of the strongest constraints on the collective expansion and transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma produced in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. In this paper, correlations and fluctuations of the anisotropic flow coefficients $v_{2}$, $v_{3}$, and $v_{4}$ are measured in Pb-Pb and Xe-Xe collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm{NN}}} = 5.02$ and $5.44$ TeV, respectively, with the ALICE detector. The Event Shape Engineering technique, based on the reduced flow vector $q_{n}$, is used to study flow correlations for different initial-state geometries. A strong anticorrelation between $v_2$ and $v_3$ and a positive correlation between $v_2$ and $v_4$ are observed. A small anticorrelation is seen between $v_3$ and $v_4$. From the $v_2$-$v_4$ correlation, the linear and nonlinear components of $v_4$ are extracted and compared to those extracted using multiparticle correlations. The linear and nonlinear components of $v_{4}$ are also measured directly as a function of $q_2$ for the first time in Pb-Pb and Xe-Xe, revealing a strong coupling of the nonlinear term to the initial-state ellipticity $\varepsilon_2$, while the linear component shows little dependence on initial-state geometry. Additionally, the coupling coefficient $χ_{4,22}$, which measures the nonlinear contribution of $v_2^2$ to $v_4$, is extracted and shows little dependence on $q_2$, except in very central collisions. The effects of flow fluctuations for constrained initial-state geometries are studied for the first time using Event Shape Engineering with the ratio of $v_2\{2\}$ and $v_2\{4\}$; the results show that collisions with the lowest $q_2$ exhibit more significant $v_2$ fluctuations compared to the unbiased ratio.
papers.title: Correlations and fluctuations of flow with event shape engineering in Pb-Pb and Xe-Xe collisions at the LHC

papers.abstract: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.
papers.title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration

papers.abstract: We report a novel solution of three-dimensional Galilean Anti-de Sitter gravity. The theory can be formulated as a topological gauge theory invariant under the doubly extended Newton-Hooke group in three dimensions. The solution possesses four conserved charges: energy, angular momentum, spin and rest mass. Interestingly, the magnitude of the spin turns out to bounded from above by the rest mass. The solution exhibits the thermal properties that define a black hole configuration in terms of its gauge theoretical description. Temperature, angular velocity and other chemical potentials are obtained from suitable regularity conditions associated with the topology of the Euclidean continuation of the solution. At zero temperature, an extreme configuration is shown to emerge provided the bound between the spin and the rest mass saturates.
papers.title: The three-dimensional Galilean black hole

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of large-scale data centers (DCs) is increasing electricity demand, market volatility, and operating costs. Battery energy storage systems (BESSs) can mitigate these challenges by shifting electricity purchases from high-price to low-price periods. This paper proposes a real-time BESS dispatch framework using polynomial diffusion models (PDMs) to forecast both electricity prices and DC loads. Leveraging the closed-form conditional expectations of PDMs, the forecasts are integrated into a dynamic programming (DP) framework to minimize electricity procurement costs. Across the evaluated BESS configurations, the proposed approach achieves 2.63 times the cost savings of a rule-based (RB) strategy.
papers.title: Joint Electricity Price and Load Forecasting for Data Center Battery Dispatch Using Polynomial Diffusion Models

papers.abstract: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $α$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.
papers.title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information

papers.abstract: We study composite optimization over the Bures--Wasserstein (BW) space of Gaussian measures. Our main observation is that a useful class of BW problems can be lifted into the Euclidean space of affine transport maps, such that the lifted problems can be solved efficiently using accelerated proximal gradient methods. For objectives whose smooth and nonsmooth components admit convex smooth and convex proximable affine lifts, respectively, our algorithm BW-FISTA achieves minimax-optimal objective gap $O(k^{-2})$ after $k$ iterations. We verify these regularity conditions for potential and interaction energies together with common spectral regularizers, and we treat stochastic gradients under a suitable noise model. As a principal application, we consider Gaussian variational inference with a log-concave, log-smooth target. Here, the resulting entropy term is handled by an efficient, exact proximal step, and we improve the previous rate of $O(k^{-1})$ to $O(k^{-2})$. We numerically verify this predicted boost with synthetic experiments.
papers.title: An Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method for Bures-Wasserstein Space

papers.abstract: Gu and Zhang asked for almost sure upper and lower bounds on the Taylor coefficients $a_n$ of $\exp(\sum_{k\ge1}X_kz^k/\sqrt{k})$ in the unit disc, and for the dependence of these bounds on the input tail. For independent, identically distributed, rotationally invariant complex inputs with $\mathbb E|X_1|^2=1$, we prove the universal almost sure bound $|a_n|=O((\log n)^{1/4})$. Almost surely, $\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|/(\log n)^{1/4}$ is positive and finite exactly when $\mathbb E[|X_1|^2\log^+|X_1|^2]<\infty$, and is zero otherwise. For each input law, we define a deterministic scale such that, almost surely, the coefficients are bounded exactly when the scale is bounded, and tend to zero exactly when it vanishes. We also determine the almost sure logarithmic growth exponent as the maximum of contributions from collective fluctuations and individual large inputs. Explicit tails exhibit distinct thresholds for boundedness and for upper bounds at the scale in the phase criteria. Examples show that neither the leading tail nor the set of finite logarithmic moments determines the almost sure phase.
papers.title: Almost sure bounds and tail phases for critical non-Gaussian holomorphic chaos

papers.abstract: The canonical cut hierarchy recursively partitions a graph along Tutte-Nash-Williams partitions, choosing the partition with the most number of parts at each step. We give a randomized almost linear-time algorithm for computing this hierarchy in undirected graphs with polynomially bounded capacities via reduction to max-flow. This yields randomized almost linear-time algorithms for computing partition connectivity, strength, both arboricity and fractional arboricity, both integral and fractional spanning tree packing numbers, and implicit representations of the principal partition sequence and a maximum fractional spanning tree packing.
papers.title: Canonical Cut Hierarchy in Almost-Linear Time via Reduction to Max-Flow

papers.abstract: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.
papers.title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion

papers.abstract: It was shown by Braverman-Finkelberg-Nakajima that the regular perverse sheaf on the affine Grassmannian of type A is isomorphic to the ring object associated to a Gelfand-Tsetlin quiver. We use this result to identify, for any finite dimensional representation $\mathbf{N}$ of a product of general linear groups, the relative Langlands dual $(T^*\mathbf{N})^\vee$ of $T^*\mathbf{N}$ with the Coulomb branch of a suitable representation. By a result of Bellamy, this implies that $(T^*\mathbf{N})^\vee$ has symplectic singularities.
papers.title: Symplectic singularities in Relative Langlands duality for products of general linear groups

papers.abstract: We present a joint Bayesian extraction of the nonrelativistic QCD long-distance matrix elements (LDMEs) for $J/ψ$, $ψ(2S)$, and $χ_c$ production, using short-distance coefficients and feed-down structure implemented in PYTHIA 8.317. Rather than fitting each charmonium state separately, we construct channel-resolved responses that link parent production to daughter feed-down and infer all LDMEs simultaneously from 286 prompt charmonium measurements in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$-13 TeV at the LHC. The extracted LDMEs provide a good description of the data, with an overall $χ^2/\mathrm{ndf}=1.18$. We also provide a positivity-constrained set that can be used directly as PYTHIA input. Using the extracted LDMEs, we predict prompt $J/ψ$ and $ψ(2S)$ cross sections at high transverse momentum in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=200$ GeV, which can be tested with RHIC data.
papers.title: Joint Bayesian Inference for Extraction of Charmonium Long Distance Matrix Elements Using PYTHIA

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, but often fail during deployment. Teaching them to recover from these failures requires substantial corrective data: existing approaches learn to recover from failures by directly associating corrective actions with the observations in which they were demonstrated. For instance, DAgger-like fine-tuning can require tens to hundreds of interactions, yet the resulting policy may still fail to generalize the learned corrections beyond the demonstrated scenarios. We hypothesize that semantics can capture the underlying reasons for failures and their corrections, enabling policies to learn from only a handful of corrective demonstrations and generalize those corrections to novel objects, and scene variations. We propose OopsieRecover, a framework that uses abduction to infer the intent behind a small set of corrective demonstrations and encodes the inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs. These costs capture when a behavior is undesirable and steer the policy toward more desirable action regions. We experiment across 6 tasks and variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks, and find that only a handful of corrective demonstrations can enable a VLA to overcome failures across a broad range of novel situations, without requiring new corrective data for each variation. Please refer to https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/oopsierecover for videos.
papers.title: OopsieRecover: Learning Transferable VLA Corrections from Semantic Interventions

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. This survey reviews these approaches using two complementary classification axes: teacher-student configuration and the role of quantum resources in the distillation process. Quantum-inspired methods are discussed separately from methods that simulate quantum computations classically or execute them on quantum hardware. We explain how measurement probabilities, expectation values, classical readouts, state overlaps, and circuit-level objectives support different transfer mechanisms. We then critically assess the presented results against baseline design, execution conditions, uncertainty, and resource costs. The evidence shows that distillation can improve selected quantum students, but benefits are task- and architecture-dependent, and several studies find negligible gains or even performance degradation. Evaluations on physical quantum hardware remain limited, with some testing individual quantum components rather than complete learning pipelines. Heterogeneous protocols and incomplete resource reporting prevent general conclusions about practical quantum advantage. We identify priorities for controlled benchmarking, noise-aware learning, reproducible evaluation, and efficient transfer between quantum and classical models.
papers.title: Quantum Knowledge Distillation: State-of-the-art, Applications and Open Problems

papers.abstract: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.
papers.title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes

papers.abstract: Precision measurements can reveal not only the presence of new physics, but also information about the dynamics that generated it. We study this question in top-pair production by comparing three top-philic scenarios: a colored scalar top partner, a colored vector-like fermion, and a spin-one $Z^\prime$ mediator. The first two contribute through loop corrections, while the $Z^\prime$ contributes at tree level. We show that the scalar and vector-like fermion scenarios match onto the same effective operator structure at low energies,making their distinction unfeasible using the EFT approach. However, near or above threshold their full loop amplitudes develop distinct momentum-dependent interference patterns. Using the top transverse momentum spectrum we find that resonant and loop-induced effects are relatively easy to distinguish, whereas separating the scalar and vector-like hypotheses is substantially more challenging. Nevertheless, their different analytic structures leave measurable information in the shape of the distribution. These results illustrate how precision differential measurements can probe the spin and dynamics of virtual new states even when they are not directly reconstructed, and motivate more powerful multidimensional analyses.
papers.title: Testing the Spin of New Physics with Top Precision Measurements

papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from limited visual demonstrations is challenging because policies must acquire both perceptual grounding and precise control, while reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation can acquire rich control behaviors from large-scale interaction with privileged information. We introduce \textbf{Latent RL Prior}, a two-stage framework that reuses this control knowledge for data-efficient visual policy learning. During privileged pretraining, we distill large-scale RL rollouts into a flow-matching action decoder conditioned on proprioception and latent task context. During visual adaptation, we freeze the decoder and learn a visual interface that maps images to its latent context using action supervision alone, without privileged labels or latent targets. The same decoder can further be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation. Across three simulated tasks, our method outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning of $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 in the low-data regime; on door lifting and bimanual assembly, it surpasses full-data baselines using $10\times$ and $5\times$ fewer demonstrations, respectively. Further analysis shows that direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation performance and training stability over routing visual predictions through the pretrained state encoder. Robustness to unseen mass variation and greater linear accessibility of contact-force information in decoder representations further provide evidence of retained RL-acquired control knowledge. Project website: https://yixiaowang7.github.io/latent-rl-prior-page/.
papers.title: Latent RL Priors for Data-Efficient Dexterous Manipulation

papers.abstract: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT. Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.
papers.title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness

papers.abstract: Generative AI and agentic coding are accelerating software development, leading to concerns about technical debt. But two less visible forms of debt, cognitive debt and intent debt, are emerging as key risks to software health. Cognitive debt is the absence or erosion of a team's shared understanding where no one can confidently explain how a system works or predict the impact of a change. Intent debt is the lack of clearly articulated goals, constraints, and rationale that explain what the system is for and guide how it should evolve. This paper presents Cognitive Tours, a tool designed to mitigate and repair cognitive and intent debt. Cognitive Tours is a web-based prototype for creating and following curated paths connecting user needs, design decisions, code, tests, and open questions. AI-assisted skills help audit existing waypoints and tours for possible problems or staleness and suggest candidates for new ones; humans decide what matters, verify relationships, and construct the narrative. This division of work deliberately preserves productive friction: the sensemaking involved in selecting, explaining, and revising a tour, which is intended to foster and share understanding. Our demonstration uses a tour of Cognitive Tours itself to introduce the tool and illustrate its design decisions and interaction mechanisms. A proposed evaluation agenda concludes the paper. A demo is available at https://cognitive-tours-demo.vercel.app/
papers.title: Cognitive Tours: Making Understanding a Deliverable in AI-Assisted Development

papers.abstract: We determine the sharp order of discrepancy in Tusnády's problem in every fixed dimension $d\ge 2$. The largest combinatorial discrepancy of $N$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to axis-parallel boxes is $Θ_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$, extending Wei's planar result and matching Nikolov's upper bound. More strongly, with high probability, this lower bound holds simultaneously for every subset obtained by deleting at most a sufficiently small fixed fraction of a uniform $N$-point sample. We apply this geometric estimate to online thinning of two independent samples of size $n$ from an unknown common distribution, where observations must be kept or discarded upon arrival. For every fixed dimension $k\ge 1$ and expected deletion budget $ρn$, with $0<ρ<2$, we prove that the minimax expected prefix discrepancy over lower orthants is $Θ_{k,ρ}((\log n)^{k+1/2})$. In dimension one, the optimal terminal discrepancy is instead $Θ_ρ((\log\log n)^{3/2})$, giving a sharp separation between the prefix and terminal objectives. For $k\ge 2$, we obtain terminal bounds differing by a factor of $\log n$. The lower bounds are based on Gaussian small-ball estimates for box-incidence matrices, while the upper bounds use stationary Metropolis thinning and, in one dimension, a terminal cancellation procedure.
papers.title: Tusnády's problem and online two-sample thinning

papers.abstract: In this paper, we prove that every complete noncompact two-sided properly embedded constant mean curvature hypersurface of finite Morse index in Euclidean space is minimal. The result holds in every dimension. We assume no bounds on curvature or volume growth. This establishes the properly embedded case of the finite-index version of do Carmo's question. For nonzero mean curvature, we use the radii of inscribed balls to define a positive weight. This weight gives a polynomial bound on weighted volume, while its reciprocal satisfies a differential inequality involving the Jacobi operator. We combine these properties with stability outside a compact set to obtain finite total area. This leads to a contradiction.
papers.title: On do Carmo's Question: The Properly Embedded Case

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.
papers.title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO

papers.abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.
papers.title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts

papers.abstract: We establish characterizations of h-dichotomies for noninvertible evolution families acting on Banach spaces, in terms of appropriate notions of expansiveness and uniform noncriticality. Our results extend the corresponding characterizations previously obtained for invertible evolution families. To the best of our knowledge, no such characterizations have previously been established for general noninvertible evolution families. A key difference is that noninvertibility makes the structure of the stable spaces more delicate: in our positive-half-line result, finite codimension must be imposed at every time, rather than only at the initial time. We show by an example that the latter, weaker condition is insufficient. We also study evolution families on the negative half-line, using duality to obtain corresponding characterizations in terms of dual expansiveness and dual uniform noncriticality. General growth rates are treated by a time-rescaling argument.
papers.title: h-dichotomies via noncritical uniformity and expansiveness for noninvertible evolution families

papers.abstract: In this note, we show that the sum of the Morse index and number of intersections of min-max geodesics achieving the p-widths of a closed surface are bounded above by $p$, improving a result from our previous work. A key idea is that deformations coming from vertex desingularization and eigenfunctions of the Jacobi operator on geodesics are sufficiently independent.
papers.title: Improved Index and Intersection bounds for Min-Max Geodesics

papers.abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.
papers.title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding

papers.abstract: We prove Conjecture 1.4 of Prochno and Strzelecki [J. Approx. Theory 277 (2022), 105736] on Gelfand numbers of embeddings between finite-dimensional Schatten classes. For $0<p\le1$ and indices bounded away from the ambient dimension by a fixed proportion, we obtain the conjectured lower bound, uniformly in the target exponent $2\le q\le\infty$. Together with the known upper estimate obtained by Hinrichs, Prochno and Vybíral [Math. Ann., 380(3-4):1563-1593, 2021], this gives the exact asymptotic order in the previously unresolved range. As a consequence, we obtain a complete all-index description by combining our result with the estimates of Hinrichs, Prochno and Vybíral and of Prochno and Strzelecki. The proof is deterministic and is based on Hilbert--Schmidt projections on rectangular matrix spaces.
papers.title: Gelfand numbers of Schatten class embeddings in the quasi-Banach range

papers.abstract: Compact gauge fields are powerful tools for controlling quantum dynamics and topological phases of matter. Non-compact gauge fields are particularly relevant for open systems, where particles or energy are exchanged with the environment. Here, we investigate the wavepacket and entanglement dynamics induced by an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field. The wavepacket undergoes non-Abelian non-compact Bloch oscillations, in which the spectrum of an auxiliary one-dimensional quantum problem determines the transition between stable oscillations and unstable amplification. In the unstable adiabatic regime, the wavepacket probes an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ topological defect, and its amplification is determined solely by a hyperbolic solid angle in Minkowski space. Threading an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field through a bosonic tight-binding model yields the bosonic Kitaev model, whose volume or super-volume entanglement scaling is governed by the stability of the gauge field. We further propose an experimental realization of an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field in a spinor condensate. Our results can be generalized to other non-compact groups and higher dimensions, providing a geometric framework for entanglement control, selective amplification, and engineering energy transfer.
papers.title: Dynamical effects induced by synthetic SU(1,1) gauge fields

papers.abstract: We consider vectors chosen randomly from high-dimensional hypersurfaces of the form $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: \sum_{j=1}^n V_j(x_j)=an\}$. These in general asymmetric surfaces generalize classical spheres and include unbounded and disconnected surfaces. We show that under mild assumptions as $n\to\infty$, any weighted sum of the random coordinates is asymptotically Gaussian, provided that no weight dominates. An explicit reduction in the variance compared to the unconstrained case is observed.
