Fair distribution of resources across links and time steps requires stochastic scheduling, motivating a diffusion framework. Via imitation learning, we train a diffusion model to sample scheduling decisions, conditioning generation on the network topology and constraint levels. The parameterization is achieved through a U-Graph Neural Network (U-GNN) to leverage the relationship between graphs and wireless networks for learning. Our approach achieves near-optimal performance, maximizing sum rate while distributing allocations across different links over time horizons. The U-GNN-based diffusion model generalizes to requirements and network sizes unseen during training, demonstrating the robustness of the approach.
papers.title: Wireless Link Scheduling with Graph Signal Diffusion

papers.abstract: We investigate the problem of scaling safe reinforcement learning (safe RL) to massively parallel training regimes, where a large number of environments are exe- cuted with short rollout horizons. Although this setting improves data throughput and wall-clock efficiency, it creates a mismatch with constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), whose safety constraints are defined over full-episode cost returns. We address this mismatch by analyzing staggered environment resets as a phase-mixture distribution over short trajectory segments. This analysis charac- terizes the bias induced by phase coverage and motivates a phase-aggregated cost estimator that reconstructs episode-level cost estimates from short rollout batches. We further incorporate finite-sample uncertainty and distribution mismatch into a constraint-tightening framework, yielding a scalable Safe RL method compatible with on-policy optimization. Using an MJX-based implementation of Safety Gym, our experiments show that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to non-massively parallel implementations while substantially reducing wall-clock training time.
papers.title: Accelerating Safe Reinforcement Learning with Massive Parallelism

papers.abstract: Parton distribution functions (PDFs) are non-perturbative inputs whose scale dependence is governed by the Dokshitzer-Gribov-Lipatov-Altarelli-Parisi (DGLAP) equations. Their numerical evaluation commonly relies on interpolation of tabulated grids. We discuss an analytic representation of collinear proton PDFs in $(x,Q^2)$, obtained by promoting the parameters of a standard $x$-space parametrisation to functions of the scale. The coefficients are reconstructed from the HERAPDF2.0 NLO set using machine-assisted fitting techniques, with sampling in $10^{-4}\le x\le 0.65$ and scales up to 1 TeV. The resulting ML-PDFs reproduce integrated distributions at the sub-percent level for most flavours, with deviations reaching about 1.5% for the strange quark at the highest scales. They satisfy valence and momentum sum rules at the percent level and reproduce representative $pp\toπ$ and $pp\toγπ$ cross sections within approximately 2% and 5%, respectively, in the kinematic regions studied. Compared with grid interpolation through LHAPDF, direct evaluation of the analytic expressions reduces the total Monte Carlo run time by about 11% and 30% in these two applications.
papers.title: Analytic parametrisations of the scale dependence of proton parton distributions

papers.abstract: Generalist Anomaly Detection (GAD) aims to detect anomalies in unseen domains using only a few reference samples. Recent normal-abnormal guided methods improve this setting by exploiting abnormal references, but their residuals often mix transferable anomaly cues with domain-specific appearance factors such as texture, geometry, and acquisition conditions. This residual domain entanglement limits cross-domain transfer and may produce spurious activations on novel domains. We propose DART, a plug-in framework for normal-abnormal guided GAD that learns to separate residuals into anomaly-relevant and domain-specific components. DART combines a Residual Disentanglement Module, which preserves anomaly-discriminative information while suppressing domain information, with Cross-Domain Meta-Training, which forms episodes across source domains to make the separation effective. The method is architecture-agnostic and can be inserted between residual computation and the detection head of existing GAD pipelines. Experiments on MVTec AD, VisA, and BraTS show consistent improvements over multiple base methods, with the largest gains under stronger domain shifts. https://github.com/aqeeelmirza/DART
papers.title: DART: Domain-Agnostic Residual Transfer for Generalist Anomaly Detection

papers.abstract: We study the supersolid order of the spin-1/2 easy-axis XXZ antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice using a fermionic parton mean-field theory built on the $π$-flux Dirac spin liquid, with the mean-field order generated by an on-site spinon interaction term and nearest-neighbor (anisotropic) spin couplings. The collective modes are obtained using the random-phase approximation (RPA). In a finite parameter region, we find the Y state as a self-consistent solution, together with the competing Y' state, which is a $90^\circ$-rotated Y state inside the order plane. The mean-field energy favors Y', even though the two states are exactly degenerate in the classical limit. However, the Y state can become lower in energy when higher-order corrections due to the fluctuations of the collective modes are considered. The Y state can also be stabilized on the mean-field level by applying small external fields, which we do in two different ways: moment-aligned local field and uniform field along the easy axis. In both cases, the RPA calculation for the stabilized Y state gives a roton minimum at the $M$ point in the excitation spectrum. A gapped pseudo-Goldstone mode above the gapless Goldstone mode is obtained as well, which has also been observed experimentally. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of tuning the spinon interaction strength and the anisotropy in spin couplings in our phenomenological model. Comparison with the recent numerical and experimental results is also discussed.
papers.title: Spin supersolid in triangular lattice easy-axis spin-1/2 antiferromagnet: a fermionic parton perspective

papers.abstract: After a runtime or API migration, an LLM-repaired procedure can run cleanly yet return wrong results, and a release check on typical test inputs ships it. We report a preregistered study of 73 tasks covering 60 documented changes in CPython, Node.js and SQLite. Every candidate is executed on the real runtimes against withheld contracts. Over the complete repair space, the all-assertions gate on typical inputs released 0.410 of wrong repairs. One edge input written from the release note cut this to 0.065, and to 0.061 on 15 unseen clusters. Three inputs from a blind GPT-5.6-luna writer that never saw the program reached 0.070. Two further frozen stages enlarged the menu to 1491 fragments and then added 233 hard distractors that match the legacy output on typical inputs. The edge input (0.058) and the frontier-model writer (0.058) passed their preregistered tests. Yet 0.168 and 0.153 of the hard wrong programs still passed. Two local-model writers failed their preregistered tests. Across four model families, the edge input cut wrong releases per attempt in all three open-weight families on all three menus, for example from 0.233 to 0.057, without lowering correct completion. Self-tests helped less. A blind AI audit flagged 34 contracts as stricter than their requirements. Dropping the disputed checks changed 0 verdicts, but class-label disputes remain open. No model-written code was executed. Artifacts are available from the authors on request.
papers.title: Accepted but Wrong: Silent Failures of LLM Code Repairs after API Migrations

papers.abstract: We give a human-readable exposition of OpenAI's construction of a group algebra in characteristic two that is not directly finite. We then adapt the argument to show that, for every prime $p$, there exists a hyperbolic group $G_p$ such that $\mathbb{F}_p[G_p]$ is not directly finite.
papers.title: A Note on the OpenAI Construction of Counterexamples to the Kaplansky Direct-Finiteness Conjecture

papers.abstract: Previous studies combined rotation periods derived from Kepler photometry, stellar parameters from previous Gaia Data Releases, and planet hosts from the NASA Exoplanet Archive to conclude that statistically planet-hosting stars rotate slower than stars without detected planets. Here, we revisit these studies by using similar Kepler rotational period sample, but with an updated Gaia DR3-based stellar parameter catalogue and an updated exoplanet catalogue. We apply minimal sample cuts in evolutionary state, metallicity, and distance, and then model the stellar rotation period as a function of effective temperature alone. For each star, we derive the ratio of its observed period to the temperature-expected period, and compare the ratio distributions for the planet-host and non-host stars. For periods shorter than 20 d, the planet-host distribution of this ratio is shifted towards longer periods; the period-ratio median is ~15% larger for hosts than for non-hosts (p_KS = 2.4 x 10^-4). We also examine the recently published TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey (TARS) and find a similar trend. However, the strongly structured period distribution precludes a robust comparison between the host and the non-host stars. Therefore, the updated analysis, using more robust stellar and planetary parameters, recovers the previously reported association, strengthening the case for a genuine connection between stellar rotation and planet occurrence.
papers.title: The slower rotation of planet-hosting stars revisited

papers.abstract: This is the first of a series of papers which will be devoted to a study of the index of mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators on closed Riemannian manifolds. The aim of the series is to discretise the index of the Dirac operator. On flat tori, this is achieved by the Wilson--Dirac operator of lattice gauge theory on a regular lattice. On a general closed Riemannian manifold, however, no regular lattice is available. As an intermediate step between the continuum Dirac operator and its discretisations, we introduce mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators on any closed Riemannian manifold, defined by integrating covariant differences over distances comparable to a fixed length scale. In this paper, we define the index of the mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators via spectral flow and prove that it agrees with that of the continuum Dirac operator at all sufficiently small scales. The proof rests on an elliptic estimate uniform in the scale and a Rellich-type compactness theorem. In the second paper, we shall pass from mesoscopic operators to discrete Wilson--Dirac operators.
papers.title: The index of mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators: I

papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish a matrix criterion for a space to be homeomorphic to a closed Euclidean ball. As applications, we prove that the normalized space of $K$-Lorentzian polynomials on an arbitrary open convex cone $K$ is homeomorphic to a closed Euclidean ball, giving an affirmative answer to Brändén and Leake's question, and we also settle Brändén's conjecture that the normalized space of homogeneous multiaffine real stable polynomials is homeomorphic to a closed Euclidean ball. In addition, our results show that the normalized space of homogeneous $K$-stable polynomials of degree $d$ is homeomorphic to a closed Euclidean ball.
papers.title: Some polynomial spaces are Euclidean balls

papers.abstract: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint.
papers.title: SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes

papers.abstract: Recent neural decoding approaches achieve strong performance by training on large collections of paired neural-behavioral recordings, but such datasets are expensive, invasive, and difficult to scale. In contrast, behavioral data is abundant and easy to collect, raising the question of whether neural decoding can benefit from decoupling behavioral and neural representation learning. We introduce BEEMO, a flexible multi-session framework that enables training with arbitrary mixtures of paired neural-behavioral recordings and unpaired behavioral data. A behavior decoder learns movement dynamics directly from behavioral trajectories, while neural activity is incorporated through cross-attention layers when available, allowing behavioral and neural supervision to scale independently. Across multiple intracortical motor datasets and tasks in nonhuman primates, we show that incorporating unpaired behavioral data improves decoding performance, particularly when transferring to new tasks, and that adding even a small amount of behavioral data from the target task further improves transfer. By decoupling neural and behavioral data, we unlock a new dimension for scaling: unpaired behavioral data, which is substantially cheaper and easier to collect than paired neural recordings, can be used directly to improve decoding performance. We further show that behavior-only pretraining, without any neural pretraining, achieves performance comparable to models pretrained on substantially larger neural datasets. Together, our results suggest that scaling behavioral data offers a practical and cost-effective path toward neural decoding models that generalize across subjects and tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/nerdslab/beemo.
papers.title: Scaling Neural Motor Decoding via Decoupled Behavioral Pretraining

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models can simulate different observers, yet it remains unclear how assigned perspectives reshape their internal representations and whether these changes govern their judgements. Here, we investigate the representational geometry of persona-conditioned visual interestingness in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Across 100 images and 53 prompting conditions, we systematically vary persona content and the linguistic framing used to introduce it, while recording behavioural ratings and layer-wise hidden states. We observe a systematic reorganisation of representational geometry across processing depth: early layers primarily encode image identity, whereas persona-specific structures emerge in later layers. Strikingly, prompt framing reshapes internal representations more strongly than persona identity, whereas persona content has a greater impact on behavioural judgements. This dissociation is further illustrated by minimal identity statements that alter representations even without changing responses. These findings demonstrate that representational distance does not necessarily reflect behavioural relevance. More broadly, they reveal how simulated perspectives emerge as distinct structures within the representational space of artificial cognitive systems, highlighting a fundamental distinction between the geometry of internal representations and their functional consequences.
papers.title: The Geometry of Simulated Perspectives: Dissociating Representation and Behaviour in a Multimodal Language Model

papers.abstract: The Characteristic Mapping (CM) method is a transport scheme which discretizes the Lagrangian flow map as a composition of spatial interpolants. This adaptive approximation technique has demonstrated novel resolution properties and the ability to efficiently simulate the fine scales of inviscid turbulent flows. In this work, we construct an extension of this approach to the solution of dissipative problems, including the Navier-Stokes equations. The extension lifts a general scalar evolution equation to a path in a group of diffeomorphisms, where the semigroup approach of the CM method can be exploited. We give an interpretation of this lift through the geometric framework of optimal transport. We then introduce a semidirect product evolution technique to perform the time stepping of the map components. The map is evolved based on the semi-Lagrangian CM approach, and its log-Jacobian is evolved explicitly by an exponential integrator. The numerical scheme is demonstrated to be high-order accurate and is tested on a range of canonical nonlinear dissipative equations. By retaining the resolution properties of the CM method, the approach shows a promising ability to simulate turbulent fluid flows across all Reynolds numbers.
papers.title: A characteristic mapping method for dissipative evolution equations

papers.abstract: This paper establishes the global well-posedness of shock solutions for a 3D spherical piston problem to the compressible Euler equations. The main mathematical challenges are the nonlinear coupling between the free shock boundary and the moving piston, alongside potential gradient catastrophes induced by spherical geometric source terms. To overcome these difficulties, we reformulate the problem using Riemann invariants and introduce a tailored directional derivative along the unperturbed piston trajectory. Then we can extend the local solution to construct a global piecewise smooth solution including a single shock under some moderate assumptions.
papers.title: Shock solutions of a 3D spherical piston problem for the compressible Euler equations

papers.abstract: Partial single-motor loss of effectiveness (LoE) changes the remaining control-authority geometry of a quadrotor and can change which control allocator performs best during emergency landing[cite: 11]. We compare three allocators in Crazyflie software-in-the-loop simulation: bounded weighted least squares (reported as PINV), a finite-candidate residual allocator (QP-lite), and the same residual allocator with scoring parameters tuned offline by the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)[cite: 11]. For this study, fault geometry is represented by the known failed-motor index[cite: 11]. At $η=0.496$ remaining effectiveness, matched development trials select CEM for M1, M3, and M4 and PINV for M2; the M3 selection is a one-trial margin (29/30 versus 28/30)[cite: 11]. After freezing this routing map, the policy achieves 117/120 safe first-contact touchdowns on fresh seeds and 115/120 in a separate randomized-order integrated-supervisor evaluation[cite: 11]. For the critical M2/PINV branch, Firth regression gives a nominal $η_{50}\approx0.4956$ with a within-model 95% bootstrap interval of approximately [0.4955, 0.4956][cite: 11]. One-factor-at-a-time $\pm10\%$ plant perturbations shift $η_{50}$ by up to 0.05495 for thrust coefficient and 0.04974 for mass; the most frequent violated first-contact criterion also changes from vertical speed in many conditions to angular rate for mass -10% and thrust-coefficient +10%[cite: 11]. At fixed $η=0.496$, PINV has a higher M2 safe count than frozen CEM in 9/11 tested plant states and ties in 2/11; the two ties are both 0/30[cite: 11]. The experiments therefore distinguish motor-conditioned allocator selection from sensitivity to plant-model mismatch[cite: 11].
papers.title: Fault-Geometry-Aware Control Allocation for Emergency Quadrotor Landing under Single-Motor Loss of Effectiveness

papers.abstract: A memory that keeps learning must also forget. The Hopfield network does not: beyond a critical number of stored patterns it falls into a state of total confusion and retrieves none of them. Parisi showed in 1986 that bounding the synaptic strength cures this pathology, since the clipping of the couplings gradually erases the oldest memories and leaves room for the new ones. In this paper we provide a thermodynamic description of the resulting network, known as the Hopfield-Parisi model. Starting from the learning rule, we show that the network is equivalent to a Hopfield model whose patterns are weighted according to their age, superimposed on a Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, both governed by the synaptic bound: a larger bound makes the memory longer, but also noisier. The theory of nonlinear networks developed in the eighties already provides, through the heuristic replica method, the equations that govern this model at any temperature, but to the best of our knowledge they have been solved only at zero temperature. We rederive them at the replica symmetric level through Guerra's interpolation and solve them at finite temperature, obtaining the phase diagram of the model together with its memory horizon, namely the largest age at which a pattern can still be retrieved. The solution shows that forgetting acts on the signal alone, the noise being the same for patterns of every age, and that the horizon is maximal at an intermediate bound which is essentially insensitive to temperature. Monte Carlo simulations of networks trained with the original learning rule support these predictions.
papers.title: Thermodynamics of Forgetting in a Bounded Hopfield Network

papers.abstract: We study the set of visible points from the origin in certain cut-and-project sets, specifically the density of the set. We generalize to all real quadratic number fields the formulas for the density found by G. Hammarhjelm, and the corresponding error bounds proved by I. Gringlaz, R. Kumar, B. Weiss. We also find the possible densities of the set of visible points in the cut-and-project set, with a constant generic lattice, and a changing window with constant volume. We also study bounds for the distance of large holes in the set of visible points of certain cut-and-project sets, generalizing theorems originally proved by P. Erdős for $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
papers.title: Density and holes of the visible points in certain cut-and-project sets

papers.abstract: We give a deterministic, strongly polynomial algorithm running in $\tilde{O}(km+k^4n)$ time that finds $k$ arc-disjoint arborescences of minimum total cost in a directed multigraph with $n$ vertices and $m$ arcs. This significantly improves upon the state of the art for $k \ge 2$ with $k=n^{o(1)}$: the prior fastest weakly polynomial and strongly polynomial algorithms take $\tilde{O}(km\sqrt{n}\log C)$ and $\tilde{O}(kmn)$ time (Gabow and Xu, 1989; Gabow, 1995), respectively. Roughly, our technique can be viewed as a way to apply a linear number of \emph{shortest} augmenting paths in near-linear total time for the special case of the weighted matroid intersection problem between the $k$-fold graphic matroid and the indegree partition matroid. This was previously done in the unweighted case by Gabow (1995), but our approach is different. As an extension, we also obtain a deterministic $\tilde{O}(km^{1+o(1)}+k^5n)$-time algorithm for minimum-cost maximum-cardinality packing of $k$ forests in undirected graphs. In particular, this finds $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees of minimum total cost, if they exist. The previous fastest algorithm takes $\tilde{O}(kn^2+m)$ time (Gabow and Westermann, 1992).
papers.title: Minimum-Cost $k$-Arborescence Packing in $\tilde O(km+k^4 n)$ Time

papers.abstract: High-resolution tropical cyclone surface wind speeds derived from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) observations can support storm structure and intensity modelling, but remain spatially and temporally sparse and unavailable near-real-time. Geostationary satellites capture cloud tops continuously in space and time, but do not directly resolve surface winds. Here, we present simple neural networks to predict 2D wind fields and storm-scale intensity metrics from geostationary imagery. Through a series of ablation studies, we find that joint prediction of 2D fields and scalar metrics from the model latent space improves the retrieval of the (radius of) maximum wind, especially for rapid intensification events.
papers.title: Nowcasting of Tropical Cyclone Wind Fields and Intensity from Geostationary Imagery

papers.abstract: Entropy has played a pivotal role in physics ever since its inception by Clausius in the early industrial age. Shannon ushered the concept into the information age by using it to describe fundamental limits of information processing, founding the field of information theory. Today, a fruitful interaction between information theory and physics is pushing our understanding of entropy forward. It has revealed, in particular, that no single notion of entropy suffices to capture all relevant properties of physical systems, making it necessary to consider a variety of entropic measures of quantum information, each with distinct features and uses. This review surveys these recent advances in a structured way, covering a comprehensive array of information measures, including Rényi and smooth entropies, together with their interrelations. Starting with a systematic characterization of entropies that motivates their definitions from natural physical principles, we discuss their applications ranging from quantum communication and cryptography to resource theories, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.
papers.title: Entropic measures of quantum information

papers.abstract: We compute Cunningham's canonical decomposition of a symmetric submodular function on $n$ elements in $O(n^3)$ time. The decomposition represents all minimum cuts in linear space. For the pair $s,t$ produced by Queyranne's algorithm, we construct in $O(n^2)$ time a digraph representing exactly the minimum $st$-cuts of the function. Using this construction in Chekuri and Xu's decomposition algorithm gives the cubic bound.
papers.title: All minimum cuts of symmetric submodular functions

papers.abstract: We consider the problem of cross-validation (CV) in time series forecasting, with a focus on global forecasting models based on deep learning. The prevailing CV strategy in forecasting is to partition data across time with the last part of each series used for testing. With global models trained on collections of time series, however, a fundamentally different approach becomes possible: partitioning across series and time. We formalize series-wise CV for global forecasting models and benchmark several instantiations, including K-fold CV, bootstrapping, and Monte Carlo CV, on 11 datasets with 10 neural network architectures. We evaluate CV procedures along five dimensions: performance estimation, overoptimism rate, model selection accuracy, regret, and downstream forecasting performance. We withhold a random fraction of series from training so that they appear only in the test set. This protocol simulates the emergence of new series not seen during training, a common scenario in global forecasting. Under this protocol, our results reveal a nuanced trade-off: series-wise CV yields better downstream forecasting accuracy by guiding model selection toward configurations that generalize across both time and series, while time-wise CV retains a slight advantage for estimating out-of-sample error.
papers.title: Series-wise Cross-validation for Global Time Series Forecasting

papers.abstract: Recent advances in speech generation have spurred the development of speech editing techniques. However, achieving high-quality speech editing remains challenging due to two key limitations. First, the major hurdle is the lack of large-scale, high-quality speech editing datasets. Constructing such datasets is costly, while open-source, scalable data pipelines remain limited. Second, the learning dynamics of speech editing models remain poorly understood. In particular, how models acquire editing capabilities and the relationship between generation and editing remain unclear. To address these challenges, we introduce VoxCanvas-41M, a large-scale bilingual dataset comprising approximately 41 million speech editing pairs. VoxCanvas-41M covers two major categories: content editing, including single-span, multi-span, and location-reference editing, and paralinguistic editing, covering the insertion and deletion of 39 classes of nonverbal events such as laughter, sighs, and coughs. Building on VoxCanvas-41M, we train VoxCanvas-Edit, an instruction-based speech editing model, demonstrating the effectiveness of our dataset in improving editing performance. Furthermore, we systematically investigate the learning dynamics of speech editing, examining how models learn different editing operations and how data scale, task interactions, and training strategies affect editing performance. The dataset, pipeline, and demos are publicly available.
papers.title: VoxCanvas-41M: A Large-Scale Bilingual Dataset for Instruction-Based Speech Editing and Its Learning Dynamics

papers.abstract: Homogeneous single-crystal growth of Ni--Mn--Ga magnetic shape-memory alloys is limited by incongruent melting, Mn reactivity, and longitudinal composition segregation. We report a modified optical floating-zone method in which growth is performed inside a transparent sapphire crucible, stabilising the molten zone while preserving optical heating and visual monitoring. The resulting crystals show improved growth reproducibility and controlled macroscopic geometry. To interpret the measured segregation profiles, a transient finite-element heat-transfer model in COMSOL Multiphysics was coupled to an effective molten-zone mass-balance calculation. The model reveals that the local solidification velocity is not fixed by the imposed translation speed but varies strongly as the molten-zone geometry evolves. The calculated solidification-front geometry is independently supported by EBSD analysis of a quenched growth interface, while the coupled mass-balance calculation reproduces the dominant features of the measured composition profiles. These results show that deviations from ideal Scheil--Pfann behaviour arise from the evolving molten-zone geometry and solidification conditions. The experimentally constrained model therefore provides a practical means of reconstructing otherwise inaccessible growth conditions and a basis for optimisation of sapphire-confined floating-zone growth of incongruently melting alloys.
papers.title: Finite-element reconstruction of molten-zone dynamics and chemical segregation in optical floating-zone grown Ni--Mn--Ga

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based molecular docking requires learning a corrective score field across a broad corruption distribution, yet individual pose errors can differ substantially in their structural consequences. This creates a post-training conflict between preserving broad score-field coverage and concentrating supervision on corrections that appear more relevant to docking geometry. Using DiffDock, a fixed-budget study compares broad continuation with torsional supervision focused on Cartesian consequence or conditional target consistency, and with a broad/focused mixture. Evaluation separates fixed score fidelity, generated-pose quality, best-of-10 sampling capacity, and confidence-selected Top-1 docking performance. At <5 Angstrom, broad continuation had the highest mean Top-1 success among trained policies, and focused or mixed supervision showed no consistent advantage under the tested budget. The starting model had better fixed score fidelity, whereas the evaluated broad-continuation model had higher mean Top-1 success with the same aggregate best-of-10 recovery. Focusing supervision on structurally consequential or more consistently specified corrections did not consistently improve returned-pose success over broad continuation.
papers.title: Geometric Relevance Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating Focused Post-Training Supervision in Diffusion Docking

papers.abstract: We describe the shifted Lagrangian geometry of curves in Radko surfaces, through their global integrations and their homotopy Poisson algebras. We construct the adjoint symplectic groupoid of the surface explicitly, show that admissible curves integrate to embedded Lagrangian subgroupoids, which are 1-shifted Lagrangians, and characterize when their shifted intersections are clean. For a component of the degeneracy locus, a canonical Hamiltonian flow on its shifted self-intersection recovers the modular period. On the infinitesimal side, the homotopy Poisson algebra of a connected admissible curve not contained in the degeneracy locus is $L_\infty$-isomorphic to its underlying cochain complex, and its $L_\infty$-isomorphism class is determined by the total contact multiplicity. The brackets of arity at least two can be removed by a change of tubular neighbourhood exactly when all contacts are transverse. At tangential contacts, the binary bracket retains the modular vector field. We establish this distinction using a general characterization of the $L_\infty$-isomorphisms induced by changes of tubular neighbourhood, valid for arbitrary coisotropic submanifolds.
papers.title: Shifted Lagrangian geometry of curves in Radko surfaces

papers.abstract: Code and circuit distances characterize how strongly quantum error correction suppresses logical errors and guide code comparisons, schedule choices and resource estimates. Yet many published distances are only upper bounds from heuristic searches. Here, we express both distances as tropical partition functions and evaluate them with rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problems, and proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values. On two benchmarks, our method certifies more instances than all other tested exact solvers combined. We certify distances for codes with up to 31,200 qubits, such as Google's modular hyperbolic codes, and for memory circuits with up to $8\times10^5$ fault mechanisms, such as those of high-rate Cornucopia codes. Our audit of 26 recent papers identifies overestimated distances and non-tight upper bounds in 10 papers, with a maximum discrepancy of at least eight. Certified distances also guide circuit design and show which defective chips remain usable. In particular, we certify circuit distance 16 for IBM's two-gross memory circuits with the standard schedule, not the assumed 18, whereas redesigned schedules reach 18 at one noisy cycle, at the cost of one more timestep per cycle. At 99.98% junction yield, keeping gross-code memory blocks with dead checks that are certified at distance 10 or more raises the estimated usable share from 53% for perfect blocks alone to 94% with an improved schedule.
papers.title: Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale

papers.abstract: Pure point spectral convergence is generally unavailable for sparse graph sequences, where Laplacian eigenvalues may remain unstable under graph growth. This poses challenges for analyzing spectral operators underlying many graph-based learning methods, including graph neural networks. We identify a class of sparse bipartite graph sequences for which eigenvalue-level spectral convergence can be recovered. Focusing on graphs with strong degree heterogeneity, we exploit the convergence properties of their line-graph sequences. Using a spectral correspondence between bipartite graph Laplacians and line-graph adjacency operators, we transfer convergence guarantees from dense line-graphs back to the original sparse graphs. This framework yields eigenvalue-level spectral convergence for a class of deterministic sparse graph sequences. We further analyze superlinear preferential attachment trees, establishing convergence to an infinite-dimensional limit operator. Numerical experiments empirically support our spectral convergence results.
papers.title: Spectral Convergence of Sparse Bipartite Graphs via the Line-Graphon

papers.abstract: Wind farm power control can help the system maintain balance and avoid blackouts. In Europe, this can be achieved through implicit balancing, where a wind farm adjusts its power setpoint in anticipation of the imbalance price using information published by the Transmission System Operator. Thereby, the wind farm helps restore system balance while also reducing its own imbalance costs resulting from forecast errors. However, implicit balancing is a challenging problem since the settlement price is unknown in advance and can be impacted by the pursued control strategy. Reinforcement learning methods could help to solve this problem, but lack the interpretability needed to be deployed on real wind farms. Therefore, we propose a policy distillation framework using explainable boosting machines (EBMs), a variant of generalized additive models, to obtain a transparent control policy. To increase the value captured by the EBM model, we introduce a value-oriented perspective to policy distillation inspired by research in the field of energy forecasting. Furthermore, we suggest to include expert knowledge during model design, such that the control strategy is also justifiable to stakeholders. Using real data of the Belgian grid and an offshore wind farm, we find that our value-oriented and expert-based controller can reduce imbalance costs by 82%, while outperforming a price threshold controller as well as a policy distillation baseline using decision trees.
papers.title: Value-oriented policy distillation for interpretable wind farm power control

papers.abstract: Akbari, Cameron, and Khosrovshahi proposed two questions concerning the null space and the image space of graphs. Although these problems have been studied in several cases, they have not yet been fully resolved. In this work, we present constructions of graphs that satisfy both the problems.
papers.title: Open Problems on the Null Space and Image Space of the Adjacency Matrix

papers.abstract: We prove an arithmetic doubling identity for the standard arithmetic theta series on $X_0(N)$ at arbitrary positive level, with constant $ψ(N)/24$ for the fixed genus-two Eisenstein series. The product comparison covers all pairs of integral indices. At rank zero, an explicit Epstein zeta correction agrees with the middle Bruhat orbit of the Eisenstein derivative. The common-component calculation combines integral CM adjunction, the cyclic difference divisor, and compact Green-current identities. It retains the different, conductor, internal contacts, and proportionality contacts at every prime, including dyadic and supersingular places. Finite intersections, curvature, and discriminant heights identify the nonpositive coefficients with an explicit modular completion. Uniform estimates for parameter derivatives give strong Fourier convergence. Green-energy estimates justify the double Petersson pairing. The full cusp lift exists as a Bochner integral and equals its Mordell--Weil projection. For $\mathbb Z/(2N)\mathbb Z$, explicit prime-power recursions determine the complete zero-component trace spectrum, including the dyadic factor. They give the scalar-to-vector Petersson norm correction and an isometric normalization on the active subspace. The Bruinier--Yang theorem then yields the scalar height formula on the specified Jacobi newform line. We also prove a double Rankin--Selberg criterion based on positive diagonal coefficients and record the paired analytic factorization with its ramified local integrals retained explicitly.
papers.title: Arithmetic theta products and doubling at arbitrary level

papers.abstract: The Gibbs state determined by a thermal reservoir does not determine how a working medium approaches it or how fluctuations accumulate over repeated cycles. We exploit this kinetic freedom in an anharmonic collective quantum Otto engine. A longitudinal interaction separates neighboring Dicke transition frequencies without changing their collective matrix elements, allowing passive spectral shaping to route finite-time transport among edges with different heat costs while preserving the contact Gibbs states. Exact edge-current identities and repeated-cycle counting statistics link this routing to mean work, hot heat, and intercycle work correlations. At fixed thermal-contact exposure, structured reservoirs can increase both mean work and long-time squared precision; equal-work controls distinguish these gains from uniform relaxation-rate changes. The useful regime is mesoscopic, bounded by spectral resolution and physical contact time. An equal-cooling example and a full-spin local-noise study test the mechanism beyond ideal engine operation, the latter retaining a one-cycle precision gain despite spin-sector mixing. In a six-transmon dressed-spectrum model, passive microwave filters at fixed integrated coupling achieve equal mean work with shorter thermal contacts, corresponding to higher contact-time-normalized output, and with long-time squared precision comparable to that of the fastest sampled flat reference. The transition pathways selected by a passive reservoir thus provide a control variable for finite-time performance and accumulated work fluctuations that is independent of thermal equilibrium.
papers.title: Finite-Time Thermodynamic Routing in an Anharmonic Collective Quantum Otto Engine

papers.abstract: A search for Higgs boson pair production where one Higgs boson decays via $H \to b \bar{b}$ and the other Higgs boson decays via $H \to WW^*\to \ell νq \bar{q}\quad (\ell=e,μ)$ is presented. This search uses the complete Run 2 data sample recorded by the ATLAS detector at the LHC from 2015 to 2018 at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $140$ fb$^{-1}$. The analysis looks for non-resonant Higgs boson pair production assuming Standard Model dynamics. No evidence for Higgs-boson pair production is observed and an upper limit at 95% confidence level is set at 35 times the Standard Model prediction. The same selection is used to target Beyond the Standard Model theories predicting the resonant production of the heavy scalars, $X$ and $S$, with $m_X > m_S > m_H$, undergoing the process $X \to SH, S \to W^+W^-, H \to b \bar{b}$. Limits are set on the resonant $X \to SH$ production for several combinations of the two scalar's masses within the $m_X$ mass range $350-3000$ GeV and $m_S$ mass range $170-2500$ GeV.
papers.title: Search for Higgs boson production in association with another Higgs or an exotic scalar boson in the $b\bar{b}W^{+}W^{-}$ single lepton final state at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV with the ATLAS experiment

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models, but most RL objectives roll out the current policy at every iteration, and with a many-step sampler these rollouts typically dominate the cost of training. Few-step models cut this cost, yet they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives are built for an instantaneous velocity with a many-step sampler. We adapt RL objectives to few-step models systematically in three phases, namely a transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation. The transformation to $x$-space expresses each objective we consider through a common policy prediction, at the clean end by default and at an explicitly marked level for transition or flow-map objectives, so that objectives stated over densities, velocities or rewards become comparable. The decomposition writes the gradient of each of these objectives as the sum of a self-regression toward a reference and a reward augmentation, so that a method reduces, at the gradient level, to a choice of anchors and weights. The adaptation computes each anchor from a few-step model at the end of its transport or along its tangent, with the instantaneous velocity recovered from the network itself or from an auxiliary network. This yields few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL in one modular codebase. In our experiments, reward-gradient-based methods are the most effective when the reward is differentiable and its gradient is affordable; otherwise DiffusionNFT-style methods generally reach high rewards in relatively few iterations despite a sometimes higher per-iteration cost. Extra inference steps show no systematic aggregate benefit in our experiments, although selected outputs visibly improve with two to four times as many sampling steps as in training.
papers.title: FewStepRL: Fine-tuning Few-step Diffusion Models with Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: Since the discovery of superconductivity in $\mathrm{MgB_2}$, metal diborides have attracted significant attention. Among these, osmium diboride ($\mathrm{OsB_2}$), crystallizing in an orthorhombic structure (space group $Pmmn$) with puckered boron layers, has been classified as a low-$κ$ Type-II superconductor ($T_c \approx 2.1~\mathrm{K}$). Here, we report experimental evidence establishing that $\mathrm{OsB_2}$ is in fact a rare nonelemental Type-I superconductor. Our identification is supported by three primary experimental hallmarks: (i) a pronounced Differential Paramagnetic Effect (DPE) peak in AC susceptibility ($χ_{ac}$) measurements under static DC magnetic fields, signaling the intermediate state; (ii) a field-induced crossover to a divergent first-order phase transition in specific heat ($C/T$); and (iii) pronounced magnetic hysteresis in field-ramped transitions indicative of supercooling.
papers.title: Experimental Evidence for Type-I Superconductivity in $\mathrm{OsB_2}$

papers.abstract: Two-phase designs provide a cost-effective framework for biomarker studies and have been widely used to reduce the burden of collecting expensive biomarker measurements. Most methodological research has focused on efficient Phase II sampling and estimation of biomarker--outcome associations. A natural subsequent step, however, is to incorporate identified biomarkers into risk prediction models, where measures of predictive performance become important inferential targets. Even for binary outcomes, methodological developments for two-phase designs that jointly address association parameters and predictive performance remain limited. Building on classical case-control and matched case-control designs developed primarily for association inference with binary outcomes, we propose a risk-matched case-control (RMCC) design that uses a scalar disease-risk score constructed from Phase I variables to define matching strata and guide Phase II sampling. To address the limitations of existing likelihood-based approaches, which typically require correct specification of the nuisance distribution of biomarkers, we develop a unified design-based inference framework based on inverse probability weighting for both association parameters and predictive performance measures, including positive predictive value and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. We further introduce target-specific weight scaling and calibration procedures and derive variance estimators that account for sampling variability in both phases. Simulation studies demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of the proposed design and inference procedures, and an application to a Taiwanese oral cancer cohort illustrates their potential utility.
papers.title: Risk-matched case-control sampling and semiparametric weight calibration for efficient biomarker assessment with binary outcomes

papers.abstract: Mathematical modeling turns an open-ended real-world problem into assumptions, a model, a solution, and a defended recommendation, and its answers matter only if they are both close to a credible reference and physically feasible; existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge, leaving those numbers unchecked. We introduce TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench), the first benchmark to make complete contest-style modeling problems agentic, verifiable, and terminal at once, over 18 real CUMCM and MCM problems (2023--2025). Each task ships the verbatim statement, official attachments, and figures in a containerized terminal; the agent returns one JSON artifact, scored on the numeric core of the final question against a reproduction of the Outstanding-award paper. Two design choices distinguish it: direction-aware, one-sided scoring, which never penalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility verification---a programmatic gate over six decidable invariant forms plus 624 Lean~4 obligations---with a hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each task is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers rather than one, so a model must be close to many accepted answers; across seven multimodal entries (three seeds each) the strongest reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58\%, while the \$2.54 open model holds 59.81\% at $1/100$ the cost. TB-MathModel turns the numeric core of modeling into a reproducible, machine-checkable signal for measuring long-horizon modeling competence and for collecting agent trajectories. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/terminal-bench-math-modeling.
papers.title: Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench: The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling

papers.abstract: Self-attention carries a quadratic cost in token count, which limits how far Vision Transformers can scale with input resolution. We introduce SSoG, a separable sum-of-Gaussians spatial operator that replaces dense self-attention with a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels, reducing the per-layer cost from $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ to subquadratic in $N$. Unlike dot-product self-attention, whose Lipschitz constant is unbounded outside a compact input domain, SSoG with fixed kernels is globally Lipschitz continuous, which, via the Picard--Lindelöf theorem, guarantees that the continuous-depth variant has a unique solution on the whole integration interval, a global guarantee that dense-attention counterparts lack in general. On CIFAR-100 at $224\times224$, in a matched discrete-Transformer setting and in the continuous setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 2.2--4.1 points across three model widths while using 8.8--16.6\% fewer parameters, with depth and training recipe held fixed. In a looped-Transformer setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 5.4--8.1 points. We further probe inference-time scaling by evaluating on inputs up to $1024\times1024$ at matched batch size: in the continuous-depth (Neural ODE) architecture, SSoG reaches up to 154\% higher throughput and over 60\% lower peak memory than dense attention, with the gap widening as resolution grows, consistent with the difference in asymptotic cost. In the discrete and looped settings, SSoG also achieves over 30\% higher throughput than dense attention at this resolution. Together, these results establish SSoG as a practical, parameter-efficient, and theoretically grounded alternative to dense attention across discrete, weight-shared, and continuous-depth Transformer variants.
papers.title: Beyond Quadratic Attention: Separable Gaussian Operators for ODE Vision Transformers

papers.abstract: We calculate the level-resolved transmon population remaining after dispersive readout with a converged open-system model. The drive and qubit-cavity coupling use the rotating-wave approximation, while the cavity is a quantized mode in a frame displaced by its classical trajectory. At a readout occupation of 80, the model leaves a persistent distribution across the first transmon levels, with p2 = 1.02 x 10^-3 and p3 = 4.10 x 10^-5 at the end of readout. These populations survive an additional drive-off wait: over 73 ns each level decays by less than 3 percent and follows its own relaxation rate, not the near-factor-of-two drop in residual cavity photons. This identifies the population as bare-level occupation rather than coherent dressing. Channel-removal and bath-model controls attribute p2 mainly to dephasing and p3 and above mainly to relaxation, unchanged across bath models though absolute values vary by up to 15 percent. We also test the coherent drive truncation. In dissipation-free transmon-only benchmarks driven by the classical cavity trajectory, the nearest-neighbour RWA drive underestimates the full charge-operator result while the drive is on. At switch-off for occupation 80, where coherent populations are hundreds of times larger than the residual values, p2(RWA)/p2(full) = 0.905 and p3(RWA)/p3(full) = 0.759, with larger discrepancies at deeper levels. One source is a parity-allowed non-nearest-neighbour charge matrix element omitted by the drive operator. A naive beyond-RWA extension with bare-basis Lindblad dissipators fails a zero-drive ground-state test and serves only as a diagnostic. A dressed-basis (secular) construction instead leaves the dressed ground state stationary at zero drive. The result is a converged RWA prediction of readout-induced population plus direct tests of where the approximation loses quantitative reliability.
papers.title: Persistent level-resolved transmon population after dispersive readout, and the limits of its open-system description

papers.abstract: In this paper, we continue our investigation of the structure of Thurston geometries with non-constant curvature. We generalize the notion of cylinders, prove that they contain the types of geodesic curves. Moreover, we formulate and prove a statement analogous to Pappus's hexagon theorem for $\SLR$ geometry.
papers.title: Pappus's hexagon theorem for geodesic curves in $\SLR$ geometry

papers.abstract: For unknown three-qubit pure states, we characterize the optimal trade-off among GHZ-class certification, binary probability readout of the three-tangle, and conditional state retention. The vanishing ideal of the null class specifies the optimal certification subspace, while a polynomial multiplication operator gives the spectral limit for binary readout. Four copies are necessary for a nonzero certificate. A fifth copy raises the optimal success probability from $τ^{2}/48$ to $5τ^{2}/72$ and permits the original unknown state to be retained, where $τ$ is the three-tangle. We obtain this gain as an instance of a general symmetry-based additional-copy theorem. At six copies the optimal certification probability is $(39+2S)τ^{2}/296$, with $S=\sum_{X}\mathrm{Tr}\,ρ_{X}^{2}$, whereas the largest exact binary probability is $τ^{2}/8$. Local Schur measurements and conditional local operations with classical communication attain these bounds. Retaining the full six-copy branch record yields a weighted estimator with lower variance than binary thinning of the same data. Explicit circuits and fixed-budget comparisons connect the success probabilities to input-copy consumption, retained quantum output, and coherent gate cost.
papers.title: Optimal finite-copy readout of three-qubit entanglement with state retention

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often present synthesized answers without making their supporting evidence easy to inspect. We study how features of these answers relate to users' subsequent accepting, checking, and challenging in 489,283 assistant-user response pairs from ShareChat and WildChat. Broad attribution language appears in 31.9% of qualifying responses, compared with explicit URLs in 1.33%, revealing a gap between claims of grounding and preserved inspectable support. Attribution, uncertainty, and other response cues generally accompany both checking and challenging; only uncertainty shows a small statistically distinguishable pooled association favoring checking. Within Technical Help, uncertainty favors checking relative to challenging; refusals and reasoning traces favor challenging in Seeking Information. Scrutiny is concentrated in some conversations, while its apparent turn-to-turn persistence becomes much smaller when conversation-level differences and response ordering are examined separately. These results suggest that supporting verification requires attention to what evidence can be inspected, which question a user is trying to resolve, and the history of the interaction.
papers.title: Signals, Evidence, and Context: User Scrutiny in Real-World LLM Conversations

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for information access, content production, and agent-based task execution, but their outputs remain vulnerable to subtle, high-risk hallucinations. To systematically evaluate and advance post-generation hallucination detection, we introduce HaluCheck, a large-scale, bilingual benchmark comprising over 42k instances spanning both factual hallucinations in text and faithfulness hallucinations in agent trajectories. HaluCheck features fine-grained, multi-level annotations for detection, localization, and correction, covering different tasks and perturbation degrees. Experiments on fourteen LLMs reveal that, while models show basic sample-level detection ability, they struggle with fine-grained localization, correction, and agent hallucination detection. Further analysis demonstrates that thinking, web search, and supervised fine-tuning each offer partial improvements, but none fully solve the problem. HaluCheck thus provides a solid basis for benchmarking and diagnosing LLM reliability across text and agent scenarios.
papers.title: From Twisted Facts to Rogue Agents: Can LLMs Reliably Detect Multi-Dimensional Hallucinations?

papers.abstract: We investigate the optimal asymptotic rate $R_q$ of perfect $q$-hash codes, a fundamental extremal problem in combinatorics, information theory, and computer science. Let $B_q=-\log_2(1-q!/q^q)/(q-1)$ denote the classical probabilistic lower bound. We prove that $R_q=B_q$ if and only if $q=2$, establishing an explicit strict improvement for every $q\ge3$ and settling the first assertion of a conjecture of Xing and Yuan (Combinatorica 43 (2023), 347--366). More significantly, we show that, for every $η>0$, $R_q\ge B_q+\exp(-(2+η)q)$ for all sufficiently large integers $q$. This improves the previously known increments of scale $\exp(-3q+O(\ln q))$ by an exponential factor. We also establish a structural limitation of the concatenation method. For pairwise uniform inner codes of subexponential length, the resulting rate bound exceeds $B_q$ by at most $\exp(-3q+o(q))$. Thus, exponentially long inner codes are necessary to achieve the new improvement scale within this framework. Our proofs combine Fourier analysis, high-dimensional simplex codes, additive permutation counts, and entropy bounds for hypergraph matchings. We further strengthen lower bounds from short inner codes and improve several known numerical estimates.
papers.title: The probabilistic bound for perfect hashing is sharp only for binary alphabets

papers.abstract: In two-tier triage a fast model decides most web requests and escalates the rest to a slow tier, so an attack the fast tier closes is never examined. We hold each of seven attack families out of training, recalibration and thresholds, splice the payloads into parameters of real browsing traffic, and compare zero-shot decision models, which return a probability for a typed question, with supervised detectors, a local language model, the OWASP Core Rule Set and an anomaly baseline. Detectors trained on the known families can give much of a held-out family a confident benign verdict: over 10 training runs, ModernBERT gives 37% to 60% of held-out path traversal a probability below 0.05 and escalates only 50% to 81% of it within a 5% benign budget, against nearly all of the same requests when traversal is known. Jev and Clef, two hosted decision models whose budget decisions do not depend on the held-out family, escalate at least 97.6% of every family within the same budget, but their undisclosed training data may contain these public families. Tests on recent exploits need controls for request shape: Jev escalates 37% of benign twins (exploit requests with the attack replaced by legitimate values), and detectors trained on older exploits learn what scanner requests look like. A search guided by Jev's probability gets 43% of held-out attacks past Jev within 300 queries, but Jev's answers vary: asked again, it escalates those requests in 60% of its answers.
papers.title: Escalate or Close: How Fast-Tier Models Handle Held-Out Web Attack Families in Two-Tier Triage

papers.abstract: Information Retrieval (IR) is much more than ad hoc web search: a large portion of the information seeking activities takes place in specific domains, often addressing work-related tasks. Examples are lawyers finding relevant prior cases for a legal case and academic researchers studying the background material for a paper. In Chapter 2 we outline the most common domain-specific tasks, datasets and applications. Domain-specific IR has a number of challenges that make set it apart from simple web search tasks: they often deal with long documents, long queries and long sessions with specific user needs. We discuss these in Chapter 3. We also address issues related to bias and fairness of models. In Chapter 4, we describe the models and methods developed for domain-specific tasks and data, addressing the specific challenges, including user aspects related to domain-specific IR tasks, dealing with queries, user models, and user interactions. We show that many of the methodological advances in domain-specific IR are transferable to other domains and even to open-domain web search. We conclude with the main takeaways and propose research directions for the near future.
papers.title: Domain-specific information retrieval

papers.abstract: Functional clustering identifies coordinated molecular profiles, but repeated numerical covariance optimization can make mixture-model fitting computationally demanding. We develop a fast functional clustering procedure for joint analysis across conditions, combining linear mean profiles on a standardized log niche coordinate with first-order structured antedependence (SAD(1)) covariance. Weighted residual statistics yield closed-form conditional covariance updates under four parameter-sharing specifications, while an innovation representation simplifies likelihood evaluation. In same-R comparisons with numerical optimization of identical conditional objectives, the closed-form solver was 91.5--201.4 times as fast, with objective agreement in all 60 targets. Under matched complete mixture fits, it achieved a 1.87--2.37-fold speedup with identical cluster assignments. Recovery simulations showed higher module classification accuracy and lower mean-curve error than $K$-means and a Gaussian mixture with shared full covariance when the mean structure was correctly specified. SAD(1) provided an additional recovery gain under strong residual correlation, whereas curved-mean controls identified the importance of an appropriate mean family. Applications to single-condition gut microbiota, paired leaf--root microbiota and three-visit human gut multi-omics illustrate the framework across different numbers of conditions. Closed-form covariance estimation makes joint functional clustering substantially faster while retaining the fitted model's likelihood and assignments.
papers.title: Fast Functional Clustering via Closed-Form Covariance Updates

papers.abstract: The explosion of generative AI systems and concerns surrounding their rapidly scaling capabilities has led to an adversarial cycle between increasingly narrow content restrictions ("guardrails") and increasingly sophisticated structured prompting techniques ("jailbreaks"). Technological frameworks surrounding such jailbreaking remain largely focused on the system's output: whether harmful or disallowed content is ultimately produced for the user. However, this approach, which draws largely from classical cybersecurity, does not address the uniquely relational dimension introduced by generative AI: in many cases the user is not just accessing a technology via an exploit, but is in conversation with it as part of the exploit. Here we present an alternative lens which centers the interaction rather than the output. Drawing on interpersonal violence scholarship, we present a novel framework of coercive control categories with a particular focus on aspects which are embodied versus disembodied. We then map how these disembodied coercive control dynamics are structurally embedded in modern AI training paradigms, and how those embeddings are exploited via a particular suite of persona-based jailbreaks. In this lens, we reframe AI safety and alignment as not merely a technical security problem, but as another surface upon which we see enacted the relational dynamics of power and control.
papers.title: "Blind Compliance": Coercive Control in AI Jailbreaking

papers.abstract: A number of results is presented concerning the extreme behaviour of products of linear operators or relations from one Hilbert space ${\mathfrak H}$ to another Hilbert space ${\mathfrak K}$. It is shown that there exists a relation $T$ from ${\mathfrak H}$ to ${\mathfrak K}$ such that the closure of the nonnegative relation $T^*T$ in ${\mathfrak H}$ is not equal to the nonnegative selfadjoint relation $T^*T^{**}$; moreover, this may happen for a singular but also for a regular (i.e., closable) relation $T$. In fact, as an extreme situation the paper contains a construction of a densely defined closable operator $T$, such that ${\rm dom\,}T^*T=\{0\}$, while $T^*T^{**}$ is a densely defined selfadjoint operator. Likewise it is shown that there exist a linear relation $T$ from ${\mathfrak H}$ to ${\mathfrak K}$ and a nonnegative everywhere defined contraction $R$ in ${\mathfrak K}$ for which the product $RT$ is singular and the product $R^{1/2} T$ is regular. Such results illustrate situations that can arise in the Lebesgue type decomposition of linear relations and the Lebesgue type decomposition of semibounded forms.
papers.title: Non-standard behaviour of semibounded forms and their representations

papers.abstract: Building on our earlier work, we present an $L^2$-$L^1$ inequality for radial Fourier eigenfunctions, relating this to the sign uncertainty principle of Bourgain, Clozel and Kahane. We also propose a generalisation of the aforementioned uncertainty principle.
papers.title: Fourier inequalities and sign uncertainty II

papers.abstract: The vast majority of cosmological simulations employ periodic boundary conditions to achieve statistical homogeneity and to mimic the infinite spatial extent of our Universe. In a cubic periodic domain the Green function breaks full rotational invariance and introduces a geometry-induced anisotropy in the gravitational interaction. We quantify how this intrinsic anisotropy affects cosmic structure growth and investigate the extent to which it biases the commonly used large-scale structure and halo-based observables in dark-matter-only simulations. We analyse an ensemble of 498 cosmological dark-matter-only $N$-body simulations in cubic $T^3$ topological manifolds, evolved to $z=0$, spanning box sizes from $L=6.25\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ to $L=100\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ at fixed mass and force resolution. We compare anisotropy-sensitive statistics across the suite, including the matter power spectrum, halo abundance, merger histories, shapes and alignments, and filament orientations. Finite periodic boundaries imprint orientation-dependent signatures aligned with the box geometry. These signatures propagate beyond the largest modes and can induce systematic shifts in both field-level and halo-level statistics. The detectable effects propagate to scales much smaller than the box size. Our results demonstrate that periodic-box anisotropy is a non-negligible source of systematics for small simulation volumes, including those commonly employed in modern hydrodynamical simulations.
papers.title: The box within the Universe: anisotropies in periodic cosmological simulations I. Dark-matter-only simulations

papers.abstract: Let $n \ge 3$, $2 \le α< n$, and $1 < p,r < \infty$ satisfy $p^{-1}+r^{-1}=1+α/n$. We prove uniqueness, up to common translations and dilations, of the normalized nonnegative extremizing pairs for the corresponding Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality. More generally, all positive finite-energy solutions of the Euler-Lagrange system belong to a single symmetry orbit. The proof compares two solutions at different relative scales. Total positivity of order two identifies the second eigenspace of an associated compact self-adjoint operator and forces each nonzero difference to change sign exactly once. The opposite orientations obtained at the two ends of the scale parameter then yield uniqueness. The same method proves radial nondegeneracy modulo dilation. We also establish strong convergence of the normalized alternating Euler-Lagrange iteration from every nonnegative, radially nonincreasing initial datum to a fixed extremizing pair, without rescaling the iterates. Square-root mass variables reduce the exclusion of several concentration profiles to a static spectral estimate and an energy-increment argument. The analysis includes sublinear exponents and the logarithmic borderline decay regimes.
papers.title: Uniqueness of Extremizers and Convergence of the Euler-Lagrange Iteration for the Critical Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev Inequality

papers.abstract: We revisit the impact of electroweak (EW) radiative corrections on the kinematic distributions of charged leptons in neutrino-induced charged-current (CC) deep inelastic scattering (DIS). These corrections are particularly relevant for observables sensitive to collinear photon radiation, such as the energy spectrum of high-energy muons detected in neutrino telescopes. To study these effects, we implement full next-to-leading order (NLO) EW corrections to CC DIS in a flexible Monte Carlo framework, supplemented with higher-order logarithmically enhanced final-state QED radiation and coherent scattering contributions. We compare our results to exclusive NLO QCD plus parton shower (PS) predictions obtained with an existing $\texttt{POWHEG-BOX}$ event generator, examining different PS models and settings. Based on this comparison, we provide recommendations for the use of the $\texttt{POWHEG-BOX}$ event generator in experimental analyses. We further assess the impact of radiative corrections on the correlation between the observed muon energy and the incoming neutrino energy, and on the mean inelasticity averaged over a realistic neutrino flux. These corrections can exceed $10\%$, and above about $10^4\,{\rm GeV}$ they receive sizeable contributions from photon-initiated and coherent $W$-boson production, which are not included in the event generator.
papers.title: DIS-secting the universe with high-energy neutrinos

papers.abstract: Over the past few years, several quantum software stacks (QSS) have been developed in response to rapid hardware advances in quantum computing. A QSS includes a quantum programming language, an optimizing compiler that translates a quantum algorithm written in a high-level language into quantum gate instructions, a quantum simulator that emulates these instructions on a classical device, and a software controller that sends analog signals to a very expensive quantum hardware based on quantum circuits. In comparison to traditional compilers and architecture simulators, QSSes are difficult to tests due to the probabilistic nature of results, the lack of clear hardware specifications, and quantum programming complexity. This work devises a novel differential testing approach for QSSes, named QDIFF with three major innovations: (1) We generate input programs to be tested via semantics-preserving, source to source transformation to explore program variants. (2) We speed up differential testing by filtering out quantum circuits that are not worthwhile to execute on quantum hardware by analyzing static characteristics such as a circuit depth, 2 qubit gate operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time. (3) We design an extensible equivalence checking mechanism via distribution comparison functions such as Kolmogorov Smirnov test and cross entropy
papers.title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks

papers.abstract: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.
papers.title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis

papers.abstract: The rapid democratization of biotechnology, enhanced by large language models (LLMs) and agentic software, is eroding longstanding barriers that have limited biosynthesis planning to experts. We present BioBulbul, an agentic system that couples LLMs with open-source biodesign tools for retrobiosynthesis, enzyme selection, gene cluster design, and DNA assembly planning. Using simple natural language prompts, BioBulbul autonomously generates plausible biosynthesis pathways and corresponding gene cluster sequences for several known small molecule toxins, demonstrating that non-experts could feasibly access them using an agentic system. Our red-teaming experiments confirm the technical viability of LLM-driven toxin biosynthesis while highlighting three principal barriers: scarcity of open-source biodesign tools, limited structured enzymatic reaction data, and the complexity of many small molecule toxin pathways. We argue that these barriers are likely to diminish within a decade, expanding the biological threat landscape. To mitigate emerging risks, we recommend expanding DNA synthesis screening to include chokepoint enzymes, extending chemical supplier controls to precursor compounds, establishing continuous AI-assisted threat surveillance pipelines, and developing robust LLM guardrails. Coordinated investment across government, industry, and AI developers is essential to safeguard against the misuse of agentic biosynthesis planning.
papers.title: Building Barricades: Red-Teaming Agentic Biosynthesis Planning

papers.abstract: Optical Network Digital Twins (ONDTs) are emerging as a key framework for representing, synchronizing, and utilizing the physical state of optical networks for quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, optimization, and intelligent operation. This survey provides a comprehensive view of ONDTs, spanning digital coherent transmission and physical-layer observability to intelligent network operations. We systematically organize ONDT technologies from ecosystem, functional, control, and implementation architecture perspectives and review the enabling technologies required to construct, synchronize, and utilize digital representations of physical optical networks. As a unifying framework to describe both ONDT design and validation, we introduce a categorization based on the following figures of merit: Fidelity, Dynamicity, and Deployability (FDD). In particular, we emphasize fit-for-purpose Fidelity, where modeling effort focuses on the physical effects of components rather than solely maximizing model accuracy, favoring scalability and generalizability. Furthermore, experimental and field validations are examined to evaluate the practical applicability of ONDT technologies. We further examine experimental and field validations, from physics-based QoT estimation and measurement-informed model refinement to field synchronization, service provisioning, multi-domain observability, and infrastructure characterization. Finally, we discuss the complementary roles of ONDTs and AI agents toward autonomous optical networks and identify key research directions for practical deployment.
papers.title: Optical Network Digital Twin: From Digital Coherent Transmission to Intelligent Network Operations

papers.abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vecτ$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at https://github.com/yufeixue-ai/ProQuant/.
papers.title: ProQuant: Progressive Quantization-aware Training for Edge MLLMs
