We reformulate the ECPM as an interconnected dynamical system: a stochastic process describing a network of locally interacting tumor cells coupled to a jump-linear system describing ECM evolution. By exploiting the sparse energy structure of the model, we characterize asymptotic ECM behavior, transition probabilities with uniform bounds, and global system convergence. In one-dimensional settings, we derive closed-form expressions for invasion time probabilities, revealing how mean invasion time depends on local ECM gradients, number of cells and their tendency to maintain a target volume. Numerical simulations validate theoretical predictions, establishing a principled foundation for analyzing haptotaxis-driven invasion in Potts-based models.
papers.title: System-Theoretic Analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models for Tumor Invasion

papers.abstract: Teleoperating a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) in complex underwater environments presents unique challenges. Dynamic, three dimensional obstacles and unseen water currents pose real risks to expensive robotic hardware in environments in which recovery can be next to impossible. This paper explores the cognitive effects of haptic feedback to improve vehicle safety in such environments. An in-water study is analysed with a ROV exposed to controlled cross-currents, with environmental information presented via a soft and vibrating haptic touchpad. Results demonstrate that while encountering an unseen cross-current significantly increases an operator's physical and temporal demand, the introduction of haptic feedback mitigates these factors and improves self-assessed performance. Interestingly, the haptic condition also produced the highest levels of mental demand and operator frustration. Despite this increased mental workload, operators drove the ROV significantly faster when receiving haptic cues compared to the current-only condition, indicating a higher level of user confidence. Ultimately, these findings suggest that while haptic feedback may initially require more cognitive processing to interpret unseen hazards, it successfully enhances operator awareness and promotes more confident navigation in hazardous environments.
papers.title: Cognitive and Behavioural Effects of Haptic Feedback for ROV Teleoperation in Hazardous Environments

papers.abstract: Post-hoc out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is mature on far-OOD yet remains weak on near-OOD. These two settings differ in their use of class-characteristic feature directions: far-OOD inputs largely fail to activate those of their predicted class, whereas near-OOD inputs activate them much as in-distribution samples do. Because the axis separating far-OOD leaves near-OOD almost indistinguishable from ID, a score optimized for one setting is misaligned with the other; where a detector already saturates far-OOD, added near-OOD sensitivity is bought partly against it. This divergence motivates a targeted near-OOD signal designed to complement existing scores. We propose PLUS (Per-class Low-dimensional sUbspace Signal). For each class, PLUS selects the $m$ most class-active neurons from a sparse autoencoder, orthonormalizes the corresponding decoder directions to form a low-dimensional subspace, and scores an input by its per-class whitened squared Mahalanobis distance $z$ within the subspace of its predicted class. Designed as a dedicated complement rather than a standalone detector, the signal $z$ is fused additively with any calibrated base score at a single, fixed weight. This weight is a single global constant: no value is adjusted per backbone, per OOD dataset, or per deployment, and all calibration statistics are estimated from ID validation data alone. When applied to 18 existing detectors spanning diverse method families, $z$ consistently improves near-OOD AUROC in all 126 detector--backbone combinations. Far-OOD performance is broadly maintained or improved, with only marginal declines where the base score is near-optimal, making $z$ a robust, detector-agnostic complement across backbones.
papers.title: Don't Replace, Complement: A Detector-Agnostic Subspace Signal for Near-OOD Detection

papers.abstract: We introduce LifeVal, a benchmark evaluating AI model performance on personalized agentic consumer tasks. LifeVal covers the most valuable life tasks that a personalized digital superassistant could automate, representing over 1.7 trillion US dollars in annual willingness-to-pay across 148 consumer task categories (e.g., managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, finding childcare). To construct our activity distribution, we conducted a new survey of willingness-to-pay for a digital superassistant across a demographically representative sample of over 3,800 consumers, cross-referencing our results against the American Time Use Survey (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) and the Multinational Time Use Study (Fisher et al., 2025). For the most valuable consumer activities, we recruited task creators to create AI evaluation tasks personalized using real ChatGPT conversations and memories, reference files, and personal context. Task creators had to pass our expertise threshold (including personally completing the task multiple times and seeing the results through in their real lives for over a year) and also write a rubric, ensuring that our evaluation measured the best personalized completion for that task. All tasks had to pass at least three rounds of human quality-control before acceptance into our final evaluation sets.
papers.title: LifeVal: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Personalized Agentic Consumer Tasks

papers.abstract: A unified approach for studying the linear eigenvalue statistics (LES) of generalized patterned random matrices was developed in Kumar, Maurya, Saha (2026). In this paper, as a continuation, we develop a unified method for studying the time-dependent LES of generalized patterned random matrices with independent process entries such as Brownian motion and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. We prove that if the limiting moment sequence of the LES of the generalized patterned random matrix with independent standard Gaussian entries is M-determinate, then under some minimal assumption on the link function, the time-dependent LES converges to a deterministic real-valued process.
papers.title: A unified approach to fluctuations of LES of time-dependent generalized patterned random matrices

papers.abstract: Online reasoning video segmentation (Online RVS) requires a model to segment query-referred objects as a video streams in, using only the frames observed so far. Existing formulations largely assume a fixed target set throughout the video, overlooking a fundamental property of streaming reasoning: as new events occur, the objects that satisfy a query may change over time. To address this, we propose a new task, Generalized Reasoning Video Segmentation (GRVS), where the target set depends on query-relevant events accumulated over the observed video history. As new evidence accumulates, the target set can evolve from empty to one or multiple objects, requiring a model to continuously maintain target validity while localizing the valid objects currently in view. To evaluate GRVS, we build Isekai, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 videos and 197 queries across 11 temporal query families, with 12,569 scoring points whose target sets are causally annotated over time. We further propose Sekai, an online framework with two complementary components: an Event Memory Reasoner (EMR) that maintains query-relevant events and evolving target states in structured memory, and a Memory-Grounded Decoder (MGD) that identifies valid targets from this memory and localizes them in the current frame. Experiments show that Sekai significantly outperforms existing online RVS methods, achieving 50.33 J&F and improving over the strongest baseline by 3.2 points. Code, example annotations, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zenastangbi/Sekai.
papers.title: Sekai: Incremental Event Memory for Generalized Reasoning Video Segmentation

papers.abstract: The online $k$-taxi problem is a natural generalization of the $k$-server problem: $k$ taxis must serve a sequence of requests in a metric space. Each request is a pair of points $(r,s)$, and the algorithm serves the request by first moving a taxi to $r$ (to pick up a passenger) and then to $s$ (to drop off the passenger). The cost is the total distance traveled by the taxis without a passenger. Previous bounds for general $k$ all depended on the number of points $n$ or the aspect ratio $Δ$ of the metric space, both of which can be infinite on general metrics, and competitive algorithms were previously known on general metrics only for $k \le 3$. In this work, we give a $9^{k-1}$-competitive randomized algorithm against adaptive online adversaries and, as a corollary, an $81^{k-1}$-competitive deterministic algorithm for the online $k$-taxi problem.
papers.title: The Online $k$-Taxi Problem Is Competitive on All Metrics

papers.abstract: Prompt-gamma (PG) imaging is a promising approach for in vivo verification in proton therapy, but existing methods are primarily limited to reconstructing the PG emission profile, which provides only indirect information on proton transport. In this work, we introduce Prompt-Gamma Time Imaging (PGTI), an iterative reconstruction method based on the PG Timing (PGT) technique that jointly estimates the PG emission distribution and the proton velocity profile from Time-Of-Flight (TOF) measurements acquired with multiple detector modules. Unlike the PG distribution, the proton velocity is directly related to the stopping power and therefore provides access to both the tissue composition traversed by the beam and a first-order estimation of the delivered dose. The method was validated using experimental data acquired with the eight-module TIARA prototype previously developed by our collaboration. The anthropomorphic RANDO head phantom was irradiated with 100 MeV protons in two anatomical configurations representative of treatment planning and delivery, providing the first demonstration of PGTI under realistic conditions. In this example, the reconstructed material sequence agreed with the reference CT; despite ten bins presenting a misclassified material, the reconstructed proton range only differed from the expected value by approximately 1 mm. These results validate both the proposed PGTI framework and the use of the TIARA detector system in a pseudo-clinical environment, extending PG imaging beyond conventional range verification.
papers.title: Experimental Assessment of Prompt Gamma Time Imaging in Complex Anatomy

papers.abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents translate model outputs into consequential actions, turning indirect prompt injection into an execution-security problem. Existing defenses constrain tool calls, trajectories, or information flows, but often leave action semantics, state dependencies, and evidence relations implicit, limiting generalization across heterogeneous tools and complicating safe updates. We present \ours{}, a dynamic ontology-guided governance framework. \ours{} grounds heterogeneous calls in a shared semantic representation and combines an executable ontology with episode-level task state to derive deterministic ready, waiting, and forbidden decisions. A waiting decision identifies an unmet but recoverable obligation, enabling bounded replanning without expanding the agent's authorization boundary. \ours{} evolves its ontology offline from verified training executions. An offline LLM proposes instance-independent action--state axioms, which are accepted only if they address ontology errors exposed by training failures, preserve logical consistency and protected entailments, and pass held-out validation before the ontology is frozen. We evaluate \ours{} on AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn under benign and indirect prompt-injection settings. \ours{} achieves a 0\% attack success rate (ASR) across all three benchmarks while improving task utility under attack compared with existing baselines. These results show that explicit semantic governance can strengthen execution security without indiscriminate blocking.
papers.title: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is commonly evaluated with standard post-deletion metrics that compare an unlearned model to one retrained on the remaining data. Such snapshot evaluations can conceal consequential differences in the features the two models encode. We prove that if an unlearned and a retrained model agree on their outputs but encode different features, a single gradient step on their prediction heads can break this agreement. We further show that deleting an arbitrarily small fraction of the data can cause retraining to select qualitatively different features, so matching retraining can require learning features that the full model never had. We then introduce a measure of feature recovery that separates missing from extraneous features. Across eight unlearning methods, models that perform well on standard metrics often fail to recover the retrained features. This mismatch predicts deviations from retraining under subsequent relearning and downstream adaptation, and directly correcting it systematically reduces these deviations.
papers.title: Do unlearning algorithms learn the right features?

papers.abstract: The National Laboratory Accelerator Study Group (NLASG) was established to assess the accelerator research and development required to advance a future high-energy Muon Collider, with particular emphasis on opportunities for coordinated contributions from U.S. national laboratories. This report examines the principal accelerator subsystems, their technical maturity, and the critical challenges that must be addressed before proceeding to a technical design. Topics include the proton driver, target and capture system, muon cooling, acceleration, collider ring, and machine-detector interface. The study identifies priority R&D activities, evaluates opportunities to leverage existing laboratory capabilities and accelerator infrastructure, and outlines a staged approach to technology demonstrations and integrated system validation. Particular emphasis is placed on developing a coordinated national research strategy that complements international efforts and establishes a technically credible path toward a future Muon Collider.
papers.title: Report of the National Lab Accelerator Study Group for a Muon Collider

papers.abstract: We study AdS form factors describing closed strings scattering off D-branes. Assuming that these form factors admit worldsheet integral representations in terms of multiple polylogarithms, we determine their leading curvature corrections around the flat-space limit by matching their pole structure to CFT data. We focus on two examples of defects in 4d $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM: a $\frac{1}{2}$-BPS 't Hooft loop, dual to a D1 brane, and a pair of giant gravitons, dual to a D3 brane. For the 't Hooft loop, the worldsheet bootstrap completely fixes the form factor, and the result passes nontrivial checks from supersymmetric localization. For the giant gravitons, the bootstrap initially leaves five free coefficients, one of which can be fixed using localization. Remarkably, imposing instead that no new operators appear in the defect channel at this order fixes all five coefficients and reproduces the localization constraint. Under this additional assumption, we therefore obtain a unique D3-brane form factor, with supersymmetric localization providing an independent check.
papers.title: Form Factors in AdS from the Worldsheet

papers.abstract: We study the Gromov-Hausdorff stability of round spheres under perturbations of Perelman's nu-entropy. We show that in dimension two almost maximal entropy, together with an area normalisation, implies Gromov-Hausdorff closeness to the round two-sphere. In contrast, in dimensions at least three, we construct smooth metrics on the sphere whose entropies converge to that of the round sphere, but which remain a definite Gromov-Hausdorff distance away from it. These metrics can be chosen conformal and uniformly bi-Lipschitz equivalent to the round metric, with the same volume as the round sphere. Finally, in dimension three, we contrast this Gromov-Hausdorff instability with a dynamical stability result: metrics with nu-entropy above that of the round shrinking cylinder converge exponentially fast to round metrics under the volume-normalised Ricci flow.
papers.title: Perelman's entropy and Gromov-Hausdorff versus dynamical stability of round spheres

papers.abstract: We study the classical apple-tasting setting, a partial feedback model in which the learner observes the true label only when it predicts $1$. A combinatorial characterization for the rates of this problem in the online adversarial setting has been studied by Raman et al. (2024). We study the self-directed setting, in which the learner can adaptively choose the order of the points it predicts on. In the realizable setting, we establish a tetrachotomy on the expected minimax number of mistakes made by any learner. Depending on the VC dimension, the $\emptyset$-centered star number, and the self-directed dimension, we show that the rates could possibly be $Θ(1)$, $O(\log n) \cap ω(1)$, $\tilde Θ(\sqrt{n})$, or $Θ(n)$. In the agnostic setting, the minimax regret is $\tilde Θ(\sqrt{n})$ or $Θ(n)$, depending on the VC dimension.
papers.title: Self-Directed Apple Tasting

papers.abstract: We report a multi-cross micro-Hall sensor fabricated from an MBE-grown GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure for high-sensitivity magnetometry. The device enables dc magnetization measurements at temperatures down to $\sim$15~mK and in dc magnetic fields up to 30 T. Bulk samples with dimensions ranging from 100~$μ$m to 1~mm can be measured with a resolution better than 1$~μ$T with a 1~$μ$A excitation at 13.77 Hz. Test-of-performance measurements were carried out by probing the field-dependent magnetization plateaus of the triangular-lattice quantum magnet K$_{2}$Co$_{2}$(SeO$_{3}$)$_{3}$ at 20~mK, the antiferromagnetic transition of K${_3}$GdTe${_2}$O${_9}$ near 220 mK via temperature-dependent magnetization, and the quantum oscillations in a ruthenium single crystal. A simple and reliable sample-mounting setup that ensures reproducible magnetic measurements is provided.
papers.title: Millikelvin magnetometry up to 30~T using a multi-cross micro-Hall sensor

papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the generalized Brézin--Gross--Witten model using its BKP integrability. By virtue of the formula for connected $n$-point functions of tau-functions of the BKP hierarchy obtained by Wang and the first-named author, we prove that the normalized generalized BGW correlators are strictly concave for fixed genus and fixed total degree. As applications, we establish the strict Schur-concavity and derive upper and lower bounds for these correlators. We also prove the strict monotonicity of normalized ordinary BGW correlators, which resolves a conjecture by Guo--Norbury--Yang--Zagier.
papers.title: Concavity of Normalized Generalized Brézin--Gross--Witten Correlators and Its Applications

papers.abstract: Infrastructure security does not establish whether an LLM agent selected an allowed tool, grounded its answer in tool output, or followed a required workflow. AgentTrustCI is a Java/JUnit 5 framework that expresses these application-layer expectations as policy, grounding, and trajectory checks over recorded traces. A deterministic replay implementation supports repeatable build-time tests; a judge interface provides an extension point for optional semantic evaluation. On 55 synthetic cases spanning seven enterprise domains, the full pipeline correctly classifies all 30 injected faults and 25 passing controls, including ten non-trivial controls, and misses none of 12 designated critical cases. Each single-layer configuration correctly classifies 35 cases because the corpus deliberately isolates ten faults per layer. A grounded answer obtained through a disallowed sequence illustrates the additional coverage of trajectory checks. Repeated measurements quantify validator execution separately from process startup and reporting. These results establish coverage of the authored regression suite, not production accuracy. We describe a production-trace validation protocol, optional LLM-judge integration, and maintenance of expectations as workflows evolve. The contribution is a practical pattern for expressing behavioral contracts within an existing Java release pipeline.
papers.title: AgentTrustCI: Build-Time Policy, Grounding, and Trajectory Tests for Java LLM Agents

papers.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors capture multiple aspects of physical interaction within a single image stream, including contact appearance, geometry, indentation depth, and tangential deformation. However, existing visuo-tactile policies often directly process tactile observations as images, making it difficult to determine which physical cues contribute to policy learning. This paper presents a controlled real-robot study that compares physically interpretable tactile signals using the LeRobot platform, enhanced with our visuo-tactile perception system. From the same tactile stream, we derive tactile RGB images, normal/depth maps, and marker-flow fields, representing contact appearance, geometry, and tangential deformation, respectively. Using identical task demonstrations and the same policy backbone, we evaluate the individual and combined contributions of these tactile cues. We further compare tactile encoders and visuo-tactile fusion strategies. Evaluation across 720 real-robot trials yields four key findings: (1) tactile perception substantially improves the overall success rate from 57.8% to 78.9%, although its contribution varies across task stages; (2) marker flow is the most effective individual cue, achieving a success rate of 74.4% and playing a particularly important role in regulating established contact; (3) cue-factorized encoding consistently improves performance, highlighting that different physical cues require tailored processing techniques; and (4) although the effectiveness of tactile fusion is task-dependent, cross-attention offers a lightweight solution with performance comparable to that of pretrained tactile encoders.
papers.title: Which Physical Tactile Cues Matter for Contact-Rich Imitation Learning? A Controlled Real-Robot Study

papers.abstract: The goal of these notes is to provide a unified and rigorous introduction to robust sequential decision-making. We offer a self-contained introduction to the main results in the field. After a concise introduction to MDPs we introduce robust MDPs with general uncertainty sets, before focusing on rectangular models of uncertainty. We make a significant effort to show connections between robust MDPs and several other popular models for sequential decision-making: MDPs with uncertain rewards, Multi-Objective MDPs and Pareto optimality, MDPs with time-varying uncertain parameters, non-rectangular robust MDPs, stochastic games, distributionally robust MDPs, and risk-averse MDPs. Having all these results in one place, within a single unifying formalism, will hopefully be useful for researchers who want to start working on this topic. The exposition combines operator and fixed point approaches, convex optimization (more specifically, duality in saddle-point problems), and game-theoretic arguments. The latter identifies robust MDPs with a certain type of two-player game; this helps build useful intuition, especially when constructing counterexamples.
papers.title: Robust Markov Decision Processes: An Introduction Using Convex Optimization and Game Theory

papers.abstract: $XV$ ($X$ is Si, Ge, Sn, or Pb, and $V$ is the carbon vacancy) color centers are promising platforms for quantum computing and quantum information science due to their favorable optical and spin properties. They are commonly fabricated by ion implantation, which inevitably introduces vacancies and carbon self-interstitials (C$_i$) into the lattice. However, the microscopic formation mechanism remains unclear, limiting the yield and stability of $XV$ centers. Here, first-principles calculations are conducted to systematically investigate the roles of $V$ and C$_i$ in $XV$ formation. We find that $XV$ formation is energetically favorable, with large binding energies and low diffusion barriers. Nevertheless, $XV$ readily captures C$_i$ to form substitutional defect $X_s$, or captures an additional $V$ to form the complex $XV_2$. Charge transition levels show that oppositely charged reactants never meet in these reactions, and that Coulomb repulsion blocks them only when both reactants carry charges of the same sign, which for the capture of C$_i$ requires strongly n- or p-type conditions. These competing defect reactions destabilize the split-vacancy configuration and could account for the low formation yield of $XV$ centers, so that they appear at concentrations well below those expected from the implanted dose. Our results elucidate the microscopic origin of this intrinsic instability and suggest that Fermi-level control may suppress defect conversions and stabilize the split-vacancy configuration.
papers.title: First-principles study of the formation of Group-IV--vacancy color centers in diamond

papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time $(\varepsilon, δ)$-edge-differentially private algorithm that releases a synthetic graph approximately preserving all cut values of a nonnegative weighted input graph $G$. Our algorithm outputs a nonnegative weighted graph $H$ such that, with probability at least $1-β$, simultaneously for all $S\subseteq V$, \[ \left|w_G(S,V\setminus S)-w_H(S,V\setminus S)\right| \leq γw_G(S,V\setminus S) + O\left(\frac{n}{γ\varepsilon} \log^7 \frac{n}{δβγ\varepsilon}\right). \] For fixed $γ, \varepsilon$ and $δ= β= n^{-10}$, the additive error is $n \operatorname{polylog} n$, improving upon the previous efficient bound of $n^{13/12 + o(1)}$. Furthermore, we establish an $Ω(n/γ\varepsilon)$ lower bound for the relevant parameter regime, showing that our result is tight up to polylogarithmic factors. Our algorithm uses a log-det-regularized SDP to generate fractional queries for multiplicative-weights updates and certify accuracy for all cuts. The privacy analysis charges privacy loss only fractionally per mechanism call, based on the amount of mass on edge coordinates retired from subsequent iterations. Our synthetic graph release yields improved error bounds for several downstream tasks in private graph analysis including correlation clustering, Max-Cut, Max-$k$-Cut, constrained cut problems and hierarchical clustering. Most notably, for unweighted complete-graph correlation clustering, we achieve the optimal $\widetilde O(n)$ additive error while reducing the best previously known approximation ratio for this additive error from several thousand to $1.387$. We also provide a formalization of our results in Lean.
papers.title: Polynomial-Time Differentially Private Synthetic Graph Release with Nearly-Linear Additive Error

papers.abstract: We consider $N$ bosons in two dimensions interacting via point interactions, modeled by the TMS Hamiltonian. We prove that their ground state energy has the asymptotic behavior $-e^{C N }$ for large $N$, for an explicit constant $C$ related to the sharp constant in the Ladyzhenskaya-Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. Such asymptotic behavior was predicted in the physics literature, based on a variant of the mean-field approximation.
papers.title: Large particle number asymptotics for point-interacting bosons in the plane

papers.abstract: Quantum steering-assisted metrology allows a trusted party (Bob) to improve local phase estimation by exploiting classical information communicated by an untrusted party (Alice). In realistic scenarios, however, the channel is subject to noise that degrades steerability and suppresses the associated metrological advantage. Here, we demonstrate that stochastic pre- and post-filtering operations can revive the violation of the metrological steering inequality (MSI) in phase-covariant amplitude-damping channels where it is initially absent, thereby activating a hidden metrological steerability and restoring their usefulness for quantum metrology. Specifically, the critical damping parameter beyond which the MSI violation is suppressed is raised from $γ_c \approx 0.5$ to $γ_c \approx 0.75$ for the largest filter strength considered. We verify this in a photonic experiment, where polarization qubits carrying the encoded phase are transmitted through an amplitude-damping channel implemented with a two-path Sagnac interferometer, and the stochastic operations are realized with glass plates at the Brewster angle. By tuning the filter strength and scanning the damping parameter over its full range, we observe the revival of the MSI violation, obtained at the cost of a reduced success probability inherent to the stochastic nature of the filtering operations. Our results establish that metrological utility and steerability can be activated through stochastic operations even when these properties are absent in the original noisy channel, extending filtering-based activation from witnesses of nonclassicality to a certified and operationally quantified metrological advantage.
papers.title: Experimental activation of hidden metrological steerability in quantum channels via stochastic filtering

papers.abstract: We demonstrate the efficacy of crowd-sourced refinement of strong gravitational lens candidate samples by citizen scientists. Binary (lens/non-lens) classification by citizen scientists has been conducted previously, and here we extend such categorisation into `definite', `probable', `possible', and `non-lenses'. This grading is a required stage ahead of any strong lens sample publication and is usually carried out by (small) teams of researchers. We compare the responses of the volunteers to those of strong lens researchers and discuss the optimal strategy for lens classification and grading in future strong lens searches. Volunteers are found to be able to correctly identify systems of each grade, and their responses can be calibrated to be comparable to those of researchers. Grade posteriors, defined as the probability that a strong lens system classified by the volunteers is a certain grade, converge most rapidly for non-lens systems. We find that one researcher classification is equivalent to only 1.9 volunteer classifications when grading such systems. There is significant disagreement in the grading of intermediate-grade lens candidates amongst both volunteers and researchers. Moving towards calibrated lens probabilities for future lens searches would help to account for such subjectivity. If the Q1 lens search was rerun with volunteers performing lens grading (and corresponding calibration), a completeness of 79% for Grades A+B (corresponding to definite + probable lenses respectively) could be achieved with 41% purity prior to researcher inspection - this would correspond to an expected 12500 true lenses (i.e. excluding contaminants) in Euclid DR1.
papers.title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). Refining the strong lens sample with Space Warps crowd-sourced science

papers.abstract: Optical work exchanged between light and time-varying matter underlies a wide range of emerging photonic technologies, yet a general geometric theory describing its generation and control has been lacking. Here we establish such a theory for coherent electromagnetic scattering. We show that the net optical work accumulated during an adiabatic modulation cycle is a geometric quantity determined by the Berry curvature of the outgoing field in parameter space. Nonzero optical work can thus be generated by cyclically modulating two or more independent system parameters. In contrast to conventional adiabatic pumping between incoherent reservoirs, optical work pumping vanishes under maximally mixed illumination. Greater illumination coherence increases the maximum work attainable through wavefront shaping. For fully coherent illumination, we derive the optimal incident wavefront and modulation trajectory that maximize the optical work per cycle. Our framework unifies time-varying photonics, optomechanics, and geometric transport within a common scattering formalism.
papers.title: Geometric Pumping of Optical Work in Coherent Wave Scattering

papers.abstract: Operator inference (OpInf) provides a nonintrusive framework for learning projection-based reduced-order models directly from data, but its standard formulations do not explicitly account for the fact that boundary actuation changes the admissible solution space of a PDE. This paper develops and evaluates a boundary-consistent, lifting-based OpInf formulation for nonlinear PDEs with time-varying inhomogeneous boundary conditions. The proposed approach decomposes the state into a known lifting component that satisfies the prescribed boundary conditions and a homogeneous component represented in a POD basis. Substituting this decomposition into the governing dynamics reveals a boundary-consistent reduced model structure in which the learned dynamics includes bilinear state-input and quadratic input-input interactions for quadratically nonlinear PDEs. The resulting operators are inferred from data, preserving the nonintrusive character of OpInf while guaranteeing boundary condition satisfaction by construction. Numerical experiments on boundary-actuated heat, Burgers, and lid-driven cavity problems show that the lifted formulation improves boundary compliance and can enhance prediction accuracy, solver stability, and computational efficiency, although these gains vary across problems and reduced model dimensions. Overall, this study establishes lifting as a principled extension of OpInf for boundary-actuated PDEs, clarifies when and how this formulation improves performance, and indicates that standard OpInf can remain an effective alternative in certain regimes.
papers.title: To lift or not to lift: Operator inference for nonlinear PDEs with boundary control

papers.abstract: Automatic cardiac motion tracking from cine cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is essential for quantifying myocardial motion abnormalities associated with cardiovascular disease. Existing methods fall into two groups: those that represent motion without anatomical correspondence across subjects and therefore limit inter-subject motion assessment; and those that represent motion with globally corresponding points, which typically require a time-consuming and error-prone semi-automatic step to fit a cardiac atlas to the subject space. To address these limitations, this study proposes CardioDrift, a fully automatic, atlas-based probabilistic framework that represents subject-specific cardiac motion on a 3D atlas mesh with globally corresponding points. The Coherent Point Drift (CPD) formulation is generalised to jointly register the atlas surfaces of multiple cardiac regions to the anatomically corresponding contours extracted from cine CMR segmentation maps throughout the cardiac cycle. Slice-shift correction is embedded in the same probabilistic model, estimating slice-wise translations that suppress the misalignment artefact limiting atlas-fitting accuracy. Evaluation on 1301 randomly selected UK Biobank subjects and the M&M dataset, CardioDrift attains Dice similarity coefficients (DSCs) of $92.23\pm8.70\%$, $82.11\pm7.56\%$, and $88.69\pm4.13\%$ for the left ventricle (LV), myocardium (Myo), and right ventricle (RV), exceeding the strongest baseline on every distance and overlap metric of both datasets.
papers.title: CardioDrift: Automatic Cardiac Motion Tracking on a 3D Atlas Mesh via Shape-aware Coherent Point Drift with Slice Shift Correction

papers.abstract: Advances in modern electronics demand the dissipation of heat fluxes approaching 1000 W cm$^{-2}$, which drives an urgent need for materials with thermal conductivity ($κ$) exceeding 1000 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. Here, by solving the Boltzmann transport equation considering both three- and four-phonon interactions, we observe that isotopically pure cubic germanium carbide (GeC) exhibits a remarkable $κ$ of 1018 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ at room temperature, which is further corroborated by state-of-the-art machine-learning molecular dynamics simulations. Two unique mechanisms underlie this anomalously high $κ$: a remarkably strong isotopic enhancement effect (289%) and a surprisingly modest suppression due to four-phonon scattering (22%)-despite the presence of a wide acoustic-optical phonon gap. Moreover, we find that GeC defies the conventional Leibfried-Schlomann formula and exhibits a non-monotonic variation of $κ$ with external hydrostatic pressure at elevated temperatures. Our findings establish isotope-enriched GeC as a material of ultrahigh $κ$ and an ideal platform for exploring exotic phonon physics.
papers.title: Anomalous thermal transport in isotope-enriched germanium carbide

papers.abstract: Search-augmented reasoning systems can reach correct answers while making errors in intermediate steps. Reliable auditing must check whether evidence $D$ covers the question $Q$, reasoning $T$ addresses $Q$, and $T$ is grounded in $D$. We introduce GraphRail, which represents requirements, evidence, and reasoning as structured claims and compares them without a generative judge or gold answer. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three reasoning frameworks, GraphRail improves error recall over generative verifiers while remaining stable under stochastic extraction. Its diagnoses can also guide online reasoning, providing a traceable way to detect and correct intermediate errors.
papers.title: Where Search Agents Go Off the Rails: Graph-Grounded Step-Level Verification

papers.abstract: API distillation campaigns try to hide model-stealing traffic by splitting requests across thousands of load-balanced accounts, which standard content classifiers often miss. However, request timestamps, specifically arrival time and stream completion time, reveal the underlying dispatching strategy, such as round-robin counters or key-shuffling pools. Using a 20 percent seed set, this timing analysis can forensically rank the remaining accounts of a campaign with 0.92 to 1.00 AUC within 20 minutes, even across thousands of real production accounts. While adaptive attackers struggle to hide rotating dispatchers using jitter, pinning keys successfully evades detection, though it can severely throttle throughput when quotas bind. Ultimately, timing exposes shared infrastructure patterns even when content filters fail.
papers.title: Fingerprinting the Dispatchers behind Distributed Model Extraction

papers.abstract: People increasingly draft a social media post themselves and then let an AI model refine it (AI-altered), a common but understudied middle case between fully human-written and fully AI-generated content. We ask whether this changes how trustworthy and transparent readers perceive the post to be, and whether they can even tell. We first analyze real ChatGPT conversations (WildChat) to find how people actually alter social media posts, which we use to design realistic alteration prompts. We then run a pre-registered, within-subjects online experiment (n=214) in which participants rate unlabeled human-written and AI-altered LinkedIn-style posts for perceived trustworthiness and transparency, and separately judge whether each post was AI-altered. We find that AI-alteration itself has no detectable effect on either perceived trustworthiness or transparency (both estimates near zero, not significant). At the same time, readers did not reliably detect AI-alteration (49\% accuracy, near chance) and defaulted to assuming human authorship when unsure. However, our analysis shows significant differences in transparency and trustworthiness ratings across the specific post, the AI model, as well as the prompt used to alter it. For instance, more detailed prompts raise both perceived trustworthiness and transparency but also make the alteration more detectable. Surprisingly, the prompt that shifted ratings most also asked the model to add one new idea absent from the original post: readers nonetheless rated this AI-invented, unverifiable content as more trustworthy and transparent.
papers.title: Perceived Trust and Transparency in AI-Altered vs. Human-Written LinkedIn Posts

papers.abstract: We construct exact static and spherically symmetric charged solutions in bumblebee gravity minimally coupled to Born--Infeld electrodynamics, taking into account a spacelike vector norm and a vanishing cosmological constant. An independently varied Lagrange multiplier enforces the norm constraint and acquires a radial profile determined by the transverse electromagnetic pressure. The solutions include purely radial configurations and configurations with constant or varying temporal amplitudes. At $ξ=κ/2$, the varying temporal amplitude introduces an independent bumblebee field strength while preserving the metric of the constant temporal configuration. Moreover, the electric field remains bounded, and the temporal configurations admit smooth extensions across a simple future horizon under explicit regularity conditions. We derive the photon sphere and shadow radii for both metric and nonlinear electromagnetic propagation. The leading nonlinear corrections enlarge the shadow at fixed geometric charge, whereas the temporal amplitude enters through the charged lapse. Comparisons with observations of Sgr~A$^*$ and M87$^*$ provide conditional bounds on the charge and nonlinear scale. In addition, the adopted planetary perihelion allowances yield an illustrative sensitivity of $|ξ|(b^2+u_0^2)\lesssim2.6\times10^{-12}$ for a neutral solar exterior.
papers.title: Born-Infeld black holes in bumblebee gravity

papers.abstract: The best known lower bound on the determinantal complexity of the 4x4 permanent is 10. In this short note, I prove that this value is exactly 15: the 4x4 permanent is the determinant of a 15x15 matrix of affine linear forms, and cannot be that of any smaller matrix. To do so, I must establish both a lower and upper bound. To establish the upper bound, I use Grenet's construction of size 2^n-1. Hence that construction is optimal at n=4 (and n=3). This now constitutes the first knwon exact value of the determinantal complexity of the permanent at n=4. Only the value at n=3 was exactly known, prior to this note. The general quadratic bound only gives 8 for n=4. To establish the lower bound, I work from a normal form at a zero of the permanent. In the first row (and column) of the normal form, the linear forms vanish on a linear space inside the singular locus of the permanent. A hessian inequality bounds the size of the matrix in terms of that space. Then, a matrix of sie 14 foces the space into any of nine corordinate types. The forcing is either up to symmetry, or else into a family that degenerates to one of them. I then rule out every case. All involved computations are exact. In respect of the claim, I have made all certificates public.
papers.title: The determinantal complexity of the 4*4 permanent is 15

papers.abstract: We give randomized algorithms for approximately counting and nearly uniformly sampling independent sets in arbitrary bipartite graphs (#BIS). At fixed accuracy, both algorithms run in $\exp(O(n^{1/3}\log^{4/3}n))$ time on $n$-vertex graphs. More generally, the same running-time dependence on the number of variables holds for approximate counting and sampling with efficiently evaluable positive log-supermodular weights on Boolean variables. A weighted Sinclair-Jerrum walk on the self-reduction tree reduces these tasks to coarse lower estimates of residual log-partition functions. We obtain these estimates by optimizing a concave relaxation of an exact variational principle on the tree; threshold smoothing certifies that the low-degree search suffices.
papers.title: Approximating #BIS in $\exp(\widetilde O(n^{1/3}))$ Time

papers.abstract: Precise and independent flux control is essential for scalable superconducting processors built from frequency-tunable qubits and couplers, but flux crosstalk undermines it. Conventional calibration methods rely either on dedicated readout channels, which tunable couplers typically lack, or on readout schemes requiring extensive prior spectroscopy of the qubit and coupler. We demonstrate two independent methods that characterize coupler flux crosstalk without directly driving or measuring the couplers. The first method is zero-knowledge characterization, which exploits intrinsic coupler-resonator coupling to yield rapid and accurate estimates with no prior qubit or coupler spectroscopy, accelerating large scale bring-up. The second method is symmetric branch cancellation, which isolates crosstalk from other dispersive effects allowing for quantifying with high precision. Combined with an improved iterative procedure, these methods suppress residual coupler crosstalk below $5\times10^{-5}$, providing a complete route from zero-knowledge initialization to high-precision crosstalk characterization in fully tunable architectures.
papers.title: Flux Crosstalk Calibration from Zero Knowledge to High Precision in Fully Tunable Superconducting Circuits

papers.abstract: Public bodies increasingly rely on AI-produced evidence, including classifications, summaries and assessments. These outputs can inform policy decisions and service delivery, making their reliability a matter of public accountability. Establishing whether this evidence can be relied upon requires testing its outputs and examining how organisations decide whether those tests are sufficient. We combine technical evaluation with analysis of AI governance requirements, informed by measurement theory and management-based regulation. We compare eight GPT-4o configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics, against human-coded labels and across unchanged repeats. Accuracy ranges from 68.2% to 70.3%, yet 24.3% of questions receive different labels, with changes in topic shares and rankings. Configurations agree more with one another than with human coding: agreement does not guarantee correctness. Under the implemented score-extraction procedure, the proportion flagged for human review ranges from 0.9% to 41.0%. We analyse 37 UK and EU policy documents. Both sets expect testing and oversight, but reporting expectations do not consistently cover changing answers, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions or review routing. Some UK guidance explicitly addresses stability. The UK sample emphasises public bodies checking their own use; the EU places substantial testing duties on providers while leaving them important choices about measures and acceptance thresholds. Without appropriate checks, evidence could misrepresent policy issues, redirect attention or resources, and leave errors undetected. Public policy should require organisations to justify reliance through checks beyond aggregate accuracy, clear responsibility, access to expertise and scrutiny of results.
papers.title: Beyond accuracy: what AI assurance needs to establish in public services

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained on static offline datasets, yet physical manipulation unfolds sequentially across stages. Because a weakness in a downstream stage remains unobservable until the policy passes earlier ones, each resolved bottleneck exposes the next hidden failure mode. This staged structure calls for Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), in which a policy iteratively executes, diagnoses failures, and updates itself. Moreover, because task completion behaves like a product of stage-level pass rates, recursive gains can multiply across generations. In physical environments, three bottlenecks obstruct compounding: terminal execution feedback rarely localizes the stage that caused a failure, failed trajectories do not supply the corrective action, and updating shared parameters can degrade previously mastered skills. We propose Compounding Physical RSI, a self-evolving policy framework that turns execution failures into heritable capability. First, automated capability-gap assessment traces failed rollouts to the task stage where progression breaks down and formulates a structured improvement objective. Second, conditioned on this objective, our remedy stage curates validated, stage-relevant experience and refines the policy via behavior-regularized offline reinforcement learning, without requiring costly online rollouts at each optimization step. Third, to safeguard existing skills, our retention stage constructs weight-space candidates between the inherited reference policy and the refined policy, evaluates them across the task suite, and promotes the best candidate as the reference state for the next generation. Evaluated across all 42 tasks of the RoboDojo-Sim benchmark, CSU-AI-07 ranks first on the leaderboard with a three-seed mean Overall Score of 26.15 and Success Rate of 20.70%, outperforming the next-best entry by 5.92 points and 5.82 percentage points.
papers.title: Compounding Physical RSI: Turning Execution Failure into Inherited Capability

papers.abstract: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
papers.title: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models

papers.abstract: Diffusion models for temporal prediction typically corrupt each future frame with independent noise, leaving temporal dependence entirely to the denoiser. We propose Dynamical State-Space Diffusion (DSSD), which learns the temporal structure of the corruption process itself. DSSD builds a temporal kernel from the damped oscillatory modes of a stable diagonal state-space model, whose learned decay rates and frequencies let the corruption capture multiple timescales and oscillatory correlations, while the denoiser architecture remains unchanged. Running this model on a finite clip, however, requires the state before the first frame, which is unobserved; starting from a zero state leaves the early frames with less noise than the diffusion schedule prescribes. We avoid this by using the Cholesky factor of the model's stationary covariance as the temporal operator. We prove that this operator is causal, exactly invertible, keeps each frame's noise variance equal to that of standard diffusion, and reduces to the identity at the clean end of the process, and that it is exactly the Kalman innovations form of the state-space model. The denoiser is trained to predict the temporally correlated noise, and sampling removes and reapplies the temporal mixing at each step. On scientific-field and robot-video datasets, DSSD outperforms diffusion baselines that share its denoiser, and the evolution of its learned modes during training shows that the temporal operator adapts to each dataset.
papers.title: Dynamical State-Space Diffusion for Spatiotemporal Prediction

papers.abstract: Solving differential equations is a promising application of quantum computing. Spectral methods, where the solution is represented by coefficients in a basis, are particularly well suited to quantum solvers because their structured discretizations can enable efficient linear-algebra operations while providing rapid convergence. Their quantum implementation, however, requires an efficient transform between amplitudes encoding function values and amplitudes encoding expansion coefficients. This work develops two key components of a quantum spectral method. First, we construct the quantum ultraspherical transform (QUT) for orthonormal ultraspherical polynomials, a basis that supports sparse and well-conditioned discretizations of differential equations. For the basis parameters $m=0$ and $1$, this transform reduces to the discrete cosine and sine transforms with known efficient circuits. Our contribution covers every fixed integer $m\geq2$: for dimensions $N$ with $N+m=2^n$, where $n$ is the number of qubits, the QUT achieves error at most $\varepsilon$ using a gate count polynomial in $n$ and $\log(1/\varepsilon)$. The construction builds on the quantum Fourier transform, augmented by approximations whose accuracy guarantees are independent of $N$. Second, we develop a quantum spectral solver for regular linear ordinary differential equations based on the QUT. Under suitable boundary conditions and data-access assumptions, preconditioning keeps condition numbers bounded independently of the basis size, allowing the solution state to be prepared at polylogarithmic cost in system size and inverse error. Together, these contributions provide a framework for quantum spectral methods with the potential to solve linear differential equations efficiently.
papers.title: Efficient quantum ultraspherical transform and a well-conditioned quantum spectral method

papers.abstract: Massive stars strongly influence their environments through their radiation, stellar winds and core-collapse supernovae, while their own evolution is strongly shaped by wind mass loss. Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars are characterised by strong, optically thick winds, and the implementation of these winds remains an important uncertainty in stellar evolution models. Recent hydrodynamically consistent atmosphere calculations predict WR mass-loss rates that depend strongly on the temperature at the wind-launching region. We investigate the effects of incorporating these latest theoretical WR wind prescriptions into single and binary stellar evolution models at Milky Way, Large Magellanic Cloud and Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) metallicities. We find that the temperature dependence of the WR wind can significantly alter the evolution of stars near the threshold for WR formation. In particular, an implementation that transitions from a hydrogen rich WNL wind prescription to a classical WR wind driven by the hot iron opacity bump causes some SMC-metallicity models to spend an extended period at temperatures of approximately 70 to 90 kK. This produces a concentration of models in the temperature range occupied by most observed SMC WR stars, a feature that has previously been difficult to explain with stellar evolution models. Our results demonstrate that incorporating physically motivated, temperature dependent WR winds can improve the agreement between stellar evolution models and observed WR populations.
papers.title: The formation and evolution of Wolf-Rayet stars with temperature-dependent winds

papers.abstract: Wiping, sanding, and inspection robots press a sliding tool on a surface with controlled force. Controlling that force needs the surface normal, which is unknown on real-world, unmapped surfaces. Surface-normal estimators can help estimate the surface normal, but they either need a friction model or assume that the instantaneous tool velocity lies along the surface; however, walking violates this assumption. We propose SCRUB, a contact-based surface-frame estimator, which lets an armless quadruped slide a body-mounted tool along near-vertical surfaces in the absence of known, axis-aligned, or vision-predicted normals. SCRUB's predictive controller presses and slides the tool using a Kalman-filter estimate of the normal from two cues: 1) A force cue measures the estimate's tilt across the motion. If friction directly opposes the motion, the cue is zero exactly when that tilt is zero, for any friction coefficient. However, if the cue's sliding direction is wrong, friction appears as a false tilt. 2) A velocity cue measures tilt along the motion. Walking and pressing move the tool in and out. SCRUB therefore subtracts the commanded press rate from the tool velocity, averages the result over each gait cycle, and treats this mean as lying along the surface. On Unitree Go1 hardware at nominal speed and load, SCRUB completed every wall traverse and column orbit. No orbit completed with either cue removed, without gait averaging, or with a fixed normal.
papers.title: SCRUB: Contact-Based Surface-Frame Estimation for Force-Motion Control with an Armless Quadruped

papers.abstract: Born out of the turbulent, dense gas of the early Universe, globular clusters (GCs) represent a significantly different star-formation mode compared to the local Universe. To quantify the initial cluster conditions, we perform the long-term dynamical evolution of GCs using the high-precision direct N-body simulation code PeTar. As the first step in a series of studies, we investigate the two low-mass outer-halo GCs, Eridanus and Whiting 1. By comparing simulated number density profiles with observations, we derive best-fit initial half-mass radii of $2.0 \pm 1.0$ pc for Eridanus and $2.5 \pm 0.5$ pc for Whiting 1, corresponding to initial surface densities of $2592.03 M_\odot pc^{-2}$ and $226.35 M_\odot pc^{-2}$, respectively -- 2-3 orders of magnitude higher than their present-day values. The absence of multiple populations (MPs) in Whiting 1 and young massive clusters (YMCs), in contrast to the MP-hosting Eridanus, supports the scenario that MP formation requires higher initial surface density and/or lower metallicity. Using the simulations as a template, we identify five high-probability extra-tidal candidates of Whiting 1 from Gaia DR3 and APOGEE DR17, which exhibit coherent kinematics and chemical abundances. Our results demonstrate that the diffuse states of low-mass GCs are the product of long-term dynamical expansion and tidal stripping, and that their primordial configurations were significantly denser.
papers.title: Investigating the initial conditions of globular clusters via $N$-body simulations: I. half-mass radius and stellar density

papers.abstract: We examine how the geometry of rotating black holes in linear, shift-symmetric Einstein--scalar--Gauss--Bonnet (EsGB) gravity changes the limiting tidal equilibria of white dwarfs (WDs). The relativistic tidal field is obtained from numerical EsGB backgrounds in a parallel-transported frame and coupled to a compressible affine model. Comparisons with Kerr black holes matched in Arnowitt--Deser--Misner (ADM) mass and angular momentum show a positive shift in the orbital frequency at the tidal fold. At fixed spin the relative correction follows an approximately quadratic dependence on the EsGB coupling, consistent with the leading response of the metric to the scalar field. Over the sampled backgrounds, the relative correction reaches order $10^{-3}$. Black hole rotation also changes the relation between the tidal fold and the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO): the sampled prograde folds remain outside the ISCO, while retrograde folds move inside it at higher spins. Orbital orientation therefore controls whether tidal equilibrium is lost before the orbital stability limit is reached. For the stellar and black hole masses considered here, the characteristic gravitational wave (GW) frequencies fall in the millihertz band relevant to planned space based interferometers. Future GW observations capable of resolving deviations from Kerr predictions could constrain the EsGB coupling.
papers.title: Quasi-equilibrium tidal folds of white dwarfs around rotating black holes in shift-symmetric Einstein--scalar--Gauss--Bonnet gravity

papers.abstract: We establish Sobolev--Poincaré inequalities for piecewise $W^{2,p}$ functions in two and three dimensions over families of general polytopic (including shape-regular simplicial and Cartesian) meshes, allowing for degenerate facets. The proposed inequalities feature control by either the broken Hessian or, more naturally for general fourth-order problems, the broken Laplacian. Important tools in their derivation are a Helmholtz decomposition in Banach--Sobolev spaces and Sobolev--Poincaré inequalities for piecewise $W^{1,p}$ functions; we avoid the use of any inverse inequality. We provide estimates with fairly general Lebesgue exponents. Applications to the stability analysis of nonconforming discretizations for second- and fourth-order, linear and nonlinear problems are exhibited.
papers.title: Sobolev--Poincaré inequalities for piecewise $W^{2,p}$ functions over general polytopic meshes

papers.abstract: In optical quantum metrology, the scaling of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) with the mean photon number is a standard benchmark for relating precision to probe resources. For phase estimation, Heisenberg scaling corresponds to a quadratic growth of the QFI with the mean photon number, which Gaussian probes can approach. Interestingly, certain non-Gaussian probes can exhibit arbitrarily large QFI even at fixed mean photon number. Here, we clarify the resource requirements underlying this behavior by introducing a constraint that separates physically admissible states from inadmissible ones: an envelope on the photon-number distribution that arises naturally from the physical limitations of state-generation methods. Building on this constraint and considering pure single-mode probes, we define a resource quantity, $N_\mathrm{RMS}$, fixed by the preparation constraints, and derive a finite bound on the QFI whose Heisenberg scaling is attainable. We identify a genuine metrological advantage of non-Gaussian states over Gaussian probes subject to the same constraints. Finally, we illustrate these results with an optical preparation model based on a universal gate set.
papers.title: Precision Limits and Non-Gaussian Advantage in Optical Phase Estimation under Preparation Constraints

papers.abstract: We establish universal nonexistence results for monotone pure-strategy equilibrium in multiunit auctions with risk-averse bidders. Fix any number of bidders greater than one and any profile of strictly increasing concave utilities, with at least one strictly risk-averse bidder. Under uniform pricing, for every supply of at least three units, we construct independent, full-support type distributions under which neither lowest-winning-bid nor highest-losing-bid pricing admits an admissible monotone equilibrium. Under discriminatory pricing, we construct a finite supply and independent, full-support type distributions that preclude monotone pure-strategy equilibrium. We extend these results to all-pay auctions and finite bid grids.
papers.title: Universal Nonexistence of Monotone Equilibrium in Multiunit Auctions with Risk Aversion

papers.abstract: We apply the quantum field theory (QFT) approach to describe the spin-flavor precession of Dirac neutrinos. The magnetic moments matrix of these neutrinos is taken to be diagonal in the mass basis. Neutrino mass eigenstates are considered to be virtual particles in the QFT approach. The neutrino contribution to the matrix element of the overall process, which includes the emission, the propagation and the detection of neutrinos, is contained in the propagators of massive neutrinos. Using the recently derived propagator of a massive neutrino, which exactly accounts for the magnetic moment interaction, we derive the transition probability of the process $ν_{e\mathrm{L}}\toν_{μ\mathrm{L}}$ under the influence of a magnetic field. The result is compared with the prediction of the standard quantum mechanical (QM) approach. We briefly discuss the possibility to derive the QFT corrections to the QM expressions.
papers.title: Quantum field theory treatment of the spin-flavor precession of Dirac neutrinos with diagonal magnetic moments

papers.abstract: We resolve one of the longest-standing open problems in algorithmic mechanism design by showing that randomization cannot yield a sublinear approximation for truthful scheduling on unrelated machines, even when truthfulness is required only in expectation. Our main technical result concerns fractional scheduling, where tasks may be split among machines. We prove that every deterministic truthful fractional mechanism on $n$ unrelated machines has worst-case approximation ratio at least $(n+1)/2$, even against the optimal integral makespan. This matches the known upper bound exactly and settles the optimal approximation ratio of truthful fractional scheduling. Since the expected allocations and payments of a truthful-in-expectation mechanism define a truthful fractional mechanism, the same lower bound applies to all truthful-in-expectation mechanisms and, in particular, to all universally truthful mechanisms. On the positive side, we give a universally truthful mechanism with approximation ratio $n/2+o(n)$. Together, these results establish the optimal leading constant $1/2$ for randomized truthful scheduling. Thus, randomization improves on the optimal deterministic approximation ratio by an asymptotic factor of two, and no more.
papers.title: Tight bounds for fractional and randomized truthful scheduling

papers.abstract: ``Emergence'' refers to the fact that different mathematical languages and theories seem to be required to describe scientific theories that operate at different spatial and temporal scales. Highly circumscribed, special cases of emergence have been investigated using many different formal tools, including coarse-graining (over space and / or time), renormalization, dimension reduction, broken symmetry, and various formulations of causality. Here we extend the mathematics of model theory to unify and extend these earlier investigations. As a preliminary application of our framework, we investigate canonical examples of emergence, including the emergence of genetics from chemistry, of psychology from neurobiology, and of different forms of collective behavior from the laws governing their constituent parts. By exploiting the power of model theory we also uncover many aspects of emergence that were previously obscured. In particular, we uncover some of the rich hierarchical structure that relates different scientific fields. For example, we show that scientific fields can be related via a collection of multiple partial orders, all defined over the same set. On the other hand, under an alternative relation among scientific fields, one which allows cycles, we show that it is possible that the set of all of scientific fields must collapse into a single scientific field. Going forward, these investigations point to the formal tools that might need to be developed in order to arrive at a deeper understanding of this emergent hierarchy of scientific reality.
papers.title: The Logic of Emergence

papers.abstract: Sparse observations of binary pulsars can leave the orbit and the pulse count across observing gaps uncertain. We present APOLLO-Timing, a Bayesian phase-orbit lattice method that fits timing parameters together with integer pulse offsets between observing sessions. PINT checks the candidate connections at fixed pulse numbers. For PSR J1912-1215, a preliminary Keplerian fit to variations in the apparent spin period and its derivative did not phase-connect 96 times of arrival (TOAs) spanning 1438.07 days in 23 sessions. Starting from its position, spin frequency F0, and first time derivative F1 estimated in that fit, with dispersion measure fixed, APOLLO-Timing recovers the orbit and a unique best-supported phase-connected solution without supplied orbital parameters. A repeat full-data blind search recovers the same pulse counts in 914.0 s, including the final fit. Setting the initial F1 to zero in the 17, 18, and 19 session subsets also recovers the reference path. The solution gives Pb = 17.526 days, x = 23.448 light-seconds, e = 2.65e-5, chi-square = 188.01, and a weighted rms residual of 5.08 microseconds. For a pulsar mass of 1.4 solar masses and inclination of 60 degrees, the inferred companion mass is 0.67 solar masses, favoring a CO/ONeMg white dwarf.
papers.title: APOLLO-Timing: Annealed Phase - Orbit Lattice Linking across Observations for Binary Pulsar Timing

papers.abstract: This chapter addresses the central reproducibility problem of research with large language models. LLM output is probabilistic and varies across models and versions, which can have significant effects on downstream statistical results. The chapter distinguishes between replicability, reproducibility, and robustness, and proposes a probabilistic standard based on the distribution of results, not identical outputs. It introduces a standardized prompt script, tests within-model variation for encoders and decoders, and develops error-structure analysis to diagnose where models err and whether their errors align. Using three datasets, the chapter shows that measurement choice can reverse the sign of downstream regression coefficients. Existing design-based corrections with gold-labeled subsamples restore validity, but come at the cost of estimate precision. The main contribution of the chapter is a stacked ensemble of open-weight models that improves precision in the correction step while retaining estimate validity.
papers.title: Replicability, Reproducibility, and Robustness in Political and Social Science Research with Large Language Models

papers.abstract: A prolongation variety of a polynomial differential system $S$ is an algebraic variety defined by the equations of $S$ and their derivatives up to a given order. We compute the geometric degree of the prolongation varieties associated with the system $x_1'=x_2^2$, $x_2'=x_1^2$ in terms of the prolongation order, thereby proving a conjecture stated by Gleb Pogudin in Section 2, Question 6 of "Some Open Problems in Differential Algebra". Our approach is motivated from the beginning by doing computational experiments in OSCAR in order to find the number of solutions of a zero-dimensional system using algebraic Thomas decomposition. The result will follow from a coprimality condition on a family of polynomials with integer coefficients, which is verified by showing that their roots satisfy a strong interlacing property. Finally, we propose an extension of the conjecture for the systems $x_1'=x_2^n$, $x_2'=x_1^n$ with $n>2$.
papers.title: On the geometric degree of the prolongation varieties of the differential system $x_1'=x_2^2$, $x_2'=x_1^2$

papers.abstract: Human Motion Prediction (HMP) aims to predict future human poses at different moments according to observed past motion sequences. Previous approaches mainly treated the prediction of different temporal moments as a single prediction task and learned the predictions of varied moments simultaneously, which would encounter a main limitation: the learning of short-term predictions (referring to ``near-future'' prediction) could be hindered by the predictions of long-term (referring to ``far-future'' prediction) motions. In this paper, we develop a novel temporal continual learning framework called Continual Prior Compensation (CPC) to progressively train HMP models, in which we divide the prediction task of motions corresponding to varied temporal moments into several subtasks and train the model in a multi-stage manner. To mitigate the prior information forgetting in the progressive training, we further introduce a learnable random variable Prior Compensation Factor (PCF) to explicitly measure the prior knowledge loss. We theoretically show that the PCF can be efficiently learned together with the model parameters by minimizing a reasonable upper bound of the objective function. The proposed CPC is further enhanced to estimate the prior information loss for each subtask and a new framework called Continual Prior Compensation++ (CPC++) with Fine-Grained Prior Compensation Factor (FGPCF) is finally developed. Our CPC and CPC++ frameworks are quite flexible and can be easily integrated with different HMP backbone models and adapted to various datasets and applications. Extensive experiments on three HMP benchmark datasets using multiple SOTA HMP backbones (PGBIG, siMLPe, MotionMixer, and LTD) demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of our frameworks.
papers.title: Human Motion Prediction via Continual Prior Compensation

papers.abstract: Concepts of avoidable paths and inherent two-rooted graphs were recently introduced for the case of induced subgraphs. In this paper, we translate this framework to the setting of not necessarily induced (NNI) subgraphs, where the structural constraints, as well as conclusions, are significantly relaxed. We develop a new sufficient condition for inherence, and use it to provide complete characterizations of inherent two-rooted paths and forks. We show that for these families, the obvious necessary condition for inherence from the induced case is sufficient in the NNI setting. To complement these results, we introduce two general methods for proving non-inherence and apply them to demonstrate the non-inherence of several classes of two-rooted trees. Keywords: subgraph, two-rooted graph, two-rooted tree, avoidable two-rooted graph, inherent two-rooted graph
papers.title: Non-induced inherent graphs

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based collaborative perception enables multiple agents to share complementary perceptual information, overcoming limitations such as occlusion and limited sensing range. Communication efficiency is a critical bottleneck, as UAVs operate under stringent bandwidth and computational constraints. However, existing spatial selection methods focus predominantly on foreground regions to reduce missed detections, neglecting perceptually ambiguous regions and leaving false detections unresolved. We propose UCP, an uncertainty-driven framework that characterizes collaborative value through observational uncertainty, identifying sensor-limited regions, and discriminative uncertainty, capturing model-level ambiguity near the decision boundary. These estimates drive spatial request and supply maps for efficient inter-agent communication, and the received messages are aggregated via U-Fusion, an uncertainty-guided cross-attention module. Experiments on three benchmarks across 3D object detection and trajectory prediction demonstrate a superior performance-bandwidth trade-off with high interpretability and strong generalizability.
papers.title: Uncertainty-Driven Efficient Communication for UAV-Based Collaborative Perception

papers.abstract: We present flash-comm, a communication library that achieves efficient transport for LLM decoding by fusing readiness synchronization with data movement. flash-comm introduces self-synchronizing transfers in which each data block carries evidence of its readiness, allowing receivers to directly validate the blocks they need without separate inter-GPU barriers. Based on this principle, a cost-guided protocol selector adapts the readiness encoding to message size and the number of participating GPUs, balancing synchronization overhead against additional data-transfer cost. flash-comm further decouples transport order from reduction order to preserve result consistency across GPUs under asynchronous data arrivals. On a server with eight NVIDIA B300 GPUs, flash-comm reduces all-reduce latency by a median of 28.8% and up to 43.7% compared with custom AR v2 (the state-of-the-art all-reduce implementation). In end-to-end decoding, flash-comm reduces time per output token (TPOT) by 1.7-6.8%. Note that all-reduce accounts for 11.4% of the baseline decoding time, which bounds the latency reduction possible from optimizing this operation alone. The same mechanism also supports standalone all-gather, reducing latency by a median of 23.8% and up to 58.9% across eight B300 GPUs.
papers.title: flash-comm: Self-Synchronizing Collective Communication for LLM Decoding

papers.abstract: Bayesian experimental design (BED) is a principled framework for intelligent data acquisition with applications across a wide range of scientific and industrial domains. However, the development and adoption of BED remains hindered by a lack of standardised software and benchmarks. Existing methods are typically implemented in bespoke codebases and evaluated on a small subset of tasks, making methods difficult to apply, compare, or extend. To address this, we present TestBED, a general-purpose, open-source toolkit for Bayesian experimental design. TestBED decomposes the BED process into modular, reusable components spanning tasks, objectives, training mechanisms, policy architectures, and evaluation procedures, together with scalable implementations of core primitives such as expected information gain estimators. We provide a wide range of these components, which can be freely composed, allowing existing methods to be reproduced within a common framework, while also enabling previously unexplored configurations and new methodologies to be easily implemented and evaluated. Using TestBED, we further conduct a large-scale benchmark of contemporary BED methods, including controlled studies of under-appreciated but surprisingly critical methodological choices, such as the importance of time embeddings in design policy architectures. By providing a modular, extensible software foundation and a reproducible benchmarking suite, we hope that TestBED will accelerate methodological research in BED and lower the barrier to its real-world application.
papers.title: TestBED: An Open-Source Toolkit for Bayesian Experimental Design

papers.abstract: U-shaped radial age profiles have recently been reported in low-mass galaxies. This type of profile differs from the usually observed positive radial age gradients of the low-mass regime. We aim to characterise the environment in which low-mass galaxies with U-shaped age profiles are more commonly found. We use the IllustrisTNG-50 hydrodynamical simulations to select a sample of galaxies with stellar masses ranging from $10^9 \, M_\odot$ to $10^{10} \, M_\odot$. Based on their radial age profiles, we classify the sample into galaxies with and without a U-shaped feature. We define a U-shaped profile as one where stellar ages decrease towards a local minimum and subsequently increase, requiring an age contrast of at least 0.4 Gyr on either side of the minimum relative to its value. We find 145 galaxies with U-shaped age profiles ($\sim 11\%$ of the sample).
