They are mostly central systems ($\sim 72\%$) and $\sim 82\%$ of them reside within low-mass halos ($M_{200} < 10^{12} \, M_\odot$). We also find that galaxies exhibiting this feature are located at large distances from galaxy groups but close to cosmic filaments, with a median distance of $\sim 265$ kpc, whereas those without U-shaped age profiles tend to be located farther away from these structures ($\sim 351$ kpc).
papers.title: Living near filaments: How environment shapes age profiles in low-mass galaxies

papers.abstract: We used medical image synthesis to create a challenging multimodal evaluation framework that exposes hallucination behaviors in frontier models. Evaluating multimodal reasoning has historically been difficult because existing medical datasets rarely pair different image modalities, such as radiographs and external clinical photographs. To address this gap, we introduce Trick-or-Treat, an adversarial multimodal medical benchmark that pairs real chest radiographs with synthetic clinical photographs to challenge models' cross-modal reasoning. For each of a wide range of conditions, we created two pairs of images, where the pairs share a single chest radiograph but contain different external photographs. In matched pairs, the chest radiograph and photograph both contain findings suggesting the same disease (e.g., varicella pneumonia suggested by lung opacities and crusted skin lesions seen in chickenpox). In mismatched pairs, the photograph depicts an alternative clinical finding that would not lead to the same unifying diagnosis (e.g. replacing crusted skin lesions with ordinary acne). Synthetic photograph generation allows clinical findings to be varied while the person's features and photographic setting stay consistent, reducing confounding. In an investigation of three frontier models, we found that models hallucinated clinically significant photograph findings in 45-57.5% of mismatched pairs, up from 25-37.5% for the same photographs shown alone. When faced with mismatched pairs, models tended to ignore mismatches and instead hallucinated findings that better matched the radiograph (e.g. misreading acne as crusted skin lesions to justify diagnosing chickenpox). Trick-or-Treat both demonstrates concerning error pattern in frontier models' medical reasoning and provides a proof of concept for the use of synthetic images in adversarial multimodal evaluation.
papers.title: Trick-or-Treat: Adversarial Evaluation of Multimodal Medical Reasoning with Synthetic Images

papers.abstract: Quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) can learn distributions that are hard to sample from classically, but their value depends on generalizing from finite training data. Here, we study how hardware noise affects this generalization. We show that, for any noise process, the generalization gap of a QCBM trained with the maximum mean discrepancy is bounded by the complexity of the distributions the noisy model can reach. Scrambled local Pauli noise contracts this complexity but biases the model towards the uniform distribution, so residual noise acts as a regularizer whose optimal strength can be intermediate. We propose GENIE, a framework that realizes a chosen noise level with capped error mitigation and selects it during training from held-out data within a fixed execution budget, with provably bounded regret. In simulations on synthetic and census data, GENIE stays close to the best of four noise-control strategies, whereas every fixed noise level falls short in many settings.
papers.title: Noise-regularized training of quantum circuit Born machines under a finite shot budget

papers.abstract: Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws. I use the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model for finding software vulnerabilities, to study how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers. Using the universe of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, I find that firms with access more than doubled their disclosures relative to Chinese and Russian tech firms without access, disclosed about 150 percent more high-impact vulnerabilities, and fixed reported flaws as quickly as before. As treated firms found more flaws themselves, external researchers, who sell their findings through bug bounties, reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms' code and more in other firms' code, without leaving the market. There is no evidence that attackers exploited the additional vulnerabilities: the share exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds, mainly because a smaller share was already exploited when disclosed, while the number exploited did not change. Frontier AI helped defenders find and fix more flaws before attackers exploited them, but its restricted release creates an asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries.
papers.title: Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense? Evidence from Project Glasswing

papers.abstract: A national digital twin was conceived as an ecosystem of twins connected through mappings to a common foundation, but the roadmap that promises to confirm those mappings are valid never says what valid means. We give the test a precise form, coherence and conservativity of the merged ontology, borrowed from logic-based alignment repair, and apply it to the Information Exchange Standard (IES), first pair by pair and then to whole hubs. Crosswalks from IES into thirteen ontologies across seven sector groups, anchored on the building ontologies BOT, Brick, and SAREF4BLDG, pass through separate stages of matching, human review, certification of each SKOS correspondence against the two class hierarchies, and reasoning with HermiT. Pair by pair, the stages catch different failures: certification alone removed all 526 conservativity violations of the raw crosswalks, review alone left 73, and together they made eleven of twelve overlapping pairs coherent and conservative. Pairwise certification does not compose. Merging the three certified building crosswalks into one hub made five Brick classes unsatisfiable, through a homonym between the IES and Brick notions of a floor that only BOT's disjointness axioms expose; rejecting that one row gave a coherent and conservative hub that entails 290 cross-ontology links nobody wrote down. The core hub is inconsistent before any crosswalk is added, because two published standards, the Open Energy Ontology and BFO 2020, contradict each other; with either one left out it is coherent and conservative. A hub, not a pair, is the unit an ecosystem of twins has to certify.
papers.title: From Certified Pairs to a Certified Hub: Reasoner-Checked Crosswalks for the Information Exchange Standard

papers.abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.
papers.title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI

papers.abstract: How much information about a graph is needed to determine its connectivity after arbitrary valid edge deletions? This question is at the heart of designing deterministic dynamic streaming algorithms for graph connectivity. Towards answering this question, we study the deterministic one-way communication problem in which Alice holds a graph $G_A = (V, E_A)$ on $n$ vertices, Bob holds a graph $G_B = (V, E_B)$ with $E_B \subseteq E_A$, and Alice sends a message $M \in \{0,1\}^m$ that allows Bob to decide whether $G_A - G_B$ is connected. Randomized sketches solve this problem using $\tilde O(n)$ bits, whereas deterministic recovery of even one surviving edge requires $Ω(n^2)$ bits. We prove an upper bound of $m = \widetilde{O}(n^{7/4})$ bits and a lower bound of $m = \widetildeΩ(n^{3/2})$ bits for deciding connectivity. Thus, connectivity admits a subquadratic deterministic representation despite the quadratic cost of edge recovery, but remains polynomially harder than its randomized counterpart. The upper bound immediately yields an $\widetilde{O}(n^{7/4})$-bit deterministic $n^2$-fault tolerant connectivity oracle, which reports the connected components of a graph $G$ after any valid set of edge deletions. We also obtain an $\tilde Ω(n f^{1/4})$-bit lower bound for deterministic $f$-fault tolerant connectivity oracles for every $f \in [1,n^2]$. Finally, we show that the separation between connectivity and edge recovery persists in deterministic single-pass dynamic streams with bounded update multiplicity. For every fixed $ε\in (0,1/3)$, our algorithm reports the connected components of the final simple graph using $\widetilde{O}(n^{15/8 + 3ε/8})$ bits (subquadratic space), provided each edge undergoes at most $n^ε$ insertion or deletion updates in total.
papers.title: Deterministic Connectivity Sketches Under Edge Deletions

papers.abstract: Controlling the shape profile of soft trunk robots extends their reach into complex regions of the workspace and enhances their use in practical applications. Recent advances in soft robot design have enabled soft trunk robots to achieve greater flexibility in conforming to complex shapes. Specifically, trunk robots whose geometries are designed as helicoids have been shown to enable extreme shape-changing capabilities. Their compliance makes them highly nonlinear, which in turn makes shape control difficult. On similar tendon-driven trunk robots, model-based controllers based on the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) have achieved high accuracy in closed-loop end-effector tracking. We extend this approach by learning an aSSM model of the full body of a trimmed-helicoid soft trunk robot from data and use this in a model predictive control (MPC) scheme to demonstrate a range of shape control tasks on hardware. On closed-loop dynamic shape regulation, our method outperforms the available linear baselines by a factor of 10. In human-in-the-loop interactive demos, our method completes section-by-section shaping and balances a tennis ball for over 25 seconds, while the linear baselines fall short. A model-free reinforcement learning policy trained for 12 hours on hardware fails on the same balancing task. These results establish aSSM-based MPC as a practical route to full-body shape control on real soft hardware.
papers.title: Dynamic Shape Control of Soft Trunk Robots

papers.abstract: Reconstructing cell lineages from 3D time-lapse microscopy requires distinguishing cell motion from division and inferring temporally consistent connections. When only a subset of cells is annotated, however, training procedures that treat unannotated regions as background or incorrect correspondences can be problematic. We propose a cell tracking pipeline that integrates detection from sparse annotations, calibration of candidate connections using image features, and joint selection of lineage graph events. For detection, we combine the outputs of 2.5D and 3D models trained to suppress erroneous background supervision at unannotated cells. We then calibrate ordinary link and division probabilities using motion features from dense flow, correspondence features from a learned cell-matching model, and features from models that identify cells immediately before division, dividing parents, and daughters immediately after division. Ordinary links, divisions represented as daughter pairs, and node inclusion are selected jointly under a surrogate objective derived from the evaluation metric, followed by gap filling and temporal coordinate refinement. The pipeline achieves an overall score of 0.9762 in 5-fold cross-validation on 199 videos from 2 zebrafish embryos. With candidates and calibrated values held fixed, joint selection outperforms a sequential method that allows replacement of existing divisions and reoptimization of ordinary links by 0.0105. The improvement arises primarily from division recovery.
papers.title: Learning to Track Cells from Sparse Annotations in 3D Time-Lapse Microscopy

papers.abstract: Stochastic simulators need suitable parameter values to reproduce observed behaviour in complex systems. Searching for these values through repeated simulations makes frequent recalibration computationally expensive. We develop an amortized optimizer that uses simulations collected in advance to learn how to choose parameters that make simulated outcomes agree with observations. Once fitted, it maps new observations to feasible parameters without further simulator calls. The method retains alternative parameter settings that can explain similar observations and compares their responses, avoiding the conflicting labels that arise when training a single parameter regressor. Historical observations also provide supervision by showing which simulated responses agree with the data, even when the underlying parameters are unknown. Experiments across four simulators compare calibration accuracy and query time. Dedicated cost analyses quantify traffic preparation and the recorded financial reuse costs. On new traffic targets, local correction more than halves query time relative to empirical and surrogate selection; a learned inverse is faster still, with similar mean error. In a retrospective comparison on real financial data, our method returns parameters about $1.07\times10^{7}$ times faster than a 10-minute Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization search, with mean calibration error 3.06% higher. Reusing simulation work across observations supports repeated parameter updates when the available time is too short for a new search.
papers.title: Amortized Optimization for Calibrating Stochastic Social Simulators

papers.abstract: The approximation of model predictive control (MPC) algorithms with neural network models has received significant attention in the power electronics research community, as a valuable tool to enable the real-time implementation of computationally expensive methods. Training machine learning models to imitate MPC algorithms typically follows a traditional supervised learning flow, with a static training data set generated through either uniform sampling or simulation. Training with uniformly distributed data allows models to maintain consistent performance throughout the entire operating space, but very small models may fail to achieve satisfactory results in the regions corresponding to expected operation. Conversely, simulation data can be used in training to obtain models that can accurately track certain trajectories but fail to achieve adequate performance in underrepresented regions. The present article proposes a method to combine the advantages of both methods, by training models on sampled data with importance weights obtained through the kernel density estimation of experimental data. This allows the training process to target specific regions of the operating space, and results in measurable performance improvements. The method is demonstrated through the imitation of a moving discretized control set MPC algorithm for a dual active bridge converter, and is validated through experimental results.
papers.title: Enhanced Imitation Learning of Model Predictive Control through Importance Weighting

papers.abstract: We determine the universal constant in the large-genus asymptotic expansion of super Weil-Petersson volumes. The argument adopts the uniform-transport strategy for shifted theta intersection numbers. The uniform large-genus theorem for normalized BGW numbers of Guo-Norbury-Yang-Zagier determines the amplitude at a simpler endpoint. The result is $C=π^{-9/2}$. We give a proof of the Griguolo-Papalini-Russo-Seminara conjecture for fixed boundary lengths and fixed descendant degrees. The boundary formula is uniform when the sum of the lengths is $o(\sqrt g)$, and we exhibit an obstruction at the $\sqrt g$ scale. We also compute the first four inverse-genus coefficients by two exact recursive methods and derive general polynomial structure results. Finally, we show that, for each fixed genus, the super Weil-Petersson volume divided by $n!$ is a polynomial in the number $n$ of marked points.
papers.title: The super Weil-Petersson asymptotic expansion and the coefficients

papers.abstract: Subgame-perfect equilibrium need not exist in continuous games with perfect information when Nature moves. Under standard regularity assumptions, we prove that weak atomic continuity of Nature's transition probabilities yields a measurable pure-strategy subgame-perfect equilibrium for finite and infinite horizons. The condition, originating in the population genetics literature, is necessary for the existence of subgame-perfect equilibrium uniformly over the remaining primitives: whenever this condition is violated, one can construct a dynamic game with no subgame-perfect equilibrium, even in behavioral strategies. The proof preserves compactness and upper hemicontinuity of continuation payoff correspondences under integration without requiring convexity.
papers.title: Weak Atomic Continuity and Subgame Perfection

papers.abstract: Persistence diagrams do not naturally live in a Hilbert space. Carrière, Cuturi, and Oudot embedded them in kernel methods through the Sliced Wasserstein kernel, built from the Sliced Wasserstein distance $\mathrm{SW}_1$, which is conditionally negative definite (CND). We study the projected ($\mathrm{SW}_p$) and reflected ($\mathrm{RW}_p$) Sliced Wasserstein distances for every order $p\ge1$, and compare them with the $p$-Wasserstein distance $d_p$ and with a reflected variant $d_p^r$, in which projection onto the diagonal is replaced by reflection across it. We show that $2^{1/p}d_p\le d_p^r\le 2d_p$ with sharp constants, so that $d_1^r=2d_1$ and $d_p^r$ inherits the stability of $d_p$, although it is a metric only for $p=1$. The distances $\mathrm{SW}_1$ and $\mathrm{RW}_1$ are CND metrics, and $\mathrm{RW}_1$ gives rise to a new positive definite kernel, stable with respect to $d_1$. For $p>1$, neither $\mathrm{SW}_p$ nor $\mathrm{RW}_p$ satisfies the triangle inequality, and rigorous interval-arithmetic certificates prove that $\mathrm{SW}_2$ and $\mathrm{RW}_2$ are not CND; numerical experiments suggest that the CND property fails for every $p$ above some $p^*\in(1,1.2]$. On diagrams with at most $N$ points, $\mathrm{SW}_p$ and $\mathrm{RW}_p$ are metrically equivalent to $d_p$ and $d_p^r$, with sharp upper constants. On an orbit recognition benchmark, the kernels built from $\mathrm{SW}_1$ and $\mathrm{RW}_1$ reach about 85% accuracy, outperform the persistence scale space kernel, perform on par with the persistence weighted Gaussian kernel, and are about one percentage point below the kernel built from $\mathrm{SW}_2$, which is not positive definite.
papers.title: Projected and Reflected Sliced Wasserstein Kernels for Persistence Diagrams

papers.abstract: Both the heart and the brain are built from electrically excitable cells, yet the emergent dynamics of these organs could not differ more. In the myocardium, a coherent traveling wave of action potentials ensures coordinated contraction; in the cerebral cortex, distributed, irregular spiking underlies efficient information processing and the generation of behavior. Here, we illuminate the principles that underlie the emergence of such distinct nonlinear dynamics using concepts from complex systems. We trace these principles across scales from ion channels and cellular action potential generation, through cellular coupling mechanisms and network architecture, to organ level dynamics and clinical phenotypes. Designed to support either synchronized waves or desynchronized information processing, the heart and the brain can thus be understood as operating on opposite sides of a synchronization phase transition. Crossing this transition implies pathological dynamics in both organs: Loss of synchrony in the heart produces arrhythmia; excess synchrony in the brain leads to epileptic seizures. We discuss how adaptation mechanisms, including plasticity, modulation, remodeling, and learning, maintain the appropriate level of (de)synchronization. Overall, we provide a unified excitable-system perspective, together with an educational notebook, to foster cross-disciplinary insights into cardiac and neural function and pathology.
papers.title: Synchronized Hearts, Desynchronized Brains: A Nonlinear Dynamics Perspective for Function and Failure

papers.abstract: We provide a counterexample to the weak Gibbs and regularity conjectures. The example is a spin-one system on the square lattice with a translation-invariant nearest-neighbor interaction. At high temperatures and high on-site field strengths, it has a unique KMS state that does not have the weak Gibbs or regularity properties.
papers.title: A Counterexample to the Weak Gibbs and Regularity Conjectures

papers.abstract: We present LeanVOA, a Lean 4 library for the theory of vertex operator algebras (VOAs), together with a companion book that sets each formalized result next to its textbook statement. The library constructs the Moonshine module $V^\natural$ and formalizes Zhu's modular invariance, Huang's tensor categories with the Verlinde formula, the Gannon-Rayhaun classification of $c=1$ VOAs, and classical freeness of the boundary admissible $L_k(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ (Arakawa-Dai) and of the minimal models $M(2,2m+3)$ (van Ekeren-Heluani). It also contains new results: graded first-order rigidity of all Virasoro minimal models and of $L_k(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ at every admissible level; classical freeness of $L_{-3/2}(\mathfrak{sl}_3)$, and of the other members of the Deligne series under stated assumptions; and a proof that graded unitarity of the boundary admissible $L_k(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ implies that of the minimal models $M(2,2n+1)$. The library declares no axiom of its own.
papers.title: Vertex Operator Algebras in Lean: a formal library and its companion book

papers.abstract: We study the limits of differentially private Gaussian mean estimation when the covariance matrix is unknown. Prior work shows that when the covariance $Σ$ is known, the optimal sample complexity can depend only on its spectrum, rather than on the ambient dimension $d$. We establish new lower bounds for Gaussian mean estimation with Euclidean error which show that private estimators cannot achieve similar guarantees when the covariance is unknown. First, when the sample size $n$ is smaller than the effective dimension $\mathrm{trace}(Σ)/\|Σ\|_{\text{op}}$, the optimal error when the covariance is unknown can be larger than the optimal error when it is known by a factor of $\sqrt{d/n}$. Second, when the sample size is larger than the effective dimension, even for diagonal covariance matrices with effective dimension bounded by $\log d$, the optimal error when the covariance is unknown can be larger than the optimal error when it is known by a factor of $\sqrt{d}/n^{3/2}$. Together, these results show that in the unknown covariance setting, exploiting anisotropic structure under differential privacy can require a dimension-dependent error or sample complexity.
papers.title: Dimension-Free Private Mean Estimation is Impossible Without the Covariance

papers.abstract: Porous carbons store energy, capture gases and purify water, and their performance depends strongly on the geometry of their pores. Atomistic models mostly simulate their synthesis by molecular dynamics, with results that depend on the interatomic potential, and return the pore network as an output rather than as a specification. Here we show that the pore network can be an input: pores drawn from a target size distribution fill a prescribed volume fraction, carbon is grown around them by stochastic ring placement, and a particle swarm recovers the construction parameters from a structural fingerprint. The search reproduces the density, surface area and pore volume of a carbon produced by quenched molecular dynamics within about 5 %, together with its pore size distribution. As a stress test, it also recovers a bimodal distribution, and the search history reveals which parameters the targets constrain and flags a failed search. A short anneal completes the network, recovering the coordination of the reference while the pore size distribution keeps its shape. Molecular dynamics still supplies the local chemistry, but the pore geometry becomes a design variable for a given application.
papers.title: Explicit pore pre-conditioning and inverse design of amorphous nanoporous carbon

papers.abstract: Blackbody radiation (BBR) poses a central challenge for quantum science with Rydberg atoms. By driving transitions to nearby opposite-parity states, BBR shortens Rydberg lifetimes and has long been suspected to trigger "avalanche" events known to cause correlated atom loss. Here, we suppress avalanche decay and establish BBR as its dominant trigger using a Rydberg atom array that operates either cryogenically or at room temperature. A $45~\text{K}$ radiation shield reduces ambient BBR, extending Rydberg $nS$ lifetimes for $n$ ranging from 50 to 75. BBR-induced decay rates are suppressed by 30%-50%, corresponding to an effective blackbody temperature $T_{\rm eff}\approx190~\text{K}$. This enables controlled comparisons of Rydberg-dressed atom arrays operating in different BBR environments. Arrays of up to 70 atoms demonstrate cryogenically suppressed avalanche rates, tracking the suppression in BBR-induced decay, for both $n=50$ and $n=60$ dressing. A parameter-free rate model agrees with the measured avalanche rates after accounting for frequency-dependent cryogenic shielding, photoionization-triggered avalanches, laser phase noise, BBR decay channels, and Rydberg interaction effects. We demonstrate a quantitative description of avalanche decay and show that improved BBR shielding should further suppress correlated loss to the $T_\text{eff}=45~\text{K}$ achievable in the current apparatus. Our results establish a route to mitigating correlated errors that otherwise impede fault-tolerant operation in neutral-atom quantum processors.
papers.title: Cryogenic suppression of correlated loss in Rydberg atom arrays

papers.abstract: Complete sensor-channel failures create a difficult form of time-series missingness: local interpolation is unavailable, and deploying a separately trained imputer for every failure pattern may be impractical. We ask whether a sequence reconstructor trained without artificial mask augmentation and then frozen can be converted into an imputer at inference time. Our method treats the missing entries of each test window as optimization variables, clamps all observations, and backpropagates through the frozen model to minimize reconstruction error only on observed coordinates. The resulting observed-self-consistency objective requires neither artificial mask augmentation nor full-channel dropout during reconstructor training. We characterize when this refinement is informative through the cross-Jacobian from missing inputs to observed residuals, and use an optional temporal-smoothness prior when that coupling is weak. Across five real-world datasets with exactly one channel synthetically masked per test window and four reconstruction architectures, no-prior test-time refinement reduces MAE relative to one-pass reconstruction in 19 of 20 dataset-backbone combinations. Compared with mask-aware imputers trained under either standard structured masks or matched full-channel dropout, the best refined reconstructor achieves the lowest MAE on two datasets and trails the strongest baseline on three. These gains require substantially more inference time and are sensitive to cross-channel coupling. Our results establish test-time self-consistency as a conditional inference-time adapter for frozen reconstruction models that complements mask-aware imputation without retraining the reconstructor.
papers.title: From Reconstruction to Imputation: Test-Time Optimization for Missing Time-Series Channels

papers.abstract: We give a dynamic algorithm that maintains a near-optimal edge coloring in constant expected time per update. For every fixed $ε>0$, the algorithm maintains a $(1+ε)Δ$ edge coloring under edge insertions and deletions in $\mathrm{poly}(1/ε)$ worst-case expected update time against an oblivious adversary, provided $Δ\geΔ_ε=\widetildeΘ(1/ε^2)$. The previous constant-time algorithm of Bhattacharya, Costa, Panski, and Solomon (BCPS) required $Δ\ge(\log n/ε^4)^{Θ(\log(1/ε)/ε)}$, where $n$ is the number of vertices. We remove this dependence on $n$, answering their open question. Our approach differs substantially from that of BCPS, which relied on coloring in locally tree-like subgraphs. Instead, we draw on distributed algorithms that organize partial coloring through successive applications of the Lovász Local Lemma (LLL). We develop a dynamic LLL solver with worst-case expected update bounds and a dynamic splitting algorithm that partitions edges into low-degree subgraphs. A key technical contribution is a bottom-up method for iterative splitting, which avoids the logarithmic overhead of maintaining successive levels. It achieves constant expected update time by adaptively choosing which levels to inspect and repair, rather than inspecting every level after each update. We believe these dynamic splitting and LLL tools can be of interest beyond edge coloring.
papers.title: Constant-Time Dynamic Edge Coloring via Dynamic Splitting and LLL

papers.abstract: Collaborative filtering (CF) is a cornerstone of recommender systems and plays a relevant role in many modern applications. CF uses user-item interaction data to discover future preferences. Although deep learning models have shown promise in CF, Embarrassingly Shallow Autoencoders for Sparse Data (EASE) has gained attention for its outstanding ranking accuracy provided by its closed-form solution. EASE relies primarily on relationships among items to fit a full-rank high-dimensional linear mapping. We hypothesize that this design limits its capacity to capture similar but not equivalent fine-grained user relationships, consequently limiting its recommendation accuracy. This paper introduces an alternative formulation based on EASE that takes advantage of user-user information. Furthermore, we propose a hybrid model that combines both user-user and item-item adjacency distributions. Our experiments reveal that the proposed models outperform EASE on well-known recommendation benchmarks, highlighting the significance of including the user alternative in shallow autoencoder studies for CF.
papers.title: Alternatives to Shallow Autoencoders for Collaborative Filtering

papers.abstract: Elastic and inelastic Compton-scattering cross sections of the deuteron were measured at HI$γ$S using a circularly polarized, quasi-monoenergetic $γ$-ray beam (61.0 MeV). Scattered $γ$ rays from a liquid deuterium target were detected at $55^\circ$, $115^\circ$, and $150^\circ$. High-resolution NaI(Tl) detectors at backward angles enabled separation of elastic and inelastic events. A $χ$EFT analysis of the data yields new neutron scalar polarizabilities, $α^n_{E1} = 12.25 \pm 1.1\mathrm{(stat)} \pm 0.3\mathrm{(BSR)} \pm 0.8\mathrm{(th)}$ and $β^n_{M1} = 2.95 \mp 1.1\mathrm{(stat)} \mp 0.3\mathrm{(BSR)} \mp 0.8\mathrm{(th)}$ (in units of $10^{-4} \mathrm{fm}^3$) reducing statistical uncertainties by 12 %.
papers.title: New Neutron Polarizabilities from Deuterium Compton Scattering at HI$γ$S

papers.abstract: It is well known that $\mathsf{VF} = \mathsf{VBP}_{3}$ (Ben-Or-Cleve'92), i.e. the width of any constant-width algebraic branching program can be reduced to width $3$ with only a polynomial overhead to size. We prove that this is not the case for the monotone equivalents. In particular, we prove that there is an infinite hierarchy $\mathsf{mVBP}_{2} \subsetneq \mathsf{mVBP}_{3} \subsetneq \ldots$ by showing that $\mathrm{imm}_{k,n}$ requires width $w$ mABPs to have depth at least $\left(\frac{k}{w-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}\left\lfloor n^{\frac{1}{(w-2)}} \right\rfloor - 1}$ whenever $3 \leq w < k$. We prove this lower bound using support-based techniques. Since this lower bound is exact instead of asymptotic, it allows some width separations even for superconstant width. Moreover, it allows us to show that the expressive power of poly-sized monotone formulas of depth $2d$ is not reached by poly-sized mABPs of width $d-1$ but a width of $2d+1$ is sufficient. We contrast this to unbounded-depth monotone formulas, which are proven to be stronger than constant-width mABPs, but weaker than $\log$-width mABPs and incomparable for most widths in between. Finally, we generalize Snir's framework (Snir'80) for showing lower bounds on the number of leaves of monotone formulas to monotone formulas of multiplication depth $d^{\times}$, giving a lower bound of $n \cdot k^{d^{\times}(n^{\frac{1}{d^{\times}}} - 1)}$ for the iterated matrix multiplication polynomial and $\left(\left(e+o(1)\right) \ln^{\circ(d^{\times}-1)}(n)\right)^n$ for the permanent.
papers.title: A Width Hierarchy of Monotone Algebraic Branching Programs

papers.abstract: Agentic research loops that let a language model propose a change, run a fixed experiment and keep whatever improves the metric work well in machine learning. In trading research the same loop is a machine for producing false discoveries: a backtest that "improves the metric" is, by default, overfit, look-ahead, a multiple-comparisons artifact, cost-free, or market drift wearing a strategy. We describe Autonomous Quant Researcher, an open-source loop built on the opposite premise: the model proposes, and only trusted code decides. Proposals are strict declarative JSON over a fixed vocabulary, so there is no model-written code to sandbox. Evaluation runs on immutable chronological stores split into discovery, validation and a final holdout that can be opened exactly once, after a durable receipt is written. Acceptance is a conjunction of absolute gates (positive edge and net P&L after costs, a positive weekly-cluster bootstrap lower bound, survival at elevated costs, per-year stability and sample floors), never a single score. Duplicates are refused before they spend a trial, and every formulation, refusal, crash and result is kept in a hash-chained, append-only ledger. We report every campaign run to date, across 0DTE options priced from traded option bars, overnight SPX verticals, daily ETF rules, technical-analysis premises, Kalshi crypto binaries, earnings options, off-exchange volume and a pre-registered alternative-data campaign. Most hypotheses fail, and we report them. Two results survive their pre-registered bars. The clearest example of the loop working is a failure: a language-model survivor that passed discovery and validation with Sharpe ratios near 3 and fell to 0.26 on its single holdout use. The value of such a loop lies less in what it finds than in how hard it is to make it report something that is not there.
papers.title: Hard to Fool: A Bounded LLM Research Loop for Quantitative Finance, and What Two Dozen Campaigns Found

papers.abstract: Large language models can solve many multi-step reasoning problems, but their reasoning remains brittle: plausible intermediate steps often lead to incorrect answers. Improving reasoning at test time requires balancing two imperfect signals: the generator, which provides diversity, and the verifier, which guides correctness. Existing approaches largely favor one side of this tradeoff. Verifier-weighted voting relies on trajectories sampled from the generator and cannot steer generation toward correct ones. By contrast, beam-style verifier-guided search can steer generation, but may over-concentrate on narrow trajectory sets and amplify verifier errors. We propose Verifier-Guided Self-Consistency (VGSC), a stochastic decoding framework that combines step-level correctness and future-outcome estimates to guide reasoning during generation. VGSC repeatedly proposes candidate next steps from the base language model and uses both signals in an acceptance/resampling procedure, while maintaining multiple trajectories for final answer-level self-consistency. We provide a probabilistic interpretation of VGSC as approximate sampling from a verifier-tilted trajectory distribution. Across multiple reasoning benchmarks, generator models, and verifier families, VGSC achieves higher average accuracy than representative baselines.
papers.title: Verifier-Guided Self-Consistency: Test-Time Reasoning with Imperfect Generators and Verifiers

papers.abstract: Accurate decoder priors are essential for high-performance quantum error correction. Theoretical noise models inevitably omit physically relevant error mechanisms, most notably correlated errors, which appear consistently in experimental error budgets yet are absent from standard models. We introduce a data-driven method for augmenting detector error models (DEMs) by discovering entirely new error mechanisms directly from experimental detector-firing statistics, going beyond most existing approaches that merely refine the probabilities of already-known mechanisms. Our method generates candidates by combining pairs of existing mechanisms as building blocks, then filters and validates them using pairwise and higher-order detector correlations. Crucially, this construction provides each newly discovered mechanism with a well-defined logical effect derived from the constituent error mechanisms, enabling its direct use in decoding. Furthermore, each mechanism is accompanied by a natural decomposition into lower-order components, preserving compatibility with the original decoder. This is particularly valuable in settings that rely on correlated graph-based decoders such as correlated matching. We evaluate the method on surface-code simulations with correlated noise and correlated-matching decoding, demonstrating that, in a realistic near-term noise scenario, DEM augmentation increases the Lambda parameter by 20% across code distances 7-15 and reduces the logical error rate by 75% at code distance 15 relative to the unaugmented DEM. On experimental data from Google's superconducting device, the augmented DEM increases the Lambda parameter by 9% across code distances 5-7 and yields a reduction of 14% in logical error rate over the baseline for distance 7. To our knowledge, this is the first data-driven DEM augmentation method that produces decomposed hyperedges with assigned logical effects.
papers.title: Discovering correlated error mechanisms: data-driven augmentation of detector error models improving decoding

papers.abstract: We study the problem of determining the maximum number of stable matchings. This classical counting problem was posed by Knuth and has been studied for five decades. We obtain a new $2.999^n$ upper bound on the number of stable matchings with $n$ men and $n$ women. This improves the best-known previous result by Palmer and Pálvölgyi. This result gets much closer to the well-known lower bound $\frac{2.28^n}{\text{poly}(n)}$. We refine their entropy-based framework by capturing broader structural relationships among stable matchings. To capture these relationships, we introduce new frameworks, including cones and supports. This establishes the $3.332^n$ bound. We also exploit relationships among local structures and use a charging argument to improve the bound to $2.999^n$.
papers.title: A Sub-$3^n$ Upper Bound on the Number of Stable Matchings

papers.abstract: Continual agents must handle urgent interaction while retaining alternatives, replaying errors, and committing safe long-term changes. A previous digital-life framework distinguishes online (busy) and offline (idle) channels, but leaves open whether these are separate programs or phases of a common process and how their operations should be ordered. Motivated by recent observations of rapidly alternating perceptual representations in primate cortex, we develop a temporal organization layer with phase-tagged micro-epochs, an observable duty cycle, independent content and resource controls, and three nested clocks separating candidate exploration from durable commitment. We give a projected duty-cycle update, state its deterministic descent guarantee and the additional noise term required for a stochastic guarantee, and specify coupled busy/idle execution contracts. Five synthetic experiments (64 seeds each) examine descent and noise, objective misalignment, gain asymmetry, resource coupling, and dropped replay logs. In the gain/noise model the best tested gain ratio is 1.55; decoupled scheduling yields 26.6% versus 11.1% success on a constructed urgent/high-load subset. A frozen-backbone Qwen3-8B prototype further checks orchestration, but its proxy outcomes are not task-benchmark evidence. The results establish a testable scheduling design and identify its conditions of validity, not machine consciousness or general-purpose agent superiority.
papers.title: Time-Division Multiplexing: The Operational Rhythm and Temporal Organization Layer of Digital Life

papers.abstract: Photosynthetic bacteria have evolved specialized light-harvesting structures to efficiently capture sunlight. Here, we investigate the ultrafast dynamics in intact cells of Gemmatimonas groenlandica, featuring unique double-ring LHh-LH1 photosynthetic complexes containing bacteriochlorophyll a. Two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy with lock-in detection allows us to directly observe primary energy-conversion processes, from excitation-energy transfer within the antenna system to the formation of a charge-separated state in the reaction center, taking place on 50 ps time scale. Through comparison with Rhodospirillum rubrum, which lacks the outer antenna ring, we use a combination of global analysis and nodal/center line slope analyses to resolve LHh-LH1 excitation energy transfer which occurs on a ~1-2 ps timescale in Gemmatimonas groenlandica.
papers.title: Unraveling Primary Energy Conversion Dynamics in Intact Cells of Gemmatimonas groenlandica

papers.abstract: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) simplifies distributed application development by offloading operational concerns to the platform, but developers remain responsible for recovering from failures. Retries require idempotent functions, which means that developers have to write complex, error-prone code that undoes or skips the already completed operations of a failed function. To address this, we propose AtomicFaaS, a platform extension that provides semantic atomicity for the external side effects of a function invocation, whether the function fails or its instance crashes, without developer-written compensation code. AtomicFaaS intercepts outbound calls and records their effects in a fault-tolerant log, from which the platform compensates leaked effects outside the failed instance. Compared with a manually implemented saga, AtomicFaaS eliminates compensation code and leaves no compensatable effects after any tested failure, while adding ~1 ms per intercepted call. Under load, it lowers the sustainable throughput of CPU-bound functions, while its latency overhead becomes negligible once calls to external services dominate the invocation time.
papers.title: AtomicFaaS: Offloading Side-Effect Compensation to the Serverless Platform

papers.abstract: In this work, we implement closed-shell Brueckner orbitals for the efficient domain-based local pair natural orbital DLPNO-CCSD(T) and DLPNO-CCSD(T)$_Λ$ methods of the free and open-source \textsc{Psi4} package. We introduce a new algorithm that allows Brueckner orbitals to be computed within the DLPNO framework, resulting in the novel DLPNO-BCCD(T) and DLPNO-BCCD(T)$_{Λ_2}$ methods. We show that DLPNO-BCCD(T) approximates its canonical BCCD(T) counterpart with significantly lower errors relative to the errors incurred by DLPNO-CCSD(T) over CCSD(T). Through a test on the S22 set of noncovalent dimers, the peak error across the set is reduced from 0.36 kcal mol$^{-1}$ to 0.25 kcal mol$^{-1}$ using normal cutoffs, and 0.28 kcal mol$^{-1}$ to 0.13 kcal mol$^{-1}$ at tight cutoffs. In addition, we show that BCCD(T)$_{Λ_2}$, a ${Λ_2}$-only implementation of Brueckner orbitals for the asymmetric triples method, generally produces the best agreement with CCSDT, compared to the (T), (T)$_Λ$, and B(T) perturbative triples corrections. This is established through benchmarks on thermochemistry tests on the barrier heights of semibullvalene and bullvalene Cope rearrangement, while the robustness of DLPNO-BCCD(T)$_{Λ_2}$ is demonstrated along bond-breaking potential energy curves, where it matches the orbital-optimized quasi-variational asymmetric renormalized-triples OQVCCDAR(T) method closely for single-bond breaking, and approximates DLPNO-CCSDT respectably even when triple bonds are stretched, at a fraction of the computational cost.
papers.title: Brueckner Orbitals in Local Pair Natural Orbital Coupled-Cluster Theory: DLPNO-BCCD(T) and DLPNO-BCCD(T)_Lambda2

papers.abstract: We study Motzkin paths satisfying the red-blue rule introduced by Wu, Eu, Ku and Shih. We answer their Question 8.5 and exhibit two new Baxter structures. Let $\mathcal M_m$ denote the set of such paths of length $m$ and $a_m=|\mathcal M_m|$. We give a combinatorial proof of \[ a_{2n-1}=\mathrm{A005802}(n),\qquad a_{2n}=\mathrm{A216947}(n) \qquad (n\geq 1). \] For the odd subsequence, we construct a bijection with $1234$-avoiding permutations which sends the initial up and terminal down runs to the initial decreasing runs of a permutation and its inverse. The boundary correspondence arising from this bijection further identifies red-blue Motzkin paths of length $2n$ with $1234$-avoiding permutations of length $n+1$ in which $1$ occurs to the left of $2$. We establish parallel binomial decompositions of this restricted permutation class and of $2$-colored noncrossing set partitions. The two decompositions have the same binomial coefficients, and their respective cores are explicitly in bijection with non-intersecting triples of lattice paths, a classical Baxter family. This establishes the even identity. Moreover, we construct a second bijection between odd-length red-blue Motzkin paths and $1234$-avoiding permutations. Under this bijection, splitting a path at its ground-level blue horizontal steps corresponds to the skew decomposition of the associated permutation.
papers.title: Baxter Structures and the Odd-Even Enumeration of Red-Blue Motzkin Paths

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate $R^\star$ as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset--receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter's leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter.
papers.title: The Behavioral Rate of Fine-Tuning: Compression as a Measure of Useful Information

papers.abstract: Machine-learning surrogates of linear peeling-ballooning stability now run in milliseconds, but they are mostly deployed as point estimators: they do not say how wrong they may be, or when a query lies outside what they were trained on. For a fusion company designing a new device, every equilibrium of interest is outside the training data of existing surrogates, so this is the case that matters. We describe a model-agnostic trust layer for stability surrogates, made of conformal error bars, out-of-distribution alarms that route doubtful cases to the physics code, and recalibration from a few simulations of a new design, and we test it with pre-registered hypotheses. On a large public dataset of JET-like equilibria with ideal-MHD growth rates, the error bars hold their nominal coverage in distribution and fall short under a shift in plasma shape; a few dozen simulations of the new shape, or routing the cases the alarms flag, restore it. On resistive BOUT++ surrogates, the bars stay calibrated on held-out runs, the alarm flags tokamaks absent from training, and a scenario scan is screened in seconds instead of hours. Across equilibria from the SPARC library and the DIII-D coil set, a surrogate trained on our own graded BOUT++ labels beats the baseline on unseen equilibria, while a surrogate trained elsewhere ranks the same cases backwards and its alarm declines them. Building our own neural-operator surrogate, the harness exposed two input defects whose fix closed its gap to a simple network. For every surrogate tested, the trust layer keeps coverage near target, with a bar width set by that surrogate's own error. Not every pre-registered hypothesis held, and we report those results and the limits of all of them.
papers.title: A trust layer for fast pedestal-stability surrogates: calibrated error bars, out-of-distribution alarms and few-shot recalibration

papers.abstract: Agent-based models (ABMs) are widely used across the biological sciences. While applications differ between biological subfields, the mathematical and statistical methods underlying ABMs largely do not, raising the question of how much knowledge is exchanged between subfields. We address this question by developing a bibliometric pipeline that combines a database keyword search with coarse- and fine-grained classification by a large language model (LLM). We apply the pipeline to the Web of Science Core Collection, classifying 22,936 ABM articles into ecology, epidemiology, oncology, other-biology, or not-biology. Using citation patterns and author overlap as proxies for knowledge exchange, we find that 83%, 81%, and 69% of citations from ecology, epidemiology, and oncology articles, respectively, go to articles in the same subfield. Furthermore, 91% of authors with at least two articles across these subfields publish exclusively within one subfield. Both proportions far exceed those expected under random assignment of subfields (permutation tests, $p \leq 0.001$). Terminology also differs, with "individual-based model" used mainly in ecology and "agent-based model" in epidemiology, oncology, and outside biology. Taken together, our results suggest limited knowledge exchange between biological subfields in ABM research, leading us to discuss opportunities for increased exchange through conferences, journals, and training.
papers.title: Limited knowledge exchange across biological subfields in agent-based modelling: an LLM-assisted bibliometric analysis

papers.abstract: We study mechanism design by an incumbent seller facing competition from an entrant seller of a substitute good. The incumbent commits to a potentially randomized mechanism before her competitor responds. A unit-demand buyer with fixed, publicly known values for the two goods observes both mechanisms and may interact with them in either order. How should a revenue-maximizing incumbent design her mechanism when her product is superior or inferior to her competitor's? We determine the incumbent's exact optimal revenue and characterize all mechanisms that obtain it. Commitment and randomization allow her to earn strictly positive revenue even against an arbitrarily superior product, despite earning nothing under posted-price (i.e., Bertrand) competition. Optimal mechanisms can require a continuum of lottery options, even though the buyer selects only one in equilibrium: unselected options shape the competitor's incentives rather than screen private buyer information. We also show that the buyer's ability to choose the interaction order can be strictly beneficial to the incumbent, even though the incumbent is always visited first at equilibrium. Finally, we show that without commitment, every pure Nash equilibrium yields Bertrand revenues even with randomized mechanisms.
papers.title: On Competing Sellers with Substitutable Goods

papers.abstract: Efficient video human pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy cost. We present SpikePose, a lightweight video pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM). The encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence, while MAM estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions. By confining temporal reasoning to a compact, lightweight module outside the spiking backbone, SpikePose helps bridge the gap between spiking and classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks. We evaluate spatial accuracy, motion errors, and estimated arithmetic energy on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset. Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Within SpikePose, adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, at a cost of only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame. Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.
papers.title: SpikePose: Lightweight Video Human Pose Estimation

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting enables efficient generalizable novel view synthesis, but existing pixel-aligned methods often generate highly redundant Gaussian primitives, causing the final representation size and rendering cost to grow rapidly with image resolution and the number of input views. We propose BudgetSplat, a budget-controllable feed-forward framework that adapts the final Gaussian representation to a user-specified preservation ratio. Rather than treating compaction as simple importance ranking, we formulate it as a joint problem of importance estimation, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy. A single trained model supports varying numbers of context views and multiple test-time budgets without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression. To realize this formulation, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision provides structure-, coverage-, and redundancy-aware guidance for learning Gaussian importance, while budget-conditioned feature modulation adapts Gaussian opacity and attributes to the requested preservation ratio. Coverage-Aware Budget Selection further combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to construct compact yet spatially distributed Gaussian representations. Experiments on indoor reconstruction and cross-dataset generalization demonstrate consistent quality--size trade-offs across different input view counts and preservation ratios, substantially reducing final representation storage and rendering cost while preserving rendering quality.
papers.title: BudgetSplat: Budget-Controllable Generalizable Gaussian Splatting

papers.abstract: Given an arbitrary finite family of Pauli observables, how sharply can they be approximated by a single measurement? We derive an exact state-space correspondence that characterises the resulting sharpness tradeoffs, establishing a link between incompatibility and preparation uncertainty. In particular, suitable ensembles of quantum states determine the full compatibility region and generate explicit parent measurements through Pauli conjugation and classical randomisation. The compatibility region depends only on the anti-commutativity graph and determines all nonuniform tradeoffs under standard noise models, including depolarising, probabilistic and generalised noise. We show that optimal sharpness tradeoffs are determined by spectral problems for signed Pauli Hamiltonians, whose ground states supply the seeds for optimal parent measurements. The correspondence also shows that magic is necessary to attain the full compatibility region of every noncommuting Pauli family. We quantify the resulting sharpness advantage and relate it to the reduced robustness of magic. Finally, we apply the framework to several structured Pauli families, obtaining exact compatibility characterisations and explicit optimal parents.
papers.title: Compatibility of Pauli Observables

papers.abstract: Thermally tuned devices pose a basic control problem. A heater on one edge of a thin plate must hold a small element at an unknown optimal temperature, and the only signal available is the device's own performance. Boundary measurements of {such} an unknown performance objective can be used to tune a diffusion process without reconstructing its spatial state. This paper studies a dual-mode extremum-seeking controller for this setting, modeled as a semilinear diffusion equation on a square with nonuniform boundary actuation. The implementation contains two scalar states and exploits the leading attenuation and \rev{$π/4$} phase \rev{lag} of the diffusion response, a property shared by every periodically heated surface. It requires neither numerical plant coefficients nor the sign of the input gain. An energy estimate first establishes exponential stability of a coupled linear diffusion and controller model. A local bound on the remaining reaction and cost nonlinearities then yields stability and disturbance estimates for the averaged system. Complete kernel and boundary-trace arguments justify a change of coordinates that compares the implemented and averaged trajectories for all time. The resulting practical stability guarantee concerns the field, input bias, and sensitivity estimate, and is unaffected by a constant cost offset under corresponding filter initialization. At fixed dither amplitude, the residual state bound decreases with the inverse square root of frequency, while the ultimate cost bound decreases with its inverse. A thermal optical-filter example illustrates the predicted trends and the conservatism of the sufficient conditions.
papers.title: Dual-Mode Extremum Seeking for Diffusion Systems with Boundary-Cost Feedback

papers.abstract: Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) offer a tunable platform for lignocellulose refining, but their solvation behavior depends on multicomponent hydrogen-bond networks rather than individual constituent properties. We develop TiNN, a thermodynamics-informed neural network that hierarchically represents HBA-HBD association and solute accommodation through a learned free-energy pathway. Trained on 938 records, TiNN achieves a test-set $R^2$ of 0.917 and generalizes to new HBA-HBD combinations and sparse conditions. Ablation identifies solute-specific stabilization as the largest contributor to prediction accuracy, while the importance of hydrogen-bond compatibility depends on the dissolution mechanism. Experimental measurements of glucose, xylan, and Kraft lignin in acidic, basic, and neutral DESs show that TiNN reduces the geometric mean solubility error from more than 23-fold with COSMO-RS to approximately 1.5-fold. Without training on fractionation data, TiNN also distinguishes DES formulations with high and low lignin and hemicellulose removal from corn stover. These results support chemically grounded solvent screening for lignocellulose fractionation.
papers.title: Thermodynamics-Informed Learning Captures Hierarchical Hydrogen-Bond Networks in Deep Eutectic Solvents

papers.abstract: The competitive equilibrium (CE) is a fundamental concept for markets, with applications to efficient and fair allocation of resources. We consider the fundamental question of computing a CE in the most basic Fisher market model where agents have linear preferences. While it is known that we can compute a CE in strongly polynomial time with linear goods, there is no known polynomial-time algorithm for CE with linear chores. Computing a CE for linear chores is known to be in CLS with no hardness results. In this paper, we prove that computing an exact CE in Fisher markets with divisible chores and linear disutilities is CLS-hard and thus CLS-complete. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first CLS-completeness result for a market equilibrium problem. On the technical side, we use the nonconvex dual Eisenberg-Gale (EG) program whose Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) points are CE [Chaudhury, Kroer, Mehta, and Nan, 2024], and the CLS-complete problem of computing a KKT point of a quadratic program [Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender, and Savani, 2024]. We show that from any exact equilibrium of the constructed market, we can recover in polynomial time an $\varepsilon$-KKT point of the input quadratic program over the unit box.
papers.title: Competitive Equilibrium for Linear Chores is CLS-complete

papers.abstract: Ground robots operating in temperate forests suffer from systematic LiDAR occlusions caused by tree trunks, creating persistent blind regions that degrade traversability estimation. In this paper, we propose FOSCo-Net, a self-supervised voxel completion framework that learns to reconstruct occluded geometry from a single scan using temporally accumulated observations as automatic supervision, and we evaluate cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs. FOSCo-Net consistently improves reconstruction quality and traversal safety, with a gated skip decoder achieving the most reliable performance and significantly reducing false obstacle predictions compared to baselines.
papers.title: FOSCo-Net: Ego-centric Voxel Completion for Forest LiDAR Occlusions

papers.abstract: Let $RG$ be the group ring of an arbitrary group $G$ over an associative and commutative ring $R$ with identity. In this paper, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for $RG$ to be Jordan nilpotent of index $n \geq 2$. In particular, we establish a connection between the study of Jordan nilpotency in group rings and the study of Lie nilpotency in these algebras. We also classify the Jordan nilpotency of $RG$, over rings of arbitrary characteristic, up to the index $6$.
papers.title: On Jordan nilpotency of index n in group rings

papers.abstract: ALICE's Event Processing Nodes (EPN) farm is CERN's largest GPU computing facility by capacity, comprising 350 GPU-based nodes and 2800 GPUs delivering approximately a total of 48\,PFLOP/s. It has successfully enabled real-time processing of heavy-ion collisions at 50\,kHz during LHC Run~3. The facility was designed for sustainability, extended hardware lifetime, and reduced operational overhead. High availability is supported by a robust technical architecture and well-defined operational practices, ensuring reliable and continuous operation throughout data taking.
papers.title: Operational Challenges in Efficient and Sustainable Operation of the Event Processing Nodes GPU Farm at the ALICE Experiment

papers.abstract: AI agents rely on third-party tools, such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, whose publishers can be authenticated and whose execution can be restricted by runtime security policies. Yet authenticity does not guarantee benign behaviour: a legitimately signed tool may perform its advertised function while concealing malicious code that leaks confidential information. We demonstrate this trust failure with a signed MCP tool that embeds sensitive data in requests to a policy-allowed destination. Meta's MCPGuard-Dynamic, a state-of-the-art runtime defence, blocks a direct exfiltration attempt in the same run, yet fails to prevent this attack in every trial. We introduce germline execution, which limits information disclosure without inspecting or trusting tool implementations. Each tool invocation runs in ephemeral copies forked from a data-free germline process, each receiving only information authorised for its destination. Even if malicious code executes, what it can disclose is bounded by the data available to its copy. Under explicit assumptions on copy confinement and a data-free germline, we prove sink noninterference for every signed release and, for releases deterministic within our replay model, show that a verified witness establishes a flow violation. Across 153 attack runs, no unauthorised disclosure was detected under germline execution, compared with 5.9-74.5% of runs under baseline defences and an ablation. Invocations served by a single copy completed in 10-49 ms, 2-28x faster than restarting the tool for every invocation, the conventional way to clear state. These results show that data-isolated execution protects agent toolchains against malicious code concealed within authenticated software.
papers.title: Signed, Sealed, Leaked: Trust Beyond Signature for MCP Toolchains

papers.abstract: This report presents findings from a Citizens' Panel convened by the SOUNDSCALE project (www.soundscale.ac.uk) to inform research priorities for distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). Across three online and in-person workshops, 48 residents from Hampshire and London explored the technology's potential uses, risks, governance, and societal implications. The report summarises their deliberations and priorities, and reflects on the challenges of involving citizens in early-stage research on an unfamiliar technology.
papers.title: Informing research priorities for distributed acoustic sensing: insights from a citizens' panel

papers.abstract: Automated vulnerability detection is critical for securing modern software systems, yet existing learning-based approaches often treat functions as independent samples and underuse the supervision provided by vulnerability-fixing patches. In this paper, we propose PatchCon, a CodeBERT-based patch-aware contrastive learning model for function-level vulnerability detection. PatchCon jointly optimizes vulnerability classification and supervised contrastive learning, and treats vulnerable-patched function pairs as hard negatives with larger contrastive weights to capture subtle security-relevant differences introduced by fixes. To evaluate patch-level discrimination, we use two pairwise metrics that measure whether a model can correctly distinguish vulnerable functions from their patched counterparts. We evaluate PatchCon on PairVul-Linux through extensive experiments, including state-of-the-art comparisons, ablation studies, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and statistical significance testing. We also conduct fine-grained analyses by Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) type, function length, and patch size, and further evaluate PatchCon on Linux kernel vulnerabilities disclosed after the training data cutoff. On PairVul-Linux, PatchCon outperforms representative pretrained code models and contrastive learning baselines on both classification and pairwise metrics, improves pairwise accuracy over the strongest reproduced baseline from 0.2060 to 0.3264, and achieves pairwise accuracy comparable to that of a GPT-4o-based large language model (LLM) method at a substantially lower cost. Among the reproduced models, PatchCon also achieves the highest pairwise accuracy on test pairs from Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries unseen during training and on newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
papers.title: PatchCon: Patch-aware Weighted Supervised Contrastive Learning for Vulnerability Detection

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks train best when they are initialised at the edge of chaos, the critical line in the plane of weight and bias variances on which the distance between two inputs neither grows nor shrinks with depth. The line is known for infinitely wide networks; at finite width it moves, and how it moves has been disputed. We treat the logarithm of the distance between two inputs through a network of width $N$ as a random walk and compute its drift and variance to order $1/N$. The edge of chaos moves to a larger weight variance, by $Δσ_w^2=-a_1/(N\,\partial_{σ_w^2}\lnχ_1)$, about $8/N$ for $\tanh$ networks at a bias variance of $0.05$, confirmed by simulations of the exact finite-width recursion. The shift describes a typical network; the average over many networks is dominated by rare networks in which the distance grows, and its critical point moves the other way, which explains why calculations and simulations have disagreed. Backpropagation follows the same random walk, so the shift applies to gradients unchanged. Along the edge of chaos, the information about the similarity of two inputs is constant until the compression over the depth exceeds about one nat, which fixes where to sit on the line. The results give an initialisation rule, Crinit, that places a network on its finite-width edge of chaos without a search. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST at width $64$ it is more accurate than the standard rules at their usual settings, by a small margin in shallow networks and a large one in deep networks, where most standard rules fail; it trains in fewer steps, and it matches or beats the standard rules with a tuned gain.
papers.title: Finite-width shift of the edge of chaos in deep neural networks

papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a finite group and $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. In our earlier work, we proved that the quasi-strongly regular Cayley graph $Γ_H(G)$ is integral whenever $H$ is normal in $G$, and raised the question of whether the converse also holds. In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively. We prove that if $Γ_H(G)$ is integral, then $H$ must be a normal subgroup of $G$. Consequently, $Γ_H(G)$ is integral if and only if $H\lhd G$. Our proof uses the irreducible representations of $G$ and the dimensions of their $H$-fixed subspaces. For a non-normal subgroup $H$, we construct a two-dimensional invariant subspace of a suitable representation operator and show that the corresponding eigenvalues are irrational.
papers.title: A characterization of a family of integral Cayley graphs

papers.abstract: Let $N=pq$ be a semiprime and let $\ell\nmid N$ be an odd prime. For $a\ne0$ modulo $\ell$, put $H_a(N;\ell)=\{ax+Nx^{-1}:x\in\F_\ell^*\}$. For a primitive root $γ$, the size of $H_γ(N;\ell)\cup H_{γ^2}(N;\ell)$ is determined by the Frobenius trace of $Y^2=(X^2-1)(X^2-γ)$. We study the resulting trace-selection problem through finite certificates, a congruence modulo $8$, and a GRH-conditional positive-density family from the CM specialization $γ=2$. Independently of this conditional result, we obtain a deterministic factorization algorithm from the residue-known coefficient lattice of Harvey and Hittmeir (\emph{Math. Comp.}, 2022). The actual babystep index is a nondegenerate quadratic image modulo each selected prime divisor of the auxiliary modulus. After a computable translation, every such image avoids a fixed set of $(\ell-χ(-1))/4$ residues. This forbidden set is optimal among translated sets that must handle both square classes of the leading coefficient. Gauss reduction, a nearby lattice-vector selection, arbitrary-point multipoint evaluation, and the unrestricted large-order algorithm of Harvey and Hittmeir (arXiv, 2026) give the bit-complexity bound $N^{1/5}\exp(-(\log(4/3)/50+o(1))\log N/\log\log N)$. Its secondary factor is asymptotically smaller than every fixed negative power of $\log N$, improving the general bound of Harvey and Hittmeir (\emph{Math. Comp.}, 2022) and the balanced-semiprime bound of Gao et al.\ (arXiv, 2025).
papers.title: Improved deterministic integer factorization by quadratic-image sieving

papers.abstract: We give negative answers to the AP-to-BAP and BAP-to-MAP questions for dual Banach spaces. More precisely, there is a separable Banach space $V$ with the metric approximation property (MAP) such that $V^*$ has the approximation property (AP) but no bounded approximation property (BAP). There is also a separable MAP space $X$, isomorphic to $\ell_1$, whose dual has BAP but no MAP. This resolves a longstanding open question explicitly stated in \cite{Oja2010}. The constructions rely on a finitely generated group without Property A and a quantitative estimate for optimal bounded approximation constants of projective tensor products.
papers.title: Dual Banach spaces with AP but without BAP

papers.abstract: The analysis of cross-diffusion systems with nonsymmetric and indefinite diffusion matrices often relies on the existence of entropies, that is, Lyapunov functionals whose dissipation often yields gradient estimates. We propose a general strategy for constructing entropies for two-species cross-diffusion systems, based on the assumption that the mobility matrix is symmetric, in accordance with Onsager's reciprocal relations. The symmetry condition leads to a linear hyperbolic equation in two variables, which can be reformulated as a linear transport system along the eigendirections of the diffusion matrix, related to the approach of Jenssen and Kogan for hyperbolic conservation laws. Positive solutions to this system yield a family of entropies parametrized by two arbitrary functions of one variable. Sufficient conditions for their existence on (possibly unbounded) characteristic rectangles are given, the mechanisms that may prevent the existence of an entropy are identified, and systems without any entropy structure are presented. The general construction recovers known entropies for models arising in physics and biology and provides new ones. For systems with an arbitrary number of components, we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of separable entropies and give a rank criterion for the uniqueness of entropies (up to affine functions). Cross-diffusion systems without symmetry of the mobility matrix are also discussed.
papers.title: Construction of entropies for cross-diffusion systems

papers.abstract: We analyze a geometric multigrid method on locally refined mesh hierarchies for non-local variational problems, focusing on the integral fractional Laplacian. For newest-vertex-bisection-generated hierarchies, we prove uniform contraction of the multigrid iteration independently of the refinement level, the smallest local mesh size, and the polynomial degree in the finite element discretization. The proof is based on an abstract Hilbert-space framework, a strengthened Cauchy--Schwarz estimate obtained from a near-/far-field decomposition of the non-local bilinear form, and a multilevel stable decomposition independent of the discretization parameters. Numerical experiments underline the theoretical findings.
papers.title: Robust Multigrid on Adaptive Meshes for the Integral Fractional Laplacian

papers.abstract: Wi-Fi~7 and 5G NR use constellations up to $4096$-QAM and $1024$-QAM at multi-gigabit peak rates. The MIMO detector must sustain these rates at a low cost. Linear MMSE detection meets these rates at low cost but loses several dB in SNR. $K$-Best detection recovers this loss, but its per-layer sorting grows with the modulation order and needs large sorting networks or deep pipelines at these rates. Box Decoding is a sort-free tree-search detector whose complexity does not depend on the QAM order, and its deterministic pruning keeps the cost fixed as the MIMO size grows. Single-step candidate pruning (SCP) is fully parallel but less accurate, while iterative candidate pruning (ICP) is more accurate, but its selection loop costs either throughput or area. This paper proposes Max-Min-Exchange Candidate Pruning (MMECP), which replaces the selection loop of ICP with a single max-min exchange without a feedback path and keeps \mbox{near-$K$-Best} performance. The paper also presents a VLSI architecture that represents each candidate by its integer constellation index, so that candidates and their distances are obtained by bit selection instead of operations on symbol values. A $4\times4$ detector synthesized in TSMC $16$\,nm detects one vector per cycle at $1$\,GHz for $64$- to $1024$-QAM and produces up to $40$\,Gb/s, while its gate count grows by $63\%$ over this range. Its normalized hardware efficiency is $2.3\times$, $12\times$ and $14\times$ that of the best compared hard-output detector at $64$-, $256$- and $1024$-QAM.
papers.title: Iteration-Free Candidate Pruning and an Index-Domain VLSI Architecture for Sort-Free MIMO Box Decoding up to 1024-QAM

papers.abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials of the latent Ewald summation (LES) type learn atomic charges from energies and forces and evaluate their electrostatic energy in reciprocal space. I formulate this long-range term as a smeared Epstein-Hurwitz lattice sum and derive its exact periodic structure: a decomposition isolating a net-charge artefact and a local self-energy, an image theorem for cells of any shape, and the forces and virial. Full charge equilibration, LES with induced charges, constrained and unconstrained LES models and fixed-charge force fields follow as successive approximations of one variational problem, whose diagonal-hardness limit is a projection of the latent charges onto fixed total charge, which I call projected latent Ewald summation (pLES). Energies and forces determine the latent charges only up to a gauge, so fragment-level rather than atom-level charge quantization is the consistent target. The latent channel is guaranteed to be a dielectric only if charge is conserved locally; charges that are local functions of the environment and conserved only globally can screen like a conductor. pLES is implemented in the atomic cluster expansion and in LAMMPS, and the exact identities hold to machine precision, also for trained models. For charged NaCl clusters, pLES recovers the total charge that an unconstrained model misses by up to 1.8 e and reduces the test errors of a short-range model from 1.44 to 0.42 meV/atom and from 37 to 13 meV/Å. In two water datasets, constrained and unconstrained models learn the same latent charges up to sign and scale.
